paragraphs: Back-propagation is often used to reduce a least-squares difference between a network’s output and a teacher signal. This paper generalizes that choice of error measure using Minkowski-r power metrics. The parameter r changes how discrepancies are combined, allowing the learning objective to express different notions of a good match.

At r equal to two, the procedure recovers standard back-propagation. Smaller values approximate a city-block measure, while large values approach a measure governed by the largest discrepancy. Changing r therefore changes which patterns of error receive emphasis during learning, even though the overall approach remains based on gradient descent.

The authors describe an implementation and report experiments indicating that different values of r suit different purposes. Potential uses include reducing the influence of noisy outliers, forming more compact clusters, and matching the statistics of a domain. They also discuss error measures that may better reflect perception in speech or vision. The finding supports treating the error metric as a meaningful modeling choice rather than assuming that squared error fits every task.
summary.tldr: Minkowski-r back-propagation varies the error metric to adapt learning to noise, clustering goals, and domain characteristics.

title: Minkowski-r Back-Propagation: Learning in Connectionist Models with Non-Euclidian Error Signals

abstract: This research investigates a new technique for unsupervised learning of nonlinear control problems. The approach is applied both to Michie and Chambers BOXES algorithm and to Barto, Sutton and Anderson's extension, the ASE/ACE system, and has significantly improved the convergence rate of stochastically based learning automata. Recurrence learning is a new nonlinear reward-penalty algorithm. It exploits information found during learning trials to reinforce decisions resulting in the recurrence of nonfailing states. Recurrence learning applies positive reinforcement during the exploration of the search space, whereas in the BOXES or ASE algorithms, only negative weight reinforcement is applied, and then only on failure. Simulation results show that the added information from recurrence learning increases the learning rate. Our empirical results show that recurrence learning is faster than both basic failure driven learning and failure prediction methods. Although recurrence learning has only been tested in failure driven experiments, there are goal directed learning applications where detection of recurring oscillations may provide useful information that reduces the learning time by applying negative, instead of positive reinforcement. Detection of cycles provides a heuristic to improve the balance between evidence gathering and goal directed search.

paragraphs: This paper introduces a learning rule for nonlinear control that uses repeated visits to nonfailing states as useful feedback. A controller can learn from what happens during an ongoing trial, rather than waiting until a failure reveals that some earlier decisions were unsuccessful.

The method, called recurrence learning, positively reinforces decisions that bring the system back to states where it has avoided failure. The researchers apply it to the BOXES algorithm and the ASE/ACE system. This adds information during exploration to methods whose basic failure-driven updates penalize decisions when a trial ends unsuccessfully.

Simulations show faster learning than both basic failure-driven learning and methods that predict failure. The tested setting is specifically failure-driven control. For tasks with an explicit destination, the authors suggest that recurring cycles could instead deserve negative reinforcement because they may signal unproductive repetition. The broader idea is to interpret recurrence according to the task: returning to a state can provide evidence of safety or evidence that progress has stalled.
summary.tldr: Rewarding returns to nonfailing states accelerates learning in the tested control systems by providing feedback before failure occurs.

title: LEARNING BY STATE RECURRENCE DETECTION

abstract: The phonological structure of human languages is intricate, yet highly constrained. Through a combination of connectionist modeling and linguistic analysis, we are attempting to develop a computational basis for the nature of phonology. We present a connectionist architecture that performs multiple simultaneous insertion, deletion, and mutation operations on sequences of phonemes, and introduce a novel additional primitive, clustering. Clustering provides an interesting alternative to both iterative and relaxation accounts of assimilation processes such as vowel harmony. Our resulting model is efficient because it processes utterances entirely in parallel using only feed-forward circuitry.

paragraphs: The paper asks how the intricate but constrained sound patterns of human languages can be explained computationally. Its approach combines linguistic analysis with connectionist modeling, using a neural architecture to represent operations on sequences of phonemes. The aim is to connect the structure of phonological processes with a concrete way of computing them.

The architecture can perform several insertions, deletions, and changes to phonemes simultaneously. It also introduces clustering as an additional primitive operation. Clustering provides a way to account for assimilation, where sounds become more alike, including vowel harmony. This gives the model another mechanism for coordinating changes across an utterance.

The central architectural claim is that these operations can be carried out entirely in parallel with feed-forward circuitry. For the assimilation processes discussed, clustering offers an alternative to repeated application of rules or relaxation toward a settled state. The contribution is therefore both a proposed explanation of phonological structure and a computational organization that makes the resulting processing efficient.
summary.tldr: A parallel feed-forward architecture models phonological changes and introduces clustering as a mechanism for assimilation.

title: A Computational Basis for Phonology

paragraphs: This paper combines neural classifiers with carefully selected speech features to recognize spoken letters independently of the speaker. For isolated letters, the system first divides the signal into broad categories. The resulting boundaries identify useful measurement locations, including vowel onset, where information important for distinguishing letters is found.

A feedforward neural network classifies letters using those features. The system achieves 96% recognition accuracy on a test set of 30 speakers. Neural classifiers also contribute to pitch tracking and to broad-category segmentation of letter sequences, giving them roles in preparing the signal as well as making the final letter decision.

The work extends to retrieving names spoken as letter sequences with pauses between letters. Searching a database of 50,000 names yields 95% first-choice retrieval. That result concerns the complete name-retrieval task, while the 96% figure concerns isolated letters. The abstract also reports the beginning of work on continuous letter classification using frame-by-frame phonetic decisions, distinguishing that ongoing direction from the completed recognition results.
summary.tldr: Feature-guided neural classifiers achieve 96% isolated-letter accuracy and 95% first-choice retrieval of names spelled with pauses.

title: Spoken Letter Recognition

abstract: This work presents an Attractor Neural Network (ANN) model of Re(cid:173) call and Recognition. It is shown that an ANN model can qualitatively account for a wide range of experimental psychological data pertaining to the these two main aspects of memory access. Certain psychological phenomena are accounted for, including the effects of list-length, word(cid:173) frequency, presentation time, context shift, and aging. Thereafter, the probabilities of successful Recall and Recognition are estimated, in order to possibly enable further quantitative examination of the model.

paragraphs: This paper proposes an attractor neural network as a common model of recall and recognition. Recall involves retrieving remembered material, while recognition involves identifying material as previously encountered. Modeling both within one architecture asks whether a shared memory mechanism can account for these different forms of access.

The authors report that the model qualitatively explains a wide range of psychological observations. These include effects associated with list length, word frequency, presentation time, changes in context, and aging. The breadth of these phenomena matters because the model is being assessed against several influences on memory rather than a single isolated effect.

The paper then estimates the probabilities of successful recall and recognition. This extends the account from reproducing qualitative patterns toward quantities that could support further numerical evaluation. The abstract presents those estimates as a basis for possible quantitative examination. Its stated result is therefore a broad qualitative account of memory access, accompanied by a step toward testing how closely the model's success rates match observed behavior.
summary.tldr: An attractor network qualitatively explains several recall and recognition phenomena and estimates their probabilities of success.

title: An Attractor Neural Network Model of Recall and Recognition

abstract: We describe a system that can track a hand in a sequence of video frames and recognize hand gestures in a user-independent manner. The system locates the hand in each video frame and determines if the hand is open or closed. The tracking system is able to track the hand to within ±10 pixels of its correct location in 99.7% of the frames from a test set containing video sequences from 18 dif(cid:173) ferent individuals captured in 18 different room environments. The gesture recognition network correctly determines if the hand being tracked is open or closed in 99.1 % of the frames in this test set . The system has been designed to operate in real time with existing hardware.

paragraphs: This paper describes a convolutional neural network system that follows a hand through video and recognizes whether it is open or closed. These are two related tasks: locating the hand establishes where to look, while gesture recognition determines its state. The system is intended to work across users, making variation between people part of the recognition problem.

The reported test set contains video sequences from 18 individuals recorded in 18 room environments. In 99.7% of test frames, the tracked position falls within 10 pixels of the correct location. The gesture network identifies the open or closed state correctly in 99.1% of frames. These figures measure different aspects of performance and should be interpreted separately.

The contribution is a combined tracking and gesture recognition system designed for real-time operation on existing hardware. Its results support reliable performance across the people and rooms represented in the test set. The demonstrated gesture vocabulary is specifically the distinction between an open hand and a closed hand.
summary.tldr: A convolutional neural network system tracks hands and recognizes open or closed gestures with high reported accuracy across multiple users and rooms.

title: A Convolutional Neural Network Hand Tracker

abstract: We examine the issue of evaluation of model specific parameters in a modified VC-formalism. Two examples are analyzed: the 2-dimensional homogeneous perceptron and the I-dimensional higher order neuron. Both models are solved theoretically, and their learning curves are com(cid:173) pared against true learning curves. It is shown that the formalism has the potential to generate a variety of learning curves, including ones displaying ''phase transitions."
originalAbstract: We examine the issue of evaluation of model specific parameters in a modified VC-formalism. Two examples are analyzed: the 2-dimensional homogeneous perceptron and the I-dimensional higher order neuron. Both models are solved theoretically, and their learning curves are com(cid:173) pared against true learning curves. It is shown that the formalism has the potential to generate a variety of learning curves, including ones displaying ''phase transitions."

paragraphs: A learning curve describes how learning performance changes as more examples become available. This paper investigates a modified VC formalism for producing such curves, focusing on how to evaluate the parameters that depend on the particular model. That focus matters because a general theoretical framework must connect to individual learning systems before it can describe their behavior.

The authors work through two examples: a two-dimensional homogeneous perceptron and a one-dimensional higher-order neuron. Both receive theoretical solutions, and the resulting learning curves are compared with their true learning curves. These examples provide concrete cases in which to examine the framework's model-specific calculations.

The stated finding is that the formalism can potentially represent several kinds of learning behavior, including curves with phase transitions. Here, the important distinction is between gradual change and a more abrupt shift in learning behavior. The examples show the framework's expressive potential, rather than restricting its predictions to one uniform shape of improvement.
summary.tldr: Two theoretically solved neuron models illustrate how a modified VC framework can generate varied learning curves, including phase transitions.

title: Examples of learning curves from a modified VC-formalism

Under the "signal estimation" paradigm, we assume the signal to be encoded in the mean firing rate of a Poisson neuron. The perfonnance of an optimal linear estimator of the signal then provides a lower bound on the capacity for signal estimation. Under the "signal detection" paradigm, the presence or absence of the signal has to be de(cid:173) tected. Perfonnance of the optimal spike detector allows us to compute a lower bound on the capacity for signal detection. We find that single synapses (for empirically measured parameter values) transmit infonna(cid:173) tion poorly but significant improvement can be achieved with a small amount of redundancy.

paragraphs: The paper analyzes a simple cortical-synapse model as an information channel. Rather than assigning it one undifferentiated performance measure, the authors consider two coding tasks: estimating a signal's value and detecting whether a signal is present. They derive closed-form lower bounds on capacity under each of these explicitly defined interpretations.

For estimation, the signal is assumed to be encoded in the mean firing rate of a Poisson neuron. The performance of an optimal linear estimator supplies the capacity lower bound. For detection, the question is whether the signal is present or absent, and the performance of an optimal spike detector supplies the corresponding bound.

With empirically measured parameter values, the analysis finds that individual synapses transmit information poorly, while a small amount of redundancy produces substantial improvement. The findings are tied to the simple synapse model and the two coding paradigms. Their significance is that transmission quality depends on both the task assigned to the signal and whether information is carried redundantly.
summary.tldr: Information-theoretic analysis finds weak transmission by individual model synapses but substantial gains from modest redundancy.

title: Synaptic Transmission: An Information-Theoretic Perspective

abstract: Long-term potentiation (LTP) has long been held as a biological substrate for associative learning. Recently, evidence has emerged that long-term depression (LTD) results when the presynaptic cell fires after the postsynaptic cell. The computational utility of LTD is explored here. Synaptic modification kernels for both LTP and LTD have been proposed by other laboratories based studies of one postsynaptic unit. Here, the interaction between time-dependent LTP and LTD is studied in small networks.
originalAbstract: Long-term potentiation (LTP) has long been held as a biological substrate for associative learning. Recently, evidence has emerged that long-term depression (LTD) results when the presynaptic cell fires after the postsynaptic cell. The computational utility of LTD is explored here. Synaptic modification kernels for both LTP and LTD have been proposed by other laboratories based studies of one postsynaptic unit. Here, the interaction between time-dependent LTP and LTD is studied in small networks.

paragraphs: This paper explores the computational role of long-term depression, or LTD, in learning. Long-term potentiation, or LTP, strengthens synaptic connections and has long been associated with associative learning. LTD concerns weakening those connections. The study asks how time-dependent strengthening and weakening interact when considered together in small networks.

The motivation includes evidence that LTD occurs when a presynaptic cell fires after the postsynaptic cell. This makes the relative timing of neural activity important to the direction of synaptic change. Earlier laboratories had proposed modification kernels for LTP and LTD based on studies involving one postsynaptic unit. Such kernels describe how timing relates to the modification of a connection.

The paper moves the investigation to interactions within small networks, where both forms of plasticity operate together. Its title frames LTD as facilitating learning in a noisy environment, while the abstract specifies the computational question and network setting. The substantive focus is how weakening participates alongside strengthening in learning, with temporal order organizing the interaction between the two.
summary.tldr: The paper studies how timing-dependent synaptic strengthening and weakening interact in small networks, exploring LTD's role in learning.

title: LTD Facilitates Learning in a Noisy Environment

abstract: Preliminary work by the authors made use of the so-called "Man(cid:173) hattan world" assumption about the scene statistics of city and indoor scenes. This assumption stated that such scenes were built on a cartesian grid which led to regularities in the image edge gra(cid:173) dient statistics. In this paper we explore the general applicability of this assumption and show that, surprisingly, it holds in a large variety of less structured environments including rural scenes. This enables us, from a single image, to determine the orientation of the viewer relative to the scene structure and also to detect target ob(cid:173) jects which are not aligned with the grid. These inferences are performed using a Bayesian model with probability distributions (e.g. on the image gradient statistics) learnt from real data.

paragraphs: The Manhattan-world assumption describes scenes as organized around a Cartesian grid. This structure produces regularities in the directions of image-edge gradients. Originally used for city and indoor scenes, the assumption offers a way to connect patterns in a two-dimensional image with the underlying orientation of the scene.

This paper investigates how broadly that assumption applies. The authors find that it holds across a large variety of less structured environments, including rural scenes. That broadens the range of images in which the statistical regularity can be useful, without making a claim that every environment has the same grid organization.

Using a Bayesian model with probability distributions learned from real data, the method draws two kinds of inference from a single image. It estimates the viewer's orientation relative to scene structure and detects target objects that are not aligned with the grid. The contribution shows how a recurring scene regularity can supply both an orientation reference and a basis for identifying objects that depart from it.
summary.tldr: Grid-related image statistics extend to varied environments and support Bayesian inference of viewer orientation and misaligned objects from one image.

title: The Manhattan World Assumption: Regularities in Scene Statistics which Enable Bayesian Inference

paragraphs: The paper introduces the import vector machine, a classifier built on kernel logistic regression. It aims to combine strong classification performance with probability estimates and a natural extension to multiple classes. The authors report that its binary classification performance matches that of support vector machines.

The model uses only a subset of training examples to index its kernel basis functions. This parallels the role of support points in an SVM, but the selected subset is typically much smaller. Fewer indexed examples make the resulting representation more compact, which the authors identify as a source of computational advantage, especially with large training datasets.

The contribution therefore combines several properties in one approach: competitive binary classification, multiclass applicability, estimated underlying probabilities, and a sparse kernel representation. The probability output provides information beyond a class label, while the subset representation addresses computation. The reported size advantage is qualified as typical; the abstract does not assert that every dataset produces fewer import vectors than support vectors.
summary.tldr: The import vector machine combines kernel logistic regression, probability estimates, multiclass classification, and a typically smaller kernel representation than an SVM.

title: Kernel Logistic Regression and the Import Vector Machine

abstract: Recent multi-agent extensions of Q-Learning require knowledge of other agents’ payoffs and Q-functions, and assume game-theoretic play at all times by all other agents. This paper proposes a fundamentally different approach, dubbed “Hyper-Q” Learning, in which values of mixed strategies rather than base actions are learned, and in which other agents’ strategies are estimated from observed actions via Bayesian in- ference. Hyper-Q may be effective against many different types of adap- tive agents, even if they are persistently dynamic. Against certain broad categories of adaptation, it is argued that Hyper-Q may converge to ex- act optimal time-varying policies. In tests using Rock-Paper-Scissors, Hyper-Q learns to significantly exploit an Infinitesimal Gradient Ascent (IGA) player, as well as a Policy Hill Climber (PHC) player. Preliminary analysis of Hyper-Q against itself is also presented.

This paper proposes a fundamentally different approach, dubbed “Hyper-Q” Learning, in which values of mixed strategies rather than base actions are learned, and in which other agents’ strategies are estimated from observed actions via Bayesian in- ference. Hyper-Q may be effective against many different types of adap- tive agents, even if they are persistently dynamic. Against certain broad categories of adaptation, it is argued that Hyper-Q may converge to ex- act optimal time-varying policies. Preliminary analysis of Hyper-Q against itself is also presented.

paragraphs: Hyper-Q addresses learning when other agents also adapt their behavior. The paper contrasts its approach with Q-learning extensions that require access to other agents’ payoffs and Q-functions and assume game-theoretic play throughout. Those requirements make the other agents’ behavior and internal information central to the learning setup.

Hyper-Q instead learns the values of mixed strategies, meaning probability distributions over actions. It estimates other agents’ strategies from their observed actions using Bayesian inference. This changes both what the learner values and how it obtains information about its opponents, creating an approach intended to handle agents whose behavior continues changing.

The authors argue that Hyper-Q may be effective against many kinds of adaptive agents and may converge to exact optimal time-varying policies against certain broad categories of adaptation. In Rock-Paper-Scissors tests, it significantly exploits both an Infinitesimal Gradient Ascent player and a Policy Hill Climber. The paper also offers preliminary self-play analysis, while keeping the broader convergence claims qualified.
summary.tldr: Hyper-Q learns mixed-strategy values and infers opponents’ strategies, showing exploitation of two adaptive Rock-Paper-Scissors players.

title: Extending Q-Learning to General Adaptive Multi-Agent Systems

abstract: We present an inﬁnite mixture model in which each component com- prises a multivariate Gaussian distribution over an input space, and a Gaussian Process model over an output space. Our model is neatly able to deal with non-stationary covariance functions, discontinuities, multi- modality and overlapping output signals. The work is similar to that by Rasmussen and Ghahramani [1]; however, we use a full generative model over input and output space rather than just a conditional model. This al- lows us to deal with incomplete data, to perform inference over inverse functional mappings as well as for regression, and also leads to a more powerful and consistent Bayesian speciﬁcation of the effective ‘gating network’ for the different experts.
originalAbstract: We present an inﬁnite mixture model in which each component com- prises a multivariate Gaussian distribution over an input space, and a Gaussian Process model over an output space. Our model is neatly able to deal with non-stationary covariance functions, discontinuities, multi- modality and overlapping output signals. The work is similar to that by Rasmussen and Ghahramani [1]; however, we use a full generative model over input and output space rather than just a conditional model. This al- lows us to deal with incomplete data, to perform inference over inverse functional mappings as well as for regression, and also leads to a more powerful and consistent Bayesian speciﬁcation of the effective ‘gating network’ for the different experts.

paragraphs: The paper presents an infinite mixture of Gaussian process experts for relationships that are difficult to describe with one uniform model. Each mixture component combines a multivariate Gaussian distribution over inputs with a Gaussian process model over outputs. This gives each expert both an input-space description and a model of the associated output behavior.

The central design choice is to model inputs and outputs jointly, rather than specifying only outputs conditional on inputs. The authors state that this construction handles changing covariance structure, discontinuities, multiple modes, and overlapping output signals. These capabilities allow the mixture to represent different kinds of behavior within the same overall modeling framework.

Joint modeling also broadens the questions the model can answer. It supports incomplete observations and inference about inputs associated with outputs, alongside ordinary regression. The authors further argue that it gives a stronger and more consistent Bayesian specification of the gating mechanism that assigns responsibility among experts. The contribution is thus a generative formulation that expands both representation and inference.
summary.tldr: An infinite mixture of Gaussian process experts jointly models inputs and outputs to support flexible regression, missing data, and inverse inference.

title: An Alternative Infinite Mixture Of Gaussian Process Experts

abstract: We present a Bayesian framework for explaining how people reason about and predict the actions of an intentional agent, based on observ- ing its behavior. Action-understanding is cast as a problem of inverting a probabilistic generative model, which assumes that agents tend to act rationally in order to achieve their goals given the constraints of their en- vironment. Working in a simple sprite-world domain, we show how this model can be used to infer the goal of an agent and predict how the agent will act in novel situations or when environmental constraints change. The model provides a qualitative account of several kinds of inferences that preverbal infants have been shown to perform, and also ﬁts quantita- tive predictions that adult observers make in a new experiment.

paragraphs: The paper models action understanding as reasoning backward from observed behavior to the goals that could explain it. Its Bayesian framework starts with a probabilistic model of how an intentional agent acts. The key assumption is that agents tend to choose rational actions for achieving their goals within the constraints of their environment.

Inverting that model lets an observer infer a goal and use it to predict future behavior. The authors demonstrate this process in a simple sprite-world setting, including predictions for unfamiliar situations and changed environmental constraints. Because the model connects goals, surroundings, and actions, it can explain behavior in terms of what the agent is trying to accomplish.

The model qualitatively accounts for several kinds of inference previously observed in preverbal infants. It also fits quantitative predictions made by adults in a new experiment. These findings support the framework as an account of aspects of human action understanding, with the rational-action assumption providing the link between visible behavior and inferred intentions.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian model infers goals and predicts actions by assuming agents tend to act rationally under environmental constraints.

title: Bayesian models of human action understanding

abstract: In supervised learning there is a typical presumption that the training and test points are taken from the same distribution. In practice this assumption is commonly violated. The situations where the training and test data are from different distributions is called covariate shift. Recent work has examined techniques for dealing with covariate shift in terms of minimisation of generalisation error. As yet the literature lacks a Bayesian generative perspective on this problem. This paper tackles this issue for regression models. Recent work on covariate shift can be understood in terms of mixture regression. Using this view, we obtain a general approach to regression under covariate shift, which reproduces previous work as a special case. The main advantages of this new formulation over previous models for covariate shift are that we no longer need to presume the test and training densities are known, the regression and density estimation are combined into a single procedure, and previous methods are reproduced as special cases of this procedure, shedding light on the implicit assumptions the methods are making.

paragraphs: This paper examines regression when training inputs and test inputs follow different distributions, a situation described as covariate shift. It develops a Bayesian generative perspective on the problem. The aim is to account for the distribution mismatch within the regression model rather than treating the mismatch as separate from prediction.

The authors show that earlier approaches to covariate shift can be understood through mixture regression. That view leads to a general procedure combining regression and density estimation. Training and test densities therefore do not have to be supplied as known quantities; estimating them is incorporated into the same procedure that learns the regression relationship.

Previous methods emerge as special cases of the formulation. This unification matters because it makes their implicit assumptions easier to understand and places them within a broader modeling framework. The paper's stated contribution is a general way to organize regression under distribution shift, with joint estimation replacing the need to begin from already-known input densities.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian mixture-regression framework jointly estimates densities and regression under covariate shift, recovering earlier methods as special cases.

title: Mixture Regression for Covariate Shift

abstract: In this paper we investigate multi-task learning in the context of Gaussian Pro- cesses (GP). We propose a model that learns a shared covariance function on input-dependent features and a “free-form” covariance matrix over tasks. This al- lows for good ﬂexibility when modelling inter-task dependencies while avoiding the need for large amounts of data for training. We show that under the assump- tion of noise-free observations and a block design, predictions for a given task only depend on its target values and therefore a cancellation of inter-task trans- fer occurs. We evaluate the beneﬁts of our model on two practical applications: a compiler performance prediction problem and an exam score prediction task. Additionally, we make use of GP approximations and properties of our model in order to provide scalability to large data sets.
originalAbstract: In this paper we investigate multi-task learning in the context of Gaussian Pro- cesses (GP). We propose a model that learns a shared covariance function on input-dependent features and a “free-form” covariance matrix over tasks. We show that under the assump- tion of noise-free observations and a block design, predictions for a given task only depend on its target values and therefore a cancellation of inter-task trans- fer occurs. We evaluate the beneﬁts of our model on two practical applications: a compiler performance prediction problem and an exam score prediction task. Additionally, we make use of GP approximations and properties of our model in order to provide scalability to large data sets.

paragraphs: This paper develops a Gaussian process model for learning several tasks together. It learns both a shared covariance function over input-dependent features and a free-form covariance matrix describing relationships among tasks. This separates similarity between inputs from dependence between tasks, providing flexibility in how tasks share information without requiring large amounts of training data.

The analysis also identifies a setting where cross-task transfer cancels. Under noise-free observations and a block design, predictions for a given task depend only on that task's target values. This is a conditional result: including a covariance structure across tasks does not by itself ensure that other tasks' observed targets influence a prediction under those conditions.

The authors evaluate the model on compiler-performance prediction and exam-score prediction. They also use Gaussian process approximations and properties of the model to support larger datasets. The contribution combines a flexible way to model task dependence, practical applications, and a precise explanation of circumstances in which the anticipated transfer between tasks disappears.
summary.tldr: A multi-task Gaussian process learns task relationships while identifying conditions under which transfer between tasks cancels.

title: Multi-task Gaussian Process Prediction

abstract: Probabilistic topic models (and their extensions) have become popular as models of latent structures in collections of text documents or images. These models are usually treated as generative models and trained using maximum likelihood estimation, an approach which may be suboptimal in the context of an overall classification problem. In this paper, we describe DiscLDA, a discriminative learning framework for such models as Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) in the setting of dimensionality reduction with supervised side information. In DiscLDA, a class-dependent linear transformation is introduced on the topic mixture proportions. This parameter is estimated by maximizing the conditional likelihood using Monte Carlo EM. By using the transformed topic mixture proportions as a new representation of documents, we obtain a supervised dimensionality reduction algorithm that uncovers the latent structure in a document collection while preserving predictive power for the task of classification. We compare the predictive power of the latent structure of DiscLDA with unsupervised LDA on the 20 Newsgroup ocument classification task.

paragraphs: Topic models describe documents through hidden topic mixtures, providing a compact representation of a collection. Their usual maximum-likelihood training aims to explain the observed data, which may be suboptimal when the final task is classification. DiscLDA brings supervised information into the learning of that reduced representation.

The method introduces a class-dependent linear transformation of the topic mixture proportions. It learns this transformation by maximizing conditional likelihood with Monte Carlo EM. The transformed mixtures then become the document representation, connecting the latent topic structure to the supervised prediction task.

This approach matters because dimensionality reduction must preserve distinctions that help predict classes, as well as uncover patterns shared across documents. DiscLDA is presented as doing both within a topic-model framework. The authors compare the predictive usefulness of its latent structure with that of unsupervised LDA on the 20 Newsgroup classification task. The abstract identifies that comparison without stating its direction or a numerical improvement, so the central stated contribution is the supervised learning framework.
summary.tldr: DiscLDA learns class-dependent transformations of topic mixtures to make low-dimensional document representations useful for classification.

title: DiscLDA: Discriminative Learning for Dimensionality Reduction and Classification

abstract: For undiscounted reinforcement learning in Markov decision processes (MDPs) we consider the total regret of a learning algorithm with respect to an optimal policy. In order to describe the transition structure of an MDP we propose a new parameter: An MDP has diameter D if for any pair of states s1,s2 there is a policy which moves from s1 to s2 in at most D steps (on average). We present a reinforcement learning algorithm with total regret O(DSAT) after T steps for any unknown MDP with S states, A actions per state, and diameter D. This bound holds with high probability. We also present a corresponding lower bound of Omega(DSAT) on the total regret of any learning algorithm. Both bounds demonstrate the utility of the diameter as structural parameter of the MDP.
originalAbstract: For undiscounted reinforcement learning in Markov decision processes (MDPs) we consider the total regret of a learning algorithm with respect to an optimal policy. In order to describe the transition structure of an MDP we propose a new parameter: An MDP has diameter D if for any pair of states s1,s2 there is a policy which moves from s1 to s2 in at most D steps (on average). We present a reinforcement learning algorithm with total regret O(DSAT) after T steps for any unknown MDP with S states, A actions per state, and diameter D. This bound holds with high probability. We also present a corresponding lower bound of Omega(DSAT) on the total regret of any learning algorithm. Both bounds demonstrate the utility of the diameter as structural parameter of the MDP.

paragraphs: This paper analyzes the accumulated cost of learning in an unknown, undiscounted Markov decision process. It measures that cost through total regret relative to an optimal policy. The question is how the learner's performance gap depends on the environment's size, the number of available actions, the time spent learning, and the structure of transitions.

To express that structure, the authors introduce the MDP diameter. A diameter of D means that, for any ordered pair of states, some policy can reach the second from the first in at most D steps on average. The definition concerns achievable expected travel times; it does not require every policy to move between states that quickly.

The paper supplies an algorithm with a high-probability regret upper bound involving diameter, states, actions, and elapsed steps. It also establishes a corresponding lower bound on the regret of any learning algorithm. Together, these results show that transition structure belongs in the analysis of learning difficulty. Diameter provides a common parameter for describing both what the proposed learner can achieve and the difficulty reflected in the lower bound.
summary.tldr: Regret upper and lower bounds identify MDP diameter as a useful structural measure of reinforcement-learning difficulty.

title: Near-optimal Regret Bounds for Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Latent tree graphical models are natural tools for expressing long range and hierarchical dependencies among many variables which are common in computer vision, bioinformatics and natural language processing problems. However, existing models are largely restricted to discrete and Gaussian variables due to computational constraints; furthermore, algorithms for estimating the latent tree structure and learning the model parameters are largely restricted to heuristic local search. We present a method based on kernel embeddings of distributions for latent tree graphical models with continuous and non-Gaussian variables. Our method can recover the latent tree structures with provable guarantees and perform local-minimum free parameter learning and efficient inference. Experiments on simulated and real data show the advantage of our proposed approach.

However, existing models are largely restricted to discrete and Gaussian variables due to computational constraints; furthermore, algorithms for estimating the latent tree structure and learning the model parameters are largely restricted to heuristic local search. We present a method based on kernel embeddings of distributions for latent tree graphical models with continuous and non-Gaussian variables. Our method can recover the latent tree structures with provable guarantees and perform local-minimum free parameter learning and efficient inference. Experiments on simulated and real data show the advantage of our proposed approach.

paragraphs: Latent tree models represent hierarchical and long-range relationships through a tree containing hidden variables. Such relationships arise in vision, bioinformatics, and language problems. The paper addresses two restrictions of existing approaches: computational pressure toward discrete or Gaussian variables, and reliance on heuristic local search when estimating tree structure and model parameters.

The authors propose representing distributions through kernel embeddings. This allows their latent tree method to handle continuous variables whose distributions need not be Gaussian. The approach covers several parts of the modeling process, including recovering the hidden tree structure, learning parameters, and carrying out inference once the model has been learned.

The paper provides provable guarantees for structure recovery and describes parameter learning that avoids local minima, together with efficient inference. Experiments on simulated and real data show advantages for the proposed approach. The contribution therefore combines broader distributional modeling with a different learning strategy, addressing both what latent trees can represent and how their structure and parameters can be estimated.
summary.tldr: Kernel embeddings enable latent tree models with continuous, non-Gaussian variables, guaranteed structure recovery, and parameter learning free of local minima.

title: Kernel Embeddings of Latent Tree Graphical Models

abstract: User preferences for items can be inferred from either explicit feedback, such as item ratings, or implicit feedback, such as rental histories. Research in collaborative filtering has concentrated on explicit feedback, resulting in the development of accurate and scalable models. However, since explicit feedback is often difficult to collect it is important to develop effective models that take advantage of the more widely available implicit feedback. We introduce a probabilistic approach to collaborative filtering with implicit feedback based on modelling the user's item selection process. In the interests of scalability, we restrict our attention to tree-structured distributions over items and develop a principled and efficient algorithm for learning item trees from data. We also identify a problem with a widely used protocol for evaluating implicit feedback models and propose a way of addressing it using a small quantity of explicit feedback data.

In the interests of scalability, we restrict our attention to tree-structured distributions over items and develop a principled and efficient algorithm for learning item trees from data. We also identify a problem with a widely used protocol for evaluating implicit feedback models and propose a way of addressing it using a small quantity of explicit feedback data.

paragraphs: Recommendation systems can learn from explicit ratings or from implicit behavior such as rental histories. This paper focuses on implicit feedback because it is more widely available, while explicit preferences can be difficult to collect. It introduces a probabilistic collaborative-filtering approach that models the process by which a user selects an item.

To make the approach scalable, the authors restrict the distribution over items to a tree structure. They develop a principled, efficient algorithm for learning the item tree from data. The tree is therefore part of the learned model, and its structure organizes how the model represents users' item selections.

The paper also examines how implicit-feedback models are evaluated. It identifies a problem in a widely used evaluation protocol and proposes a remedy using a small amount of explicit feedback. This contribution connects model design with the evidence used to assess it: behavioral histories provide the main modeling input, while limited explicit preference information helps address the stated evaluation problem.
summary.tldr: A probabilistic recommender learns item-selection trees from implicit feedback and addresses an evaluation problem using limited explicit feedback.

title: Learning Label Trees for Probabilistic Modelling of Implicit Feedback

abstract: This paper describes a third-generation parameter server framework for distributed machine learning. This framework offers two relaxations to balance system performance and algorithm efficiency. We propose a new algorithm that takes advantage of this framework to solve non-convex non-smooth problems with convergence guarantees. We present an in-depth analysis of two large scale machine learning problems ranging from $\ell_1$-regularized logistic regression on CPUs to reconstruction ICA on GPUs, using 636TB of real data with hundreds of billions of samples and dimensions. We demonstrate using these examples that the parameter server framework is an effective and straightforward way to scale machine learning to larger problems and systems than have been previously achieved.
originalAbstract: This paper describes a third-generation parameter server framework for distributed machine learning. This framework offers two relaxations to balance system performance and algorithm efficiency. We propose a new algorithm that takes advantage of this framework to solve non-convex non-smooth problems with convergence guarantees. We present an in-depth analysis of two large scale machine learning problems ranging from $\ell_1$-regularized logistic regression on CPUs to reconstruction ICA on GPUs, using 636TB of real data with hundreds of billions of samples and dimensions. We demonstrate using these examples that the parameter server framework is an effective and straightforward way to scale machine learning to larger problems and systems than have been previously achieved.

paragraphs: Training very large models across multiple machines requires attention to both the learning algorithm and the system that supports it. This paper presents a third-generation parameter server framework for distributed machine learning. Its design includes two relaxations intended to balance system performance against the efficiency of the learning algorithm.

The authors also propose an optimization algorithm that takes advantage of this framework. It addresses problems that are both non-convex and non-smooth, and comes with convergence guarantees. This links the system design to an analyzed learning procedure, making the contribution about how distributed computation and optimization work together.

The evaluation examines L1-regularized logistic regression on CPUs and reconstruction independent component analysis on GPUs. These examples use 636 TB of real data, with hundreds of billions of samples and dimensions. From these large-scale studies, the authors report that the framework offers an effective and straightforward route to scaling machine learning beyond previously achieved problem and system sizes. The evidence spans two substantially different learning workloads and hardware settings.
summary.tldr: A parameter server framework couples distributed-system relaxations with a convergent optimization algorithm and demonstrates large-scale learning on CPU and GPU workloads.

title: Communication Efficient Distributed Machine Learning with the Parameter Server

abstract: We consider the problem of Bayesian parameter estimation for deep neural networks, which is important in problem settings where we may have little data, and/ or where we need accurate posterior predictive densities p(y|x, D), e.g., for applications involving bandits or active learning. One simple approach to this is to use online Monte Carlo methods, such as SGLD (stochastic gradient Langevin dynamics). Unfortunately, such a method needs to store many copies of the parameters (which wastes memory), and needs to make predictions using many versions of the model (which wastes time).We describe a method for “distilling” a Monte Carlo approximation to the posterior predictive density into a more compact form, namely a single deep neural network. We compare to two very recent approaches to Bayesian neural networks, namely an approach based on expectation propagation [HLA15] and an approach based on variational Bayes [BCKW15]. Our method performs better than both of these, is much simpler to implement, and uses less computation at test time.
originalAbstract: We consider the problem of Bayesian parameter estimation for deep neural networks, which is important in problem settings where we may have little data, and/ or where we need accurate posterior predictive densities p(y|x, D), e.g., for applications involving bandits or active learning. One simple approach to this is to use online Monte Carlo methods, such as SGLD (stochastic gradient Langevin dynamics). Unfortunately, such a method needs to store many copies of the parameters (which wastes memory), and needs to make predictions using many versions of the model (which wastes time).We describe a method for “distilling” a Monte Carlo approximation to the posterior predictive density into a more compact form, namely a single deep neural network. We compare to two very recent approaches to Bayesian neural networks, namely an approach based on expectation propagation [HLA15] and an approach based on variational Bayes [BCKW15]. Our method performs better than both of these, is much simpler to implement, and uses less computation at test time.

paragraphs: Bayesian neural-network prediction accounts for uncertainty about model parameters when predicting an output. This can matter when data are scarce or when applications such as bandits and active learning need accurate predictive distributions. Monte Carlo methods offer one approach, but they require storing many parameter samples and making predictions with many versions of the network.

The paper proposes compressing that collection of predictions into a single deep neural network. Its target is the Monte Carlo approximation to the posterior predictive distribution: the output distribution obtained by accounting for parameter uncertainty. Distillation makes this predictive information available in a more compact form, reducing the need to retain and evaluate many separate models.

The authors compare their method with Bayesian neural-network approaches based on expectation propagation and variational Bayes. They report better performance, simpler implementation, and less computation at prediction time in those comparisons. The contribution is a way to make approximate Bayesian prediction more economical by learning a single network to represent the sampled models' predictive behavior.
summary.tldr: Bayesian dark knowledge distills Monte Carlo predictive distributions into one neural network, reducing storage and prediction costs.

title: Bayesian dark knowledge

abstract: For structured estimation problems with atomic norms, recent advances in the literature express sample complexity and estimation error bounds in terms of certain geometric measures, in particular Gaussian width of the unit norm ball, Gaussian width of a spherical cap induced by a tangent cone, and a restricted norm compatibility constant. However, given an atomic norm, bounding these geometric measures can be difficult. In this paper, we present general upper bounds for such geometric measures, which only require simple information of the atomic norm under consideration, and we establish tightness of these bounds by providing the corresponding lower bounds. We show applications of our analysis to certain atomic norms, especially k-support norm, for which existing result is incomplete.
originalAbstract: For structured estimation problems with atomic norms, recent advances in the literature express sample complexity and estimation error bounds in terms of certain geometric measures, in particular Gaussian width of the unit norm ball, Gaussian width of a spherical cap induced by a tangent cone, and a restricted norm compatibility constant. However, given an atomic norm, bounding these geometric measures can be difficult. In this paper, we present general upper bounds for such geometric measures, which only require simple information of the atomic norm under consideration, and we establish tightness of these bounds by providing the corresponding lower bounds. We show applications of our analysis to certain atomic norms, especially k-support norm, for which existing result is incomplete.

paragraphs: Atomic norms provide a framework for structured estimation, but analyzing their statistical behavior can require difficult geometric calculations. Existing results express sample requirements and estimation errors through quantities such as Gaussian widths and restricted norm compatibility constants. Those expressions are useful only when the relevant quantities can themselves be bounded.

This paper develops general upper bounds that require relatively simple information about the atomic norm being studied. The analysis covers the Gaussian width of its unit ball, a Gaussian width associated with a tangent cone, and the restricted norm compatibility constant. It therefore addresses a recurring technical obstacle between specifying a structured estimator and understanding its statistical guarantees.

The authors also provide corresponding lower bounds to establish tightness of their upper bounds. They demonstrate applications to particular atomic norms, especially the k-support norm, for which earlier results were incomplete. The contribution is a reusable analytical route to sample-complexity and error guarantees, reducing the need to solve each difficult geometric bounding problem from scratch.
summary.tldr: General, tight geometric bounds simplify the analysis of structured estimators using atomic norms, including the k-support norm.

title: Structured Estimation with Atomic Norms: General Bounds and Applications

abstract: Unsupervised learning of structured predictors has been a long standing pursuit in machine learning. Recently a conditional random field auto-encoder has been proposed in a two-layer setting, allowing latent structured representation to be automatically inferred. Aside from being nonconvex, it also requires the demanding inference of normalization. In this paper, we develop a convex relaxation of two-layer conditional model which captures latent structure and estimates model parameters, jointly and optimally. We further expand its applicability by resorting to a weaker form of inference---maximum a-posteriori. The flexibility of the model is demonstrated on two structures based on total unimodularity---graph matching and linear chain. Experimental results confirm the promise of the method.

Recently a conditional random field auto-encoder has been proposed in a two-layer setting, allowing latent structured representation to be automatically inferred. Aside from being nonconvex, it also requires the demanding inference of normalization. In this paper, we develop a convex relaxation of two-layer conditional model which captures latent structure and estimates model parameters, jointly and optimally. We further expand its applicability by resorting to a weaker form of inference---maximum a-posteriori. paragraphs: Learning structured predictors without supervision requires discovering hidden structure while estimating the model that describes it. The paper considers a two-layer conditional modeling approach related to conditional random field autoencoders. Existing work in this setting faces both nonconvex optimization and the computational burden of calculating normalization quantities during inference.

The authors develop a convex relaxation that jointly captures latent structure and estimates model parameters. The optimality claim belongs to this relaxed formulation. Bringing both tasks into one convex problem provides a way to address their interdependence while avoiding the nonconvex formulation identified in the earlier approach.

The paper also expands applicability by using maximum a posteriori inference, which asks for a most probable configuration and imposes a weaker inference requirement. It demonstrates the model on graph matching and linear-chain structures using total unimodularity. Experimental results are described as promising. The contribution combines a different optimization formulation with reduced inference demands and demonstrations on two distinct structured problems.
summary.tldr: A convex relaxation jointly learns latent structure and model parameters while reducing inference requirements to maximum a posteriori inference.

title: Convex Two-Layer Modeling with Latent Structure

abstract: Feature selection is one of the most fundamental problems in machine learning. An extensive body of work on information-theoretic feature selection exists which is based on maximizing mutual information between subsets of features and class labels. Practical methods are forced to rely on approximations due to the difficulty of estimating mutual information. We demonstrate that approximations made by existing methods are based on unrealistic assumptions. We formulate a more flexible and general class of assumptions based on variational distributions and use them to tractably generate lower bounds for mutual information. These bounds define a novel information-theoretic framework for feature selection, which we prove to be optimal under tree graphical models with proper choice of variational distributions. Our experiments demonstrate that the proposed method strongly outperforms existing information-theoretic feature selection approaches.
originalAbstract: Feature selection is one of the most fundamental problems in machine learning. An extensive body of work on information-theoretic feature selection exists which is based on maximizing mutual information between subsets of features and class labels. Practical methods are forced to rely on approximations due to the difficulty of estimating mutual information. We demonstrate that approximations made by existing methods are based on unrealistic assumptions. We formulate a more flexible and general class of assumptions based on variational distributions and use them to tractably generate lower bounds for mutual information. These bounds define a novel information-theoretic framework for feature selection, which we prove to be optimal under tree graphical models with proper choice of variational distributions. Our experiments demonstrate that the proposed method strongly outperforms existing information-theoretic feature selection approaches.

paragraphs: Feature selection seeks a useful subset of input variables. Information-theoretic methods often try to maximize mutual information between that subset and the class label, measuring how informative the selected variables are about the prediction target. Directly estimating this quantity is difficult, so practical methods rely on approximations.

The authors argue that existing approximations rest on unrealistic assumptions and introduce a more flexible family based on variational distributions. These distributions allow them to construct tractable lower bounds on mutual information. The bounds become the basis of a new feature-selection framework, replacing difficult direct estimation with an explicitly bounded objective.

The paper proves optimality under tree graphical models when the variational distributions are chosen appropriately. Both the tree structure and the distribution choice qualify that theoretical result. Experiments also show strong improvements over existing information-theoretic selection methods. Together, the results give the framework a conditional theoretical foundation and empirical support for using more flexible assumptions when assessing which feature subsets are informative.
summary.tldr: Variational lower bounds support feature selection with conditional optimality for tree graphical models and strong reported empirical performance.

title: Variational Information Maximization for Feature Selection

abstract: We give a novel formal theoretical framework for unsupervised learning with two distinctive characteristics. First, it does not assume any generative model and based on a worst-case performance metric. Second, it is comparative, namely performance is measured with respect to a given hypothesis class. This allows to avoid known computational hardness results and improper algorithms based on convex relaxations. We show how several families of unsupervised learning models, which were previously only analyzed under probabilistic assumptions and are otherwise provably intractable, can be efficiently learned in our framework by convex optimization.
originalAbstract: We give a novel formal theoretical framework for unsupervised learning with two distinctive characteristics. First, it does not assume any generative model and based on a worst-case performance metric. Second, it is comparative, namely performance is measured with respect to a given hypothesis class. This allows to avoid known computational hardness results and improper algorithms based on convex relaxations. We show how several families of unsupervised learning models, which were previously only analyzed under probabilistic assumptions and are otherwise provably intractable, can be efficiently learned in our framework by convex optimization.

paragraphs: The paper proposes a theoretical framework for unsupervised learning that does not start by specifying a probabilistic process that generated the data. Instead, it evaluates performance using a worst-case criterion. This changes the basis of the learning guarantee: success is assessed without relying on a particular generative account of the observations.

A second defining choice is to make the guarantee comparative. The learner is judged relative to a specified class of hypotheses, which establishes the benchmark it should compete against. The framework also accommodates improper learning through convex relaxations: the algorithm can use a broader set of solutions than the class defining the comparison.

Within this framework, the authors show that convex optimization can efficiently learn several families previously analyzed using probabilistic assumptions and otherwise subject to computational hardness results. The significance is tied to the new formulation of success. It provides a way to obtain efficient, comparative guarantees without claiming that the previously intractable formulations themselves have become easy.
summary.tldr: A comparative, worst-case framework enables efficient convex approaches to some unsupervised learning problems without assuming a generative model.

title: A Non-generative Framework and Convex Relaxations for Unsupervised Learning

abstract: The additive model is one of the most popularly used models for high dimensional nonparametric regression analysis. However, its main drawback is that it neglects possible interactions between predictor variables. In this paper, we reexamine the group additive model proposed in the literature, and rigorously define the intrinsic group additive structure for the relationship between the response variable $Y$ and the predictor vector $\vect{X}$, and further develop an effective structure-penalized kernel method for simultaneous identification of the intrinsic group additive structure and nonparametric function estimation. The method utilizes a novel complexity measure we derive for group additive structures. We show that the proposed method is consistent in identifying the intrinsic group additive structure. Simulation study and real data applications demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method as a general tool for high dimensional nonparametric regression.

However, its main drawback is that it neglects possible interactions between predictor variables. In this paper, we reexamine the group additive model proposed in the literature, and rigorously define the intrinsic group additive structure for the relationship between the response variable $Y$ and the predictor vector $\vect{X}$, and further develop an effective structure-penalized kernel method for simultaneous identification of the intrinsic group additive structure and nonparametric function estimation. The method utilizes a novel complexity measure we derive for group additive structures. We show that the proposed method is consistent in identifying the intrinsic group additive structure. Simulation study and real data applications demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method as a general tool for high dimensional nonparametric regression.

paragraphs: Additive regression models simplify high-dimensional prediction by combining separate contributions from predictor variables. Their weakness is that they can miss interactions: the relationship between a response and one predictor may depend on another predictor. This paper revisits group additive modeling, which allows predictors to contribute jointly within groups.

The authors formally define the intrinsic group additive structure relating predictors to the response. They then develop a kernel method that identifies this structure while estimating the associated nonparametric functions. A newly derived measure of structural complexity supplies the penalty, so choosing the grouping and fitting its predictive functions become parts of the same estimation procedure.

The paper establishes consistency for identifying the intrinsic grouping structure and evaluates the method in simulations and real-data applications. These results support its use for high-dimensional nonparametric regression when interactions need to be represented. The central contribution is to make the grouping itself a target of learning, rather than treating all predictor effects as separate or assuming the relevant interaction groups are already known.
summary.tldr: A complexity-penalized kernel method jointly learns interacting predictor groups and their regression functions, with a structure-identification consistency result.

title: Group Additive Structure Identification for Kernel Nonparametric Regression

abstract: Off-policy model-free deep reinforcement learning methods using previously collected data can improve sample efficiency over on-policy policy gradient techniques. On the other hand, on-policy algorithms are often more stable and easier to use. This paper examines, both theoretically and empirically, approaches to merging on- and off-policy updates for deep reinforcement learning. Theoretical results show that off-policy updates with a value function estimator can be interpolated with on-policy policy gradient updates whilst still satisfying performance bounds. Our analysis uses control variate methods to produce a family of policy gradient algorithms, with several recently proposed algorithms being special cases of this family. We then provide an empirical comparison of these techniques with the remaining algorithmic details fixed, and show how different mixing of off-policy gradient estimates with on-policy samples contribute to improvements in empirical performance. The final algorithm provides a generalization and unification of existing deep policy gradient techniques, has theoretical guarantees on the bias introduced by off-policy updates, and improves on the state-of-the-art model-free deep RL methods on a number of OpenAI Gym continuous control benchmarks.

title: Interpolated Policy Gradient: Merging On-Policy and Off-Policy Gradient Estimation for Deep Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Background: Deep learning models are typically trained using stochastic gradient descent or one of its variants. These methods update the weights using their gradient, estimated from a small fraction of the training data. It has been observed that when using large batch sizes there is a persistent degradation in generalization performance - known as the "generalization gap" phenomenon. Identifying the origin of this gap and closing it had remained an open problem. Contributions: We examine the initial high learning rate training phase. We find that the weight distance from its initialization grows logarithmically with the number of weight updates. We therefore propose a "random walk on a random landscape" statistical model which is known to exhibit similar "ultra-slow" diffusion behavior. Following this hypothesis we conducted experiments to show empirically that the "generalization gap" stems from the relatively small number of updates rather than the batch size, and can be completely eliminated by adapting the training regime used. We further investigate different techniques to train models in the large-batch regime and present a novel algorithm named "Ghost Batch Normalization" which enables significant decrease in the generalization gap without increasing the number of updates. To validate our findings we conduct several additional experiments on MNIST, CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100 and ImageNet. Finally, we reassess common practices and beliefs concerning training of deep models and suggest they may not be optimal to achieve good generalization.

summary.tldr: Experiments link the large-batch generalization gap to too few updates and show that revised training regimes can eliminate it.

title: Train longer, generalize better: closing the generalization gap in large batch training of neural networks

abstract: Collecting the large datasets needed to train deep neural networks can be very difficult, particularly for the many applications for which sharing and pooling data is complicated by practical, ethical, or legal concerns. However, it may be the case that derivative datasets or predictive models developed within individual sites can be shared and combined with fewer restrictions. Training on distributed data and combining the resulting networks is often viewed as continual learning, but these methods require networks to be trained sequentially. In this paper, we introduce distributed weight consolidation (DWC), a continual learning method to consolidate the weights of separate neural networks, each trained on an independent dataset. We evaluated DWC with a brain segmentation case study, where we consolidated dilated convolutional neural networks trained on independent structural magnetic resonance imaging (sMRI) datasets from different sites. We found that DWC led to increased performance on test sets from the different sites, while maintaining generalization performance for a very large and completely independent multi-site dataset, compared to an ensemble baseline.

The paper considers situations where sharing derived datasets or predictive models may face fewer restrictions. Its goal is to combine learning from separate datasets through the networks trained on them.

The authors frame it as a continual learning method, addressing the sequential training requirement of existing approaches discussed in the abstract. The key organizational change is that networks trained separately on independent datasets become the inputs to consolidation.

The evaluation uses brain segmentation with dilated convolutional networks trained on structural MRI datasets from different sites. Compared with an ensemble baseline, DWC improves performance on test sets from those sites while maintaining generalization on a very large, completely independent multi-site dataset. These results distinguish improved performance within the participating sites from preserved performance on independent data, providing evidence for model consolidation in this case study.
summary.tldr: DWC combines independently trained networks, improving site-specific brain segmentation while maintaining generalization on an independent multi-site dataset.

title: Distributed Weight Consolidation: A Brain Segmentation Case Study

abstract: We advocate Laplacian K-modes for joint clustering and density mode finding, and propose a concave-convex relaxation of the problem, which yields a parallel algorithm that scales up to large datasets and high dimensions. We optimize a tight bound (auxiliary function) of our relaxation, which, at each iteration, amounts to computing an independent update for each cluster-assignment variable, with guar- anteed convergence. Therefore, our bound optimizer can be trivially distributed for large-scale data sets. Furthermore, we show that the density modes can be obtained as byproducts of the assignment variables via simple maximum-value operations whose additional computational cost is linear in the number of data points. Our formulation does not need storing a full affinity matrix and computing its eigenvalue decomposition, neither does it perform expensive projection steps and Lagrangian-dual inner iterates for the simplex constraints of each point. Fur- thermore, unlike mean-shift, our density-mode estimation does not require inner- loop gradient-ascent iterates. It has a complexity independent of feature-space dimension, yields modes that are valid data points in the input set and is appli- cable to discrete domains as well as arbitrary kernels. We report comprehensive experiments over various data sets, which show that our algorithm yields very competitive performances in term of optimization quality (i.e., the value of the discrete-variable objective at convergence) and clustering accuracy.

paragraphs: Laplacian K-modes combines clustering with finding density modes, which represent concentrated regions of the data. This paper proposes a concave-convex relaxation that makes the problem amenable to parallel computation. These results support a formulation that makes joint clustering and mode finding more scalable without requiring those expensive intermediate operations.

title: Scalable Laplacian K-modes

abstract: Applications of optimal transport have recently gained remarkable attention as a result of the computational advantages of entropic regularization. However, in most situations the Sinkhorn approximation to the Wasserstein distance is replaced by a regularized version that is less accurate but easy to differentiate. In this work we characterize the differential properties of the original Sinkhorn approximation, proving that it enjoys the same smoothness as its regularized version and we explicitly provide an efficient algorithm to compute its gradient. We show that this result benefits both theory and applications: on one hand, high order smoothness confers statistical guarantees to learning with Wasserstein approximations. On the other hand, the gradient formula allows to efficiently solve learning and optimization problems in practice. Promising preliminary experiments complement our analysis.

paragraphs: Optimal transport provides a way to compare distributions, and entropic regularization has made its computation more practical. In learning applications, however, obtaining gradients is also important. The paper addresses a common substitution: replacing the original Sinkhorn approximation to Wasserstein distance with a less accurate regularized version because that alternative is easier to differentiate.

The authors characterize the differential properties of the original approximation and prove that it has the same smoothness as the regularized version. They also give an efficient algorithm for computing its gradient. Together, these results address both the mathematical question of whether suitable derivatives exist and the computational question of how to obtain them.

The consequences extend in two directions. Higher-order smoothness supports statistical guarantees for learning with Wasserstein approximations, while the gradient formula makes practical learning and optimization possible with the original approximation. The paper includes promising preliminary experiments, so its empirical evidence is presented as an initial complement to the analysis. Its main contribution is establishing the properties and computational tools needed to use this approximation more directly.
summary.tldr: The original Sinkhorn approximation has the same smoothness as its regularized alternative and admits efficient gradient computation.

title: Differential Properties of Sinkhorn Approximation for Learning with Wasserstein Distance

abstract: Successful approaches to program induction require a hand-engineered domain-specific language (DSL), constraining the space of allowed programs and imparting prior knowledge of the domain. We contribute a program induction algorithm that learns a DSL while jointly training a neural network to efficiently search for programs in the learned DSL. We use our model to synthesize functions on lists, edit text, and solve symbolic regression problems, showing how the model learns a domain-specific library of program components for expressing solutions to problems in the domain.
