paragraphs: Accuracy counts every incorrect emotion label as an error of the same severity. Yet some emotions are psychologically closer than others: confusing excitement with awe differs from confusing it with anger. This paper develops evaluation measures for visual emotion recognition that account for those differences, aiming to reflect the character of a model’s mistakes.

The proposed approach uses distances on Mikel’s emotion wheel, a psychological representation of relationships among emotions. Those distances allow evaluation to distinguish between nearby and more distant confusions. As a result, assessment includes information that a simple count of correct predictions leaves out: how far an incorrect emotional interpretation lies from the intended one.

Experiments in semi-supervised emotion recognition and a user study find the proposed measures more effective than accuracy for assessing performance and more consistent with human emotional cognition. The contribution is an evaluation perspective grounded in psychological similarity. It gives researchers a way to judge whether a system’s errors resemble relatively close emotional confusions or more substantial misreadings of an image.
summary.tldr: Emotion-wheel-based metrics evaluate visual emotion recognition by accounting for the psychological severity of different mistakes.

title: To Err Like Human: Affective Bias-Inspired Measures for Visual Emotion Recognition Evaluation

abstract: Time series analysis is widely used in many fields such as power energy, economics, and transportation, including different tasks such as forecasting, anomaly detection, classification, etc. Missing values are widely observed in these tasks, and often leading to unpredictable negative effects on existing methods, hindering their further application. In response to this situation, existing time series imputation methods mainly focus on restoring sequences based on their data characteristics, while ignoring the performance of the restored sequences in downstream tasks. Considering different requirements of downstream tasks (e.g., forecasting), this paper proposes an efficient downstream task-oriented time series imputation evaluation approach. By combining time series imputation with neural network models used for downstream tasks, the gain of different imputation strategies on downstream tasks is estimated without retraining, and the most favorable imputation value for downstream tasks is given by combining different imputation strategies according to the estimated gain.

paragraphs: Time-series imputation fills gaps in sequences used for forecasting, anomaly detection, classification, and other tasks. This paper argues that restoring a sequence according to its data characteristics overlooks an important question: whether the filled-in values help the eventual task. Different downstream uses can place different requirements on the same missing observations.

The proposed evaluation approach connects candidate imputation strategies with the neural networks used for downstream prediction. It estimates how much each strategy benefits the downstream task without retraining those networks. This provides a task-oriented basis for judging alternative ways of filling gaps while avoiding retraining as part of that estimation.

The method then combines imputation strategies according to their estimated benefits to obtain values favorable to the downstream task. Its central contribution is to make the needs of the consuming model part of imputation evaluation and selection. The approach therefore links gap filling to intended use, rather than assessing reconstructed sequences solely through their own characteristics.
summary.tldr: The method evaluates and combines time-series imputations by estimating their downstream-task benefits without retraining the task model.

title: Task-oriented Time Series Imputation Evaluation via Generalized Representers

abstract: Recent studies reveal that large language models (LLMs) often struggle to resolve conflicting instructions embedded within hierarchical prompts, resulting in decreased compliance with system-level directives and compromising the reliability of safety-critical applications. While earlier approaches attempt to improve instruction hierarchy awareness through prompt engineering or embedding-level modifications, they typically lack structural modeling and either offer limited gains or require extensive fine-tuning. In this work, we introduce $\textbf{FocalLoRA}$, a parameter-efficient and structure-aware framework that strengthens hierarchical instruction adherence by selectively optimizing structurally critical attention heads, referred to as $\textit{focal heads}$, which exhibit heightened sensitivity to instruction conflicts. Experiments across multiple models and a dedicated benchmark demonstrate that FocalLoRA markedly enhances system instruction compliance with minimal tuning cost. For instance, on Llama-8B, fine-tuning only 0.0188\% of parameters yields a 35.52\% $\uparrow$ in system instruction compliance.

paragraphs: Language models can struggle when a prompt contains instructions that conflict across different priority levels. A lower-priority instruction may pull the model away from a system-level directive, weakening reliable instruction following. FocalLoRA targets this problem by making the hierarchy of instructions a focus of parameter-efficient adaptation.

The framework identifies attention heads that are especially sensitive to instruction conflicts and calls them focal heads. It selectively optimizes these structurally important components. This concentrates training on parts of the model associated with conflict sensitivity, rather than requiring extensive fine-tuning throughout the network. The approach connects a structural observation about attention with a targeted training strategy.

Experiments across several models and a dedicated benchmark report substantially better system-instruction compliance at low tuning cost. For Llama-8B, updating only 0.0188% of parameters yields a reported 35.52% increase in compliance. The finding indicates that selective changes to conflict-sensitive attention heads can deliver meaningful improvements in hierarchical instruction adherence within the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: FocalLoRA improves instruction-hierarchy adherence by selectively tuning attention heads that are sensitive to conflicting instructions.

title: Don’t Forget the Enjoin: FocalLoRA for Instruction Hierarchical Alignment in Large Language Models

abstract: Image fusion is a fundamental and important task in computer vision, aiming to combine complementary information from different modalities to fuse images. In recent years, diffusion models have made significant developments in the field of image fusion. However, diffusion models often require complex computations and redundant inference time, which reduces the applicability of these methods. To address this issue, we propose RFfusion, an efficient one-step diffusion model for image fusion based on Rectified Flow. We incorporate Rectified Flow into the image fusion task to straighten the sampling path in the diffusion model, achieving one-step sampling without the need for additional training, while still maintaining high-quality fusion results. Furthermore, we propose a task-specific variational autoencoder (VAE) architecture tailored for image fusion, where the fusion operation is embedded within the latent space to further reduce computational complexity. To address the inherent discrepancy between conventional reconstruction-oriented VAE objectives and the requirements of image fusion, we introduce a two-stage training strategy. This approach facilitates the effective learning and integration of complementary information from multi-modal source images, thereby enabling the model to retain fine-grained structural details while significantly enhancing inference efficiency. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method outperforms other state-of-the-art methods in terms of both inference speed and fusion quality.

paragraphs: Image fusion combines complementary information from images captured through different modalities. RFfusion addresses this computational burden by using Rectified Flow to straighten the sampling trajectory, enabling one-step generation while maintaining high-quality fused images.

The one-step sampling mechanism is described as requiring no additional training, while the overall framework includes its proposed two-stage training strategy. The contribution therefore combines a shorter generation procedure with a representation designed for fusion, addressing both the cost of sampling and the preservation of useful image information.
summary.tldr: RFfusion combines one-step Rectified Flow sampling with a fusion-specific latent representation to improve image-fusion speed and quality.

title: Efficient Rectified Flow for Image Fusion

abstract: The problem of optimally covering a given compact subset of $\mathbb{R}^N$ with a preassigned number $n$ of Euclidean metric balls has a long-standing history and it is well-recognized to be computationally hard. This article establishes a numerically viable algorithm for obtaining optimal covers of compact sets via two key contributions. The first is a foundational result establishing Lipschitz continuity of the marginal function of a certain parametric non-convex maximization problem in the optimal covering problem, and it provides the substrate for numerical gradient algorithms to be employed in this context. The second is an adaptation of a stochastically smoothed numerical gradient-based (zeroth-order) algorithm for a non-convex minimization problem, that, equipped with randomized restarts, spurs global convergence to an optimal cover. Several numerical experiments with complicated nonconvex compact sets demonstrate the excellent performance of our techniques.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to cover a compact region of Euclidean space using a fixed number of balls as effectively as possible. Even describing a complicated region does not make finding its optimal cover easy: the underlying optimization is computationally hard and nonconvex. The authors develop a numerical approach that connects a mathematical regularity result to a practical search procedure.

Their first contribution establishes Lipschitz continuity for a marginal function arising from a parameterized maximization problem within the covering formulation. In plain language, this controls how sharply that function can change when its inputs change. That regularity provides a foundation for applying numerical gradient methods to the covering problem.

The algorithm then uses stochastic smoothing and function evaluations to obtain gradient-like search directions, together with randomized restarts. The authors establish global convergence to an optimal cover for their approach. Numerical experiments on complicated nonconvex compact sets also show strong performance. The contribution therefore combines a justification for the optimization procedure with evidence that it can handle geometrically difficult covering examples.
summary.tldr: The paper combines a continuity result, stochastic smoothing, and randomized restarts to numerically search for optimal geometric covers.

title: A Computationally Viable Numerical Gradient-based Technique for Optimal Covering Problems

abstract: We propose an inference-time scaling approach for pretrained flow models. Recently, inference-time scaling has gained significant attention in LLMs and diffusion models, improving sample quality or better aligning outputs with user preferences by leveraging additional computation. For diffusion models, particle sampling has allowed more efficient scaling due to the stochasticity at intermediate denoising steps. On the contrary, while flow models have gained popularity as an alternative to diffusion models--offering faster generation and high-quality outputs--efficient inference-time scaling methods used for diffusion models cannot be directly applied due to their deterministic generative process. To enable efficient inference-time scaling for flow models, we propose three key ideas: 1) SDE-based generation, enabling particle sampling in flow models, 2) Interpolant conversion, broadening the search space and enhancing sample diversity, and 3) Rollover Budget Forcing (RBF), an adaptive allocation of computational resources across timesteps to maximize budget utilization. Our experiments show that SDE-based generation and variance-preserving (VP) interpolant-based generation, improves the performance of particle sampling methods for inference-time scaling in flow models. Additionally, we demonstrate that RBF with VP-SDE achieves the best performance, outperforming all previous inference-time scaling approaches.

For diffusion models, particle sampling has allowed more efficient scaling due to the stochasticity at intermediate denoising steps. On the contrary, while flow models have gained popularity as an alternative to diffusion models--offering faster generation and high-quality outputs--efficient inference-time scaling methods used for diffusion models cannot be directly applied due to their deterministic generative process. To enable efficient inference-time scaling for flow models, we propose three key ideas: 1) SDE-based generation, enabling particle sampling in flow models, 2) Interpolant conversion, broadening the search space and enhancing sample diversity, and 3) Rollover Budget Forcing (RBF), an adaptive allocation of computational resources across timesteps to maximize budget utilization. Our experiments show that SDE-based generation and variance-preserving (VP) interpolant-based generation, improves the performance of particle sampling methods for inference-time scaling in flow models. Additionally, we demonstrate that RBF with VP-SDE achieves the best performance, outperforming all previous inference-time scaling approaches.

paragraphs: This paper studies how pretrained flow models can use additional generation-time computation to improve outputs. Particle-sampling techniques already exploit randomness during diffusion generation, but they do not transfer directly to flow models because the latter use a deterministic generation process. The proposed approach changes generation so that this kind of search becomes available.

The method has three parts. Stochastic differential equation generation introduces randomness that enables particle sampling. Interpolant conversion broadens the search space and increases sample diversity. Rollover Budget Forcing then allocates computational resources adaptively across timesteps, aiming to make fuller use of the available computation budget.

Experiments show that stochastic generation and variance-preserving interpolants improve particle-based inference-time scaling for flow models. Combining Rollover Budget Forcing with the variance-preserving stochastic formulation produces the best reported performance, exceeding the previous approaches compared in the study. The contribution is therefore both a way to enable search within flow generation and a strategy for distributing the computation that search consumes.
summary.tldr: Stochastic generation and adaptive compute allocation enable more effective inference-time scaling for pretrained flow models.

title: Inference-Time Scaling for Flow Models via Stochastic Generation and Rollover Budget Forcing

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable achievements across diverse applications; however, they remain plagued by spurious correlations and the generation of hallucinated content. Despite extensive efforts to enhance the resilience of LLMs, existing approaches either rely on indiscriminate fine-tuning of all parameters, resulting in parameter inefficiency and lack of specificity, or depend on post-processing techniques that offer limited adaptability and flexibility. This study introduces a novel Causality-driven Robust Optimization (CdRO) approach that selectively updates model components sensitive to causal reasoning, enhancing model causality while preserving valuable pretrained knowledge to mitigate overfitting. Our method begins by identifying the parameter components within LLMs that capture causal relationships, achieved through comparing the training dynamics of parameter matrices associated with the original samples, as well as augmented counterfactual and paraphrased variants. These comparisons are then fed into a lightweight logistic regression model, optimized in real time to dynamically identify and adapt the causal components within LLMs. The identified parameters are subsequently optimized using an enhanced policy optimization algorithm, where the reward function is designed to jointly promote both model generalization and robustness. Extensive experiments across various tasks using twelve different LLMs demonstrate the superior performance of our framework, underscoring its significant effectiveness in reducing the model’s dependence on spurious associations and mitigating hallucinations.

paragraphs: Language models can depend on misleading associations and produce hallucinated content. This paper proposes Causality-driven Robust Optimization, or CdRO, to address these problems through selective parameter updates. Its aim is to strengthen components associated with causal reasoning while preserving useful pretrained knowledge and reducing overfitting.

CdRO compares how parameter matrices behave during training on original examples, counterfactual variants, and paraphrases. These comparisons feed a lightweight logistic regression model that is updated in real time to identify relevant components dynamically. The selected parameters are then trained with an enhanced policy optimization algorithm whose reward encourages both generalization and robustness. This makes the choice of what to update part of the optimization process itself.

Experiments across multiple tasks and twelve language models report superior performance, reduced reliance on spurious associations, and fewer hallucinations. The findings support the authors' approach of directing training toward components identified through these data comparisons. The stated outcome is improved resilience and mitigation of hallucinations, rather than their complete elimination.
summary.tldr: CdRO dynamically selects and trains language-model components associated with causal reasoning to reduce spurious associations and hallucinations.

title: Boosting Resilience of Large Language Models through Causality-Driven Robust Optimization

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have achieved state-of-the-art results across diverse domains, yet their development remains reliant on vast amounts of publicly available data, raising concerns about data scarcity and the lack of access to domain-specific, sensitive information. Federated Learning (FL) presents a compelling framework to address these challenges by enabling decentralized fine-tuning on pre-trained LLMs without sharing raw data. However, the compatibility and performance of pre-trained LLMs in FL settings remain largely under explored. We introduce the FlowerTune LLM Leaderboard, a first-of-its-kind benchmarking suite designed to evaluate federated fine-tuning of LLMs across four diverse domains: general NLP, finance, medical, and coding. Each domain includes federated instruction-tuning datasets and domain-specific evaluation metrics. Our results, obtained through a collaborative, open-source and community-driven approach, provide the first comprehensive comparison across 26 pre-trained LLMs with different aggregation and fine-tuning strategies under federated settings, offering actionable insights into model performance, resource constraints, and domain adaptation. This work lays the foundation for developing privacy-preserving, domain-specialized LLMs for real-world applications.

paragraphs: FlowerTune studies how pretrained language models behave when fine-tuned through federated learning. This setting allows decentralized training without sharing raw data, making it relevant to specialized or sensitive information that may be unavailable in public datasets. The paper addresses the limited understanding of which models and training strategies work well in that setting.

The authors introduce a leaderboard and benchmarking suite covering general language tasks, finance, medicine, and coding. Each domain includes instruction-tuning datasets arranged for federated use and evaluation metrics suited to that domain. The comparison spans 26 pretrained language models and examines different methods for aggregating learning across participants and for fine-tuning the models.

The reported contribution is a broad, community-driven comparison that connects model performance with resource constraints and domain adaptation. This gives researchers a common basis for assessing federated fine-tuning choices across several kinds of task. Its significance lies in making decentralized adaptation more systematically measurable and supporting the development of domain-specialized models trained without centralizing participants' raw data.
summary.tldr: FlowerTune benchmarks federated fine-tuning across 26 language models and four domains, comparing performance, training strategies, and resource constraints.

title: FlowerTune: A Cross-Domain Benchmark for Federated Fine-Tuning of Large Language Models

abstract: Transformers can implement both generalizable algorithms (e.g., induction heads) and simple positional shortcuts (e.g., memorizing fixed output positions). In this work, we study how the choice of pretraining data distribution steers a shallow transformer toward one behavior or the other. Focusing on a minimal trigger-output prediction task -- copying the token immediately following a special trigger upon its second occurrence -- we present a rigorous analysis of gradient-based training of a single-layer transformer. In both the infinite and finite sample regimes, we prove a transition in the learned mechanism: if input sequences exhibit sufficient diversity, measured by a low “max-sum” ratio of trigger-to-trigger distances, the trained model implements an induction head and generalizes to unseen contexts; by contrast, when this ratio is large, the model resorts to a positional shortcut and fails to generalize out-of-distribution (OOD). We also reveal a trade-off between the pretraining context length and OOD generalization, and derive the optimal pretraining distribution that minimizes computational cost per sample. Finally, we validate our theoretical predictions with controlled synthetic experiments, demonstrating that broadening context distributions robustly induces induction heads and enables OOD generalization. Our results shed light on the algorithmic biases of pretrained transformers and offer conceptual guidelines for data-driven control of their learned behaviors.

paragraphs: A transformer can solve a training task through a reusable rule or through a positional shortcut that breaks when contexts change. This paper studies how the pretraining distribution influences that choice in a single-layer transformer. Its task is deliberately minimal: when a special trigger appears again, copy the token that followed its earlier occurrence.

The authors analyze gradient-based training with both finite and infinite samples. They prove a transition governed by a measure of diversity in trigger-to-trigger distances, called the max-sum ratio. Sufficient diversity, expressed through a low ratio, leads to an induction head that generalizes to unseen contexts. A large ratio instead leads to a positional shortcut and failure outside the training distribution.

The analysis also identifies a tradeoff between pretraining context length and out-of-distribution generalization, and derives a pretraining distribution minimizing computational cost per sample. Controlled synthetic experiments support the predictions: broadening context distributions induces induction heads and enables generalization. Within this simplified setting, the work shows how data design can steer the algorithm a model learns, rather than merely change its training accuracy.
summary.tldr: For a minimal copying task, the paper proves that sufficient training-context diversity steers a single-layer transformer from positional shortcuts toward generalizable induction heads.

title: From Shortcut to Induction Head: How Data Diversity Shapes Algorithm Selection in Transformers

abstract: We present **AgMMU**, a challenging real‑world benchmark for evaluating and advancing vision-language models (VLMs) in the knowledge‑intensive domain of agriculture. Unlike prior datasets that rely on crowdsourced prompts, AgMMU is distilled from 116,231 authentic dialogues between everyday growers and USDA-authorized Cooperative Extension experts. Through a three‑stage pipeline: automated knowledge extraction, QA generation, and human verification, we construct (i) AgMMU, an evaluation set of 746 multiple‑choice questions (MCQs) and 746 open‑ended questions (OEQs), and (ii) AgBase, a development corpus of 57,079 multimodal facts covering five high-stakes agricultural topics: insect identification, species identification, disease categorization, symptom description, and management instruction. AgMMU has three key advantages:- **Authentic \& Expert‑Verified**: All facts, images, and answers originate from real farmer and gardener inquiries answered by credentialed specialists, ensuring high‑fidelity agricultural knowledge.- **Complete Development Suite**: AgMMU uniquely couples a dual‑format evaluation benchmark (MCQ and OEQ) with AgBase, a large‑scale training set, enabling both rigorous assessment and targeted improvement of VLMs.- **Knowledge‑intensive Challenge**: Our tasks demand the synergy of nuanced visual perception and domain expertise, exposing fundamental limitations of current general‑purpose models and charting a path toward robust, application‑ready agricultural AI.Benchmarking 12 leading VLMs reveals pronounced gaps in fine‑grained perception and factual grounding. Open‑sourced models trail after proprietary ones by a wide margin. Simple fine‑tuning on AgBase boosts open-sourced model performance on challenging OEQs for up to 11.6\% on average, narrowing this gap and also motivating future research to propose better strategies in knowledge extraction and distillation from AgBase. We hope AgMMU stimulates research on domain‑specific knowledge integration and trustworthy decision support in agriculture AI development.

paragraphs: AgMMU evaluates whether vision-language models can combine visual detail with agricultural expertise. Its evidence comes from 116,231 real exchanges between growers and USDA-authorized Cooperative Extension experts. An automated extraction and question-generation pipeline, followed by human verification, turns these exchanges into a benchmark and a development corpus. This connects evaluation to questions people actually ask about agricultural problems.

The benchmark contains 746 multiple-choice questions and 746 open-ended questions. Its companion corpus, AgBase, provides 57,079 multimodal facts covering insect and species identification, disease categorization, symptom description, and management instruction. Pairing evaluation with development data matters because researchers can both measure weaknesses and train models using knowledge from the same specialist domain.

Testing 12 leading models reveals substantial weaknesses in fine-grained perception and factual grounding, with open-source models trailing proprietary models. Fine-tuning on AgBase improves open-ended performance, with reported average gains reaching up to 11.6%. The results indicate that domain-specific training can narrow the observed gap and that strong general-purpose capabilities do not automatically supply detailed agricultural understanding.
summary.tldr: AgMMU uses expert-answered agricultural questions to expose vision-language model weaknesses and provides training data that helps narrow them.

title: AgMMU: A Comprehensive Agricultural Multimodal Understanding Benchmark

abstract: We address the problem of looking into the water from the air, where we seek to remove image distortions caused by refractions at the water surface. Our approach is based on modeling the different water surface structures at various points in time, assuming the underlying image is constant. To this end, we propose a model that consists of two neural-field networks. The first network predicts the height of the water surface at each spatial position and time, and the second network predicts the image color at each position. Using both networks, we reconstruct the observed sequence of images and can therefore use unsupervised training. We show that using implicit neural representations with periodic activation functions (SIREN) leads to effective modeling of the surface height spatio-temporal signal and its derivative, as required for image reconstruction. Using both simulated and real data we show that our method outperforms the latest unsupervised image restoration approach. In addition, it provides an estimate of the water surface.

paragraphs: Images taken from above water can be distorted as light passes through its moving surface. This paper seeks to recover the underlying image by modeling how the surface changes across a sequence. Its key assumption is that the scene being viewed remains constant while the water produces different distortions over time.

The method uses two neural fields. One predicts surface height at each position and time; the other predicts the underlying image's color at each position. Together, they reconstruct the observed image sequence. Training can therefore use the observations themselves as the reconstruction target, allowing the model to learn without supervised image-restoration examples.

The authors find that SIREN networks, which use periodic activation functions, effectively represent both the changing surface height and the derivatives needed for image reconstruction. Tests on simulated and real data outperform the latest unsupervised restoration approach in the reported comparison. The method also estimates the water surface, connecting image recovery to an explicit account of the physical distortion that produced the observations.
summary.tldr: Two neural fields jointly recover a constant underwater image and a changing water surface by reconstructing observed distorted frames.

title: Looking Into the Water by Unsupervised Learning of the Surface Shape

abstract: Recent studies have demonstrated the efficacy of using Reinforcement Learning (RL) in building reasoning models that articulate chains of thoughts prior to producing final answers. However, despite ongoing advances that aim at enabling reasoning for vision-language tasks, existing open-source visual reasoning models typically generate reasoning content with pure natural language, lacking explicit integration of visual information. This limits their ability to produce clearly articulated and visually grounded reasoning chains. To this end, we propose Grounded Reasoning with Images and Texts (GRIT), a novel method for training MLLMs to think with images. GRIT introduces a grounded reasoning paradigm, in which models generate reasoning chains that interleave natural language and explicit bounding box coordinates. These coordinates point to regions of the input image that the model consults during its reasoning process. Additionally, GRIT is equipped with a reinforcement learning approach, GRPO-GR, built upon the GRPO algorithm. GRPO-GR employs robust rewards focused on the final answer accuracy and format of the grounded reasoning output, which eliminates the need for data with reasoning chain annotations or explicit bounding box labels. As a result, GRIT achieves exceptional data efficiency, requiring as few as 20 image-question-answer triplets from existing datasets. Comprehensive evaluations demonstrate that GRIT effectively trains MLLMs to produce coherent and visually grounded reasoning chains, showing a successful unification of reasoning and grounding abilities. All code, data, and checkpoints will be released.

paragraphs: Visual reasoning models often explain their answers entirely in words, leaving the image regions they consult implicit. GRIT trains multimodal language models to combine written reasoning with explicit references to the input image. Its reasoning chains interleave text and bounding box coordinates, connecting steps in the explanation to particular visual regions.

The training method, GRPO-GR, builds on the GRPO reinforcement learning algorithm. Its rewards emphasize final-answer correctness and the required grounded reasoning format. This avoids requiring training examples annotated with complete reasoning chains or explicit bounding box labels. The model instead learns from image–question–answer triplets while being rewarded for producing answers and reasoning in the intended form.

The authors report that training can work with as few as twenty such triplets from existing datasets. Their evaluations show coherent reasoning chains that incorporate visual grounding, supporting the possibility of learning both abilities together with little annotated task data. The contribution is a training approach and output format that make visual references explicit within the reasoning process.
summary.tldr: GRIT uses reinforcement learning to teach multimodal models to interleave textual reasoning with image-region coordinates using sparse answer-level supervision.

title: GRIT: Teaching MLLMs to Think with Images

abstract: Few-shot segmentation aims to segment unseen categories from just a handful of annotated examples. This requires mechanisms to identify semantically related objects across images and accurately produce masks. We note that Segment Anything 2 (SAM2), with its prompt-and-propagate mechanism, provides strong segmentation capabilities and a built-in feature matching process. However, we show that its representations are entangled with task-specific cues optimized for object tracking, which impairs its use for tasks requiring higher level semantic understanding. Our key insight is that, despite its class-agnostic pretraining, SAM2 already encodes rich semantic structure in its features. We propose SANSA (Semantically AligNed Segment Anything 2), a framework that makes this latent structure explicit, and repurposes SAM2 for few-shot segmentation through minimal task-specific modifications. SANSA achieves state-of-the-art on few-shot segmentation benchmarks designed to assess generalization and outperforms generalist methods in the popular in-context setting. Additionally, it supports flexible promptable interaction via points, boxes, or scribbles, and remains significantly faster and more compact than prior approaches. Code at: https://github.com/ClaudiaCuttano/SANSA.

paragraphs: Few-shot segmentation asks a model to outline objects from previously unseen categories using only a few annotated examples. Success requires matching objects by semantic meaning across images and producing accurate masks. SAM2 already offers strong mask generation and feature matching, making it a useful starting point for this task.

The authors find that SAM2’s features contain rich semantic information despite class-agnostic pretraining. However, this information is mixed with cues tailored to object tracking, which hinders tasks requiring higher-level semantic understanding. SANSA makes the existing semantic structure explicit and adapts SAM2 for few-shot segmentation with minimal task-specific changes.

SANSA reports state-of-the-art results on few-shot benchmarks designed to test generalization and outperforms generalist methods in the in-context setting. It also supports interaction through points, boxes, and scribbles, while being substantially faster and more compact than prior approaches. The findings show that making existing semantics accessible can extend a segmentation model’s capabilities without requiring a large task-specific redesign.
summary.tldr: SANSA exposes semantic structure already present in SAM2 to enable efficient segmentation of unseen categories from a few examples.

title: SANSA: Unleashing the Hidden Semantics in SAM2 for Few-Shot Segmentation

abstract: In this work, we present GPDiT, a Generative Pre-trained Autoregressive Diffusion Transformer that unifies the strengths of diffusion and autoregressive modeling for long-range video synthesis, within a continuous latent space. Instead of predicting discrete tokens, GPDiT autoregressively predicts future latent frames using a diffusion loss, enabling natural modeling of motion dynamics and semantic consistency across frames. This continuous autoregressive framework not only enhances generation quality but also endows the model with representation capabilities. Additionally, we introduce a lightweight causal attention variant and a parameter-free rotation-based time-conditioning mechanism, improving both the training and inference efficiency. Extensive experiments demonstrate that GPDiT achieves strong performance in video generation quality, video representation ability, and few-shot learning tasks, highlighting its potential as an effective framework for video modeling in continuous space.

paragraphs: Long-range video synthesis requires a model to generate new content while maintaining motion and meaning across successive frames. GPDiT combines autoregressive modeling, which predicts future frames from earlier context, with diffusion-based learning. It carries out this process in a continuous latent space, where frames have numerical representations rather than discrete token identities.

The model predicts future latent frames autoregressively using a diffusion loss. This connects sequential prediction with a training objective suited to continuous generation, supporting motion dynamics and semantic consistency. The authors also introduce a lightweight causal attention mechanism and time conditioning based on rotations that adds no parameters. Both changes are intended to improve training and inference efficiency.

Experiments report strong results in video generation, video representation, and learning from few examples. The representation findings matter because they indicate that the framework learns useful video features alongside its generative ability. Taken together, the results support continuous autoregressive diffusion as a promising framework for video modeling across generation and representation tasks.
summary.tldr: GPDiT combines autoregressive frame prediction with diffusion learning in continuous latent space for video generation and representation.

title: Generative Pre-trained Autoregressive Diffusion Transformer

abstract: Neurosymbolic (NeSy) predictors combine neural perception with symbolic reasoning to solve tasks like visual reasoning. However, standard NeSy predictors assume conditional independence between the symbols they extract, thus limiting their ability to model interactions and uncertainty --- often leading to overconfident predictions and poor out-of-distribution generalisation. To overcome the limitations of the independence assumption, we introduce _neurosymbolic diffusion models_ (NeSyDMs), a new class of NeSy predictors that use discrete diffusion to model dependencies between symbols. Our approach reuses the independence assumption from NeSy predictors at each step of the diffusion process, enabling scalable learning while capturing symbol dependencies and uncertainty quantification. Across both synthetic and real-world benchmarks — including high-dimensional visual path planning and rule-based autonomous driving — NeSyDMs achieve state-of-the-art accuracy among NeSy predictors and demonstrate strong calibration.

paragraphs: Neurosymbolic predictors combine neural perception with symbolic reasoning. A common simplification assumes that extracted symbols are conditionally independent, even when they interact. The paper argues that this limits the representation of uncertainty and dependencies, contributing to overconfident predictions and poor generalization outside the training distribution.

Neurosymbolic diffusion models address the issue by modeling symbols through a discrete diffusion process. Each individual step retains the independence assumption used by conventional predictors, keeping learning scalable. Across the sequence of steps, however, the model captures dependencies between symbols. This separates the computational convenience of a local assumption from the richer relationships represented by the overall process.

Experiments span synthetic and real-world benchmarks, including high-dimensional visual path planning and rule-based autonomous driving. The models achieve state-of-the-art accuracy among the neurosymbolic predictors evaluated and show strong calibration, meaning their confidence better reflects predictive reliability. The contribution is a way to combine scalable symbol prediction with joint dependency modeling and uncertainty quantification within the same neurosymbolic framework.
summary.tldr: Neurosymbolic diffusion models capture symbol dependencies across discrete diffusion steps, improving accuracy and confidence calibration.

title: Neurosymbolic Diffusion Models

abstract: LLMs have demonstrated unprecedented capabilities in natural language processing, yet their practical deployment remains hindered by persistent factuality and faithfulness hallucinations. While existing methods address these hallucination types independently, they inadvertently induce performance trade-offs, as interventions targeting one type often exacerbate the other. Through empirical and theoretical analysis of activation space dynamics in LLMs, we reveal that these hallucination categories share overlapping subspaces within neural representations, presenting an opportunity for concurrent mitigation. To harness this insight, we propose SPACE, a unified framework that jointly enhances factuality and faithfulness by editing shared activation subspaces. SPACE establishes a geometric foundation for shared subspace existence through dual-task feature modeling, then identifies and edits these subspaces via a hybrid probe strategy combining spectral clustering and attention head saliency scoring. Experimental results across multiple benchmark datasets demonstrate the superiority of our approach.
originalAbstract: LLMs have demonstrated unprecedented capabilities in natural language processing, yet their practical deployment remains hindered by persistent factuality and faithfulness hallucinations. While existing methods address these hallucination types independently, they inadvertently induce performance trade-offs, as interventions targeting one type often exacerbate the other. Through empirical and theoretical analysis of activation space dynamics in LLMs, we reveal that these hallucination categories share overlapping subspaces within neural representations, presenting an opportunity for concurrent mitigation. To harness this insight, we propose SPACE, a unified framework that jointly enhances factuality and faithfulness by editing shared activation subspaces. SPACE establishes a geometric foundation for shared subspace existence through dual-task feature modeling, then identifies and edits these subspaces via a hybrid probe strategy combining spectral clustering and attention head saliency scoring. Experimental results across multiple benchmark datasets demonstrate the superiority of our approach.

paragraphs: This paper addresses two forms of language-model hallucination: failures of factual correctness and failures to remain faithful to the information being used. Methods that target these problems separately can create trade-offs, improving one while worsening the other. The authors investigate whether the model's internal representations offer a common point of intervention.

Their empirical and theoretical analysis finds overlapping activation subspaces associated with the two hallucination categories. SPACE builds on this overlap by editing shared subspaces to improve both properties together. It uses dual-task feature modeling to establish a geometric foundation for their existence, then combines spectral clustering with attention-head saliency scoring to identify and edit them.

Experiments across multiple benchmarks report superior results for this unified approach. The significance is that the two problems need not always be treated as independent targets: shared internal structure can provide an opportunity for concurrent mitigation. SPACE turns that observation into a concrete intervention strategy, linking an analysis of activation geometry to changes intended to improve both factuality and faithfulness.
summary.tldr: SPACE edits shared activation subspaces to jointly reduce factuality and faithfulness hallucinations, addressing trade-offs from separate interventions.

title: One SPACE to Rule Them All: Jointly Mitigating Factuality and Faithfulness Hallucinations in LLMs

abstract: This paper investigates the role of explicit thinking process in rule-based reinforcement fine-tuning (RFT) for multi-modal large language models (MLLMs). We first extend \textit{Thinking-RFT} to image classification task, using verifiable rewards for fine-tuning~(FT). Experiments show {Thinking-RFT} significantly outperforms supervised FT and yields a cross-dataset generalization effect. We then rethink and question whether explicit thinking in RFT is always necessary and beneficial. Challenging the convention that explicit thinking is crucial for the success of RFT, we introduce \textit{No-Thinking-RFT}, exploring RFT without thinking by introducing a simple equality accuracy reward. We evaluate No-Thinking-RFT on six diverse tasks across different model sizes and types. Experiment results reveal four key findings: \textbf{(1).} Visual perception tasks do not require thinking during RFT, as No-Thinking-RFT consistently outperforms or matches Thinking-RFT across model sizes and types. \textbf{(2).} Models with limited capabilities struggle to generate high-quality CoT for RFT, making Thinking-RFT less effective than No-Thinking-RFT. \textbf{(3).} There are inconsistencies between the answers in the thinking tags and answer tags for some responses of Thinking-RFT, which show lower average accuracy than the overall accuracy. \textbf{(4).} The performance gain of No-Thinking-RFT mainly stems from improved learning during no thinking FT and the avoidance of inference overthinking, as evidenced by the partial gains from appending empty thinking tags at inference time of Thinking-RFT. We hypothesize that explicit thinking before verifiable answers may hinder reward convergence and reduce performance in certain scenarios. To test this, we propose \textit{Think-After-Answer}, which places thinking after the answer to mitigate this effect for experimental verification. Lastly, we conduct a pilot study to explore whether MLLMs can learn when to think during RFT, introducing an \textit{Adaptive-Thinking} method. Experiments show that model converges to either thinking or not depending on model capability, achieving comparable or better performance than both Thinking and No-Thinking-RFT. Our findings suggest MLLMs can adaptively decide to think or not based on their capabilities and task complexity, offering insights into the thinking process in RFT.

A pilot Adaptive-Thinking method learns to think or refrain depending on model capability, reaching comparable or better performance than either fixed strategy. The findings suggest that explicit reasoning should depend on capabilities and task complexity.
summary.tldr: Explicit reasoning does not consistently help visual reinforcement fine-tuning, and a pilot adaptive method learns whether to use it.

title: To Think or Not To Think: A Study of Thinking in Rule-Based Visual Reinforcement Fine-Tuning

abstract: The growing prevalence of streaming data and increasing concerns over data privacy pose significant challenges for traditional nonparametric regression methods, which are often ill-suited for real-time, privacy-aware learning. In this paper, we tackle these issues by first proposing a novel one-pass online functional stochastic gradient descent algorithm that leverages the Huber loss (H-FSGD), to improve robustness against outliers and heavy-tailed errors in dynamic environments. To further accommodate privacy constraints, we introduce a locally differentially private extension, Private H-FSGD (PH-FSGD), designed to real-time, privacy-preserving estimation. Theoretically, we conduct a comprehensive non-asymptotic convergence analysis of the proposed estimators, establishing finite-sample guarantees and identifying optimal step size schedules that achieve optimal convergence rates. In particular, we provide practical insights into the impact of key hyperparameters, such as step size and privacy budget, on convergence behavior. Extensive experiments validate our theoretical findings, demonstrating that our methods achieve strong robustness and privacy protection without sacrificing efficiency.

paragraphs: This paper combines three requirements for regression: learning from a stream, resisting unreliable observations, and protecting privacy. Traditional nonparametric regression methods can be poorly suited to this combination, especially when data must be processed as they arrive. The authors develop an online method that needs only one pass through the observations.

Their H-FSGD algorithm uses functional stochastic gradient descent with the Huber loss to improve robustness to outliers and heavy-tailed errors. A second version, PH-FSGD, adds local differential privacy for real-time private estimation. These versions address the robustness and privacy requirements within the same overall approach to sequential learning.

The theoretical analysis provides finite-sample convergence guarantees and identifies step-size schedules achieving optimal convergence rates. It also examines how step size and privacy budget affect convergence, connecting practical tuning decisions to statistical behavior. Experiments support the analysis and report strong robustness and privacy protection while retaining efficiency. The contribution is therefore both an online learning procedure and an account of how its central parameters govern performance under the studied conditions.
summary.tldr: H-FSGD and its private extension provide one-pass robust regression with finite-sample guarantees and guidance on learning-rate and privacy choices.

title: Online robust locally differentially private learning for nonparametric regression

abstract: This paper describes a new online convex optimization method which incorporates a family of candidate dynamical models and establishes novel tracking regret bounds that scale with comparator’s deviation from the best dynamical model in this family. Previous online optimization methods are designed to have a total accumulated loss comparable to that of the best comparator sequence, and existing tracking or shifting regret bounds scale with the overall variation of the comparator sequence. In many practical scenarios, however, the environment is nonstationary and comparator sequences with small variation are quite weak, resulting in large losses. The proposed dynamic mirror descent method, in contrast, can yield low regret relative to highly variable comparator sequences by both tracking the best dynamical model and forming predictions based on that model. This concept is demonstrated empirically in the context of sequential compressive observations of a dynamic scene and tracking a dynamic social network.

paragraphs: Online optimization evaluates a learner by comparing its accumulated loss with that of a reference sequence of decisions. Existing tracking-regret bounds often grow with how much that sequence changes. In a nonstationary environment, however, a useful reference may need to change substantially, making low-variation comparisons a poor reflection of the task.

The paper introduces dynamic mirror descent with a family of candidate dynamical models. The method tracks a suitable model and uses it to form predictions. Its regret bounds depend on how far the comparator departs from the best dynamics in the family, shifting attention from the total amount of change to how well that change follows a model.

This distinction allows low regret relative to highly variable comparator sequences when their evolution is sufficiently well captured by the candidate dynamics. The authors demonstrate the idea using sequential compressive observations of a changing scene and tracking a dynamic social network. The contribution is a way to exploit predictable structure within nonstationarity.
summary.tldr: Dynamic mirror descent bounds tracking regret through mismatch with candidate dynamical models, allowing meaningful comparisons with rapidly changing reference sequences.

title: Dynamical Models and tracking regret in online convex programming

abstract: In real crowdsourcing applications, each label from a crowd usually comes with a certain cost. Given a pre- fixed amount of budget, since different tasks have different ambiguities and different workers have different expertises, we want to find an optimal way to allocate the budget among instance-worker pairs such that the overall label quality can be maximized. To address this issue, we start from the simplest setting in which all workers are assumed to be perfect. We formulate the problem as a Bayesian Markov Decision Process (MDP). Using the dynamic programming (DP) algorithm, one can obtain the optimal allocation policy for a given budget. However, DP is computationally intractable. To solve the computational challenge, we propose a novel approximate policy which is called optimistic knowledge gradient. It is practically efficient while theoretically its consistency can be guaranteed. We then extend the MDP framework to deal with inhomogeneous workers and tasks with contextual information available. The experiments on both simulated and real data demonstrate the superiority of our method.

paragraphs: Crowdsourced labels cost money, and a fixed budget must be divided among tasks and workers. Tasks differ in ambiguity, while workers differ in expertise, so choosing which instance-worker pair to fund affects overall label quality. This paper treats that allocation as a sequential decision problem in which each purchased label informs later choices.

The authors begin with a setting that assumes perfect workers and formulate allocation as a Bayesian Markov decision process. Dynamic programming can produce an optimal policy for a specified budget, but it is computationally intractable. The proposed optimistic knowledge gradient policy supplies a practically efficient approximation with a theoretical consistency guarantee.

The framework is then extended to heterogeneous workers and tasks with contextual information. These extensions bring worker differences and task descriptions into the allocation problem. Experiments on simulated and real data report superior performance for the proposed method. The contribution combines a formal account of optimal budget allocation with an approximation that makes sequential allocation practical.
summary.tldr: An optimistic knowledge gradient policy efficiently approximates Bayesian budget allocation for crowdsourced labeling.

title: Optimistic Knowledge Gradient Policy for Optimal Budget Allocation in Crowdsourcing

abstract: Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods are often deemed far too computationally intensive to be of any practical use for large datasets. This paper describes a methodology that aims to scale up the Metropolis-Hastings (MH) algorithm in this context. We propose an approximate implementation of the accept/reject step of MH that only requires evaluating the likelihood of a random subset of the data, yet is guaranteed to coincide with the accept/reject step based on the full dataset with a probability superior to a user-specified tolerance level. This adaptive subsampling technique is an alternative to the recent approach developed in (Korattikara et al, ICML’14), and it allows us to establish rigorously that the resulting approximate MH algorithm samples from a perturbed version of the target distribution of interest, whose total variation distance to this very target is controlled explicitly. We explore the benefits and limitations of this scheme on several examples.

paragraphs: Metropolis-Hastings sampling can become expensive on large datasets because its accept-or-reject decision requires likelihood evaluation across the data. This paper proposes an approximate version of that decision using a random subset. Adaptive subsampling aims to reduce the amount of data processed while retaining explicit probabilistic control over the decision.

The method guarantees that the subsampled decision agrees with the full-data decision with probability above a user-specified tolerance level. This is a probability guarantee, so disagreement remains possible. The authors also establish a distribution-level result: the approximate algorithm samples from a perturbed target distribution whose total variation distance from the intended target is explicitly controlled.

These two guarantees connect a local computational shortcut to its effect on the sampling distribution. The paper examines benefits and limitations through several examples. Its contribution is therefore a controlled approximation to Metropolis-Hastings, giving a way to reason about both reduced likelihood computation and the distributional error introduced by using only part of the data.
summary.tldr: Adaptive subsampling reduces Metropolis-Hastings likelihood work while explicitly controlling decision agreement and deviation from the target distribution.

title: Towards scaling up Markov chain Monte Carlo: an adaptive subsampling approach

abstract: Dimensionality reduction techniques extract low-dimensional structure from high-dimensional data and are widespread in machine learning research. In practice, due to lacking labeled data, the unsupervised dimensionality reduction algorithms are more desired. Among them, Principal Component Analysis (PCA) is the most widely used approach. In recent research, several robust PCA algorithms were presented to enhance the robustness of PCA model. However, all existing robust PCA methods incorrectly center the data using the L2-norm distance to calculate the mean, which actually is not the optimal mean due to the L1-norm used in the objective functions. It is non-trivial to remove the optimal mean in the robust PCA, because of the sparsity-inducing norms used in the robust formulations. In this paper, we propose novel robust PCA objective functions with removing optimal mean automatically. We naturally integrate the mean calculation into the dimensionality reduction optimization, such that the optimal mean can be obtained to enhance the dimensionality reduction. Both theoretical analysis and empirical studies demonstrate our new methods can more effectively reduce data dimensionality than previous robust PCA methods.

paragraphs: Principal component analysis reduces the number of dimensions needed to represent data, and robust variants seek to make that representation less sensitive to problematic observations. This paper identifies a mismatch in the robust PCA methods it discusses: they center data using an L2-based mean even though their objectives use an L1 norm.

The center that suits one distance measure need not be optimal for another. Consequently, calculating the center separately can leave the dimensionality reduction procedure working around a point that does not fit its own objective. The paper proposes robust PCA objectives that incorporate calculation of the mean directly into the dimensionality reduction optimization.

This joint treatment allows the optimal mean to be determined and removed as part of fitting the representation. The authors emphasize that sparsity-inducing norms make this integration nontrivial. Their theoretical analysis and empirical studies show more effective dimensionality reduction than previous robust PCA methods. The contribution is to make centering consistent with the robust objective being optimized.
summary.tldr: Jointly optimizing the data center and robust PCA representation resolves an objective mismatch and improves dimensionality reduction in the reported analysis and experiments.

title: Optimal Mean Robust Principal Component Analysis

abstract: We propose minimum regret search (MRS), a novel acquisition function for Bayesian optimization. MRS bears similarities with information-theoretic approaches such as entropy search (ES). However, while ES aims in each query at maximizing the information gain with respect to the global maximum, MRS aims at minimizing the expected simple regret of its ultimate recommendation for the optimum. While empirically ES and MRS perform similar in most of the cases, MRS produces fewer outliers with high simple regret than ES. We provide empirical results both for a synthetic single-task optimization problem as well as for a simulated multi-task robotic control problem.

paragraphs: Bayesian optimization must decide which evaluation to request next before ultimately recommending a solution. This paper proposes minimum regret search, an acquisition function that makes those evaluation decisions with the final recommendation in mind. Its objective is to minimize expected simple regret, meaning the performance shortfall of the recommended solution relative to the optimum.

The method is closely related to information-based approaches such as entropy search, but the objectives differ. Entropy search chooses queries to gain information about the global maximum. Minimum regret search instead values queries according to their effect on the expected quality of the eventual recommendation. This connects the sampling decision directly to the outcome the optimization procedure will deliver.

Experiments cover a synthetic single-task problem and a simulated robotic control problem involving multiple tasks. The two methods perform similarly in most evaluated cases, but minimum regret search produces fewer outliers with high simple regret. The reported advantage therefore concerns reducing particularly poor recommendations, rather than a broad claim that it improves every optimization run.
summary.tldr: Minimum regret search chooses evaluations to improve the final recommendation and empirically produces fewer high-regret outliers than entropy search.

title: Minimum Regret Search for Single- and Multi-Task Optimization

abstract: This paper solves a specialized regression problem to obtain sampling probabilities for records in databases. The goal is to sample a small set of records over which evaluating aggregate queries can be done both efficiently and accurately. We provide a principled and provable solution for this problem; it is parameterless and requires no data insights. Unlike standard regression problems, the loss is inversely proportional to the regressed-to values. Moreover, a cost zero solution always exists and can only be excluded by hard budget constraints. A unique form of regularization is also needed. We provide an efficient and simple regularized Empirical Risk Minimization (ERM) algorithm along with a theoretical generalization result. Our extensive experimental results significantly improve over both uniform sampling and standard stratified sampling which are de-facto the industry standards.

paragraphs: The paper learns sampling probabilities for database records so that aggregate queries can be evaluated accurately and efficiently on a small sample. This turns sample construction into a specialized regression problem. The proposed solution is parameterless and does not require prior insights into the data.

The optimization differs from ordinary regression in several ways. Its loss is inversely proportional to the predicted values, a zero-cost solution must be ruled out through hard budget constraints, and a distinctive form of regularization is required. These features make the sampling budget and regularization central parts of the formulation rather than optional additions.

The authors develop a simple, efficient algorithm based on regularized empirical risk minimization and provide a theoretical generalization result. Extensive experiments show significant improvements over uniform sampling and standard stratified sampling. The contribution is a principled way to learn which records deserve sampling probability under a limited budget, with both formal support and evidence of better query-oriented sampling in the reported evaluations.
summary.tldr: A specialized regression method learns database sampling probabilities under a hard budget and significantly improves on standard sampling methods in experiments.

title: Stratified Sampling Meets Machine Learning

abstract: This paper considers the problem of canonical-correlation analysis (CCA) and, more broadly, the generalized eigenvector problem for a pair of symmetric matrices. These are two fundamental problems in data analysis and scientific computing with numerous applications in machine learning and statistics. We provide simple iterative algorithms, with improved runtimes, for solving these problems that are globally linearly convergent with moderate dependencies on the condition numbers and eigenvalue gaps of the matrices involved. We obtain our results by reducing CCA to the top-k generalized eigenvector problem. We solve this problem through a general framework that simply requires black box access to an approximate linear system solver. Instantiating this framework with accelerated gradient descent we obtain a running time of \order\fracz k \sqrtκρ \log(1/ε) \log \left(kκ/ρ\right) where z is the total number of nonzero entries, κis the condition number and ρis the relative eigenvalue gap of the appropriate matrices. Our algorithm is linear in the input size and the number of components k up to a \log(k) factor. This is essential for handling large-scale matrices that appear in practice. To the best of our knowledge this is the first such algorithm with global linear convergence. We hope that our results prompt further research and ultimately improve the practical running time for performing these important data analysis procedures on large data sets.

paragraphs: The paper develops faster iterative algorithms for canonical correlation analysis and the generalized eigenvector problem involving two symmetric matrices. These computations are important in data analysis and scientific computing, but large matrices make runtime a central concern. The authors focus on convergence guarantees together with favorable scaling in the input size.

They reduce canonical correlation analysis to computing the top k generalized eigenvectors. A general solution framework then needs only access to an approximate linear-system solver as a black box. This modular reduction makes solving linear systems the computational building block for the broader eigenvector and correlation problems.

Using accelerated gradient descent within the framework gives a runtime linear in the number of nonzero input entries and nearly linear in the number of requested components. The algorithms have global linear convergence, with dependencies on matrix condition numbers and eigenvalue gaps. Here, linear convergence describes geometric progress toward accuracy. The contribution establishes theoretical runtime and convergence improvements; the authors frame improved practical performance on large datasets as a hoped-for consequence.
summary.tldr: A framework based on approximate linear-system solves yields globally linearly convergent algorithms for generalized eigenvectors and canonical correlation analysis.

title: Efficient Algorithms for Large-scale Generalized Eigenvector Computation and Canonical Correlation Analysis

abstract: In this paper, we explore theoretical properties of training a two-layered ReLU network $g(\mathbf{x}; \mathbf{w}) = \sum_{j=1}^K \sigma(\mathbf{w}_j^\top\mathbf{x})$ with centered $d$-dimensional spherical Gaussian input $\mathbf{x}$ ($\sigma$=ReLU). We train our network with gradient descent on $\mathbf{w}$ to mimic the output of a teacher network with the same architecture and fixed parameters $\mathbf{w}^*$. We show that its population gradient has an analytical formula, leading to interesting theoretical analysis of critical points and convergence behaviors. First, we prove that critical points outside the hyperplane spanned by the teacher parameters (“out-of-plane“) are not isolated and form manifolds, and characterize in-plane critical-point-free regions for two-ReLU case. On the other hand, convergence to $\mathbf{w}^*$ for one ReLU node is guaranteed with at least $(1-\epsilon)/2$ probability, if weights are initialized randomly with standard deviation upper-bounded by $O(\epsilon/\sqrt{d})$, in accordance with empirical practice. For network with many ReLU nodes, we prove that an infinitesimal perturbation of weight initialization results in convergence towards $\mathbf{w}^*$ (or its permutation), a phenomenon known as spontaneous symmetric-breaking (SSB) in physics. We assume no independence of ReLU activations. Simulation verifies our findings.

paragraphs: This paper studies a two-layer ReLU network trained to reproduce a fixed teacher network with the same architecture. Inputs follow a centered spherical Gaussian distribution. The authors derive an analytical expression for the population gradient, making it possible to examine training behavior through an explicit mathematical formula.

The formula reveals structure in the critical points. Points outside the hyperplane spanned by the teacher weights occur in continuous families rather than as isolated points. For two ReLU units, the analysis also identifies regions within that hyperplane containing no critical points. These results describe different parts of the optimization landscape without assuming independent ReLU activations.

For multiple units, the authors prove a convergence result involving an infinitesimal perturbation of initialization, interpreted as spontaneous symmetry breaking. Simulations support the findings. The conclusions therefore connect initialization and convergence within the stated Gaussian teacher–student setting.
summary.tldr: An explicit population-gradient formula reveals critical-point structure and conditional convergence behavior for Gaussian-input ReLU teacher–student networks.

title: An Analytical Formula of Population Gradient for two-layered ReLU network and its Applications in Convergence and Critical Point Analysis

abstract: Deep multitask networks, in which one neural network produces multiple predictive outputs, can offer better speed and performance than their single-task counterparts but are challenging to train properly. We present a gradient normalization (GradNorm) algorithm that automatically balances training in deep multitask models by dynamically tuning gradient magnitudes. We show that for various network architectures, for both regression and classification tasks, and on both synthetic and real datasets, GradNorm improves accuracy and reduces overfitting across multiple tasks when compared to single-task networks, static baselines, and other adaptive multitask loss balancing techniques. GradNorm also matches or surpasses the performance of exhaustive grid search methods, despite only involving a single asymmetry hyperparameter $\alpha$. Thus, what was once a tedious search process that incurred exponentially more compute for each task added can now be accomplished within a few training runs, irrespective of the number of tasks. Ultimately, we will demonstrate that gradient manipulation affords us great control over the training dynamics of multitask networks and may be one of the keys to unlocking the potential of multitask learning.

paragraphs: A multitask neural network produces several predictions from one model, potentially improving speed and predictive performance. Training is difficult because the tasks must share a learning process. GradNorm addresses this coordination problem by automatically balancing training through adjustments to gradient magnitudes.

The method dynamically tunes those magnitudes instead of leaving task balance fixed throughout training. It has one asymmetry hyperparameter, alpha. This makes the approach appealing when manually searching over combinations of task weights would require an increasingly expensive collection of training runs as more tasks are added.

Across the evaluated architectures, regression and classification tasks, and synthetic and real datasets, GradNorm improves accuracy and reduces overfitting relative to single-task networks, static alternatives, and other adaptive balancing methods. It also matches or exceeds exhaustive grid search performance in the reported comparisons. The findings support gradient manipulation as a practical means of controlling multitask training, with the paper describing a few training runs as sufficient regardless of task count.
summary.tldr: GradNorm dynamically balances multitask gradient magnitudes, improving reported accuracy while reducing the need for expensive task-weight searches.

title: GradNorm: Gradient Normalization for Adaptive Loss Balancing in Deep Multitask Networks

abstract: Over the course of the past decade, a variety of randomized algorithms have been proposed for computing approximate least-squares (LS) solutions in large-scale settings. A longstanding practical issue is that, for any given input, the user rarely knows the actual error of an approximate solution (relative to the exact solution). Likewise, it is difficult for the user to know precisely how much computation is needed to achieve the desired error tolerance. Consequently, the user often appeals to worst-case error bounds that tend to offer only qualitative guidance. As a more practical alternative, we propose a bootstrap method to compute a posteriori error estimates for randomized LS algorithms. These estimates permit the user to numerically assess the error of a given solution, and to predict how much work is needed to improve a "preliminary" solution. In addition, we provide theoretical consistency results for the method, which are the first such results in this context (to the best of our knowledge). From a practical standpoint, the method also has considerable flexibility, insofar as it can be applied to several popular sketching algorithms, as well as a variety of error metrics. Moreover, the extra step of error estimation does not add much cost to an underlying sketching algorithm. Finally, we demonstrate the effectiveness of the method with empirical results.

paragraphs: Randomized least-squares algorithms make large problems more manageable by computing approximate solutions. A practical difficulty remains: users often cannot tell how far a particular approximation is from the exact solution or how much additional computation would meet their accuracy target. Worst-case bounds may provide only broad guidance for that specific input.

This paper proposes a bootstrap method for estimating error after an approximate solution has been computed. These a posteriori estimates let users assess a solution numerically and predict the work needed to improve a preliminary result. The method thus connects an existing approximate answer with a practical decision about whether further computation is worthwhile.

The authors establish theoretical consistency results and demonstrate effectiveness empirically. They also emphasize flexibility: the method applies to several popular sketching algorithms and multiple error measures, rather than depending on a single solver or definition of accuracy. Its additional computational cost is reported to be small relative to the underlying sketching algorithm. The contribution makes randomized optimization results easier to assess and refine for individual problems.
summary.tldr: A low-overhead bootstrap method estimates the error of randomized least-squares solutions and helps predict the computation needed to improve them.

title: Error Estimation for Randomized Least-Squares Algorithms via the Bootstrap

abstract: Despite the great advances made by deep learning in many machine learning problems, there is a relative dearth of deep learning approaches for anomaly detection. Those approaches which do exist involve networks trained to perform a task other than anomaly detection, namely generative models or compression, which are in turn adapted for use in anomaly detection; they are not trained on an anomaly detection based objective. In this paper we introduce a new anomaly detection method—Deep Support Vector Data Description—, which is trained on an anomaly detection based objective. The adaptation to the deep regime necessitates that our neural network and training procedure satisfy certain properties, which we demonstrate theoretically. We show the effectiveness of our method on MNIST and CIFAR-10 image benchmark datasets as well as on the detection of adversarial examples of GTSRB stop signs.
