paragraphs: A neural network used for anomaly detection may first be trained for a different purpose, such as generating or compressing data. Its outputs are then adapted to identify unusual examples. This paper asks whether the network can instead be trained directly with an objective designed for anomaly detection.

The proposed method, Deep Support Vector Data Description, takes that direct approach. Moving the method into a deep-learning setting requires the network and its training procedure to satisfy particular properties. The authors demonstrate these requirements theoretically, making the design of the network and the way it is trained part of the contribution.

Experiments show the method's effectiveness on MNIST and CIFAR-10, as well as in detecting adversarial examples of stop signs from GTSRB. These demonstrations connect the anomaly-focused objective to both image benchmarks and manipulated inputs. The findings support training specifically for anomaly detection in these settings, with the theoretical work explaining why the deep adaptation requires care.
summary.tldr: Deep Support Vector Data Description trains a neural network directly for anomaly detection and demonstrates effectiveness on image and adversarial-example tasks.

title: Deep One-Class Classification

abstract: We propose a novel distributed inference algorithm for continuous graphical models, by extending Stein variational gradient descent (SVGD) to leverage the Markov dependency structure of the distribution of interest. Our approach combines SVGD with a set of structured local kernel functions defined on the Markov blanket of each node, which alleviates the curse of high dimensionality and simultaneously yields a distributed algorithm for decentralized inference tasks. We justify our method with theoretical analysis and show that the use of local kernels can be viewed as a new type of localized approximation that matches the target distribution on the conditional distributions of each node over its Markov blanket. Our empirical results show that our method outperforms a variety of baselines including standard MCMC and particle message passing methods.

We justify our method with theoretical analysis and show that the use of local kernels can be viewed as a new type of localized approximation that matches the target distribution on the conditional distributions of each node over its Markov blanket. paragraphs: Inference in a continuous graphical model must account for dependencies among variables, potentially in a high-dimensional distribution. This paper extends Stein variational gradient descent so that its computations explicitly use the model's Markov structure. The aim is to reduce difficulties associated with high dimensionality while enabling distributed inference.

The method uses structured local kernel functions defined over each node's Markov blanket, the local collection of variables relevant to its conditional relationships. These local kernels organize the inference procedure around the dependency structure. The resulting algorithm can distribute its computations, making the same design useful for decentralized inference tasks.

The theoretical analysis interprets the method as a localized approximation that matches the target's nodewise conditional distributions over their Markov blankets. This describes the particular probabilistic relationships the approximation preserves. Experiments report improvements over several baselines, including standard MCMC and particle message passing. Together, the analysis and empirical findings support using graphical structure to shape the approximation rather than treating the distribution as an undifferentiated high-dimensional object.
summary.tldr: Local Markov-blanket kernels extend Stein variational inference into a distributed method that alleviates high-dimensional inference difficulties.

title: Stein Variational Message Passing for Continuous Graphical Models

abstract: The iteratively reweighted least squares method (IRLS) is a popular technique used in practice for solving regression problems. Various versions of this method have been proposed, but their theoretical analyses failed to capture the good practical performance. In this paper we propose a simple and natural version of IRLS for solving $\ell_\infty$ and $\ell_1$ regression, which provably converges to a $(1+\epsilon)$-approximate solution in $O(m^{1/3}\log(1/\epsilon)/\epsilon^{2/3} + \log m/\epsilon^2)$ iterations, where $m$ is the number of rows of the input matrix. Interestingly, this running time is independent of the conditioning of the input, and the dominant term of the running time depends sublinearly in $\epsilon^{-1}$, which is atypical for the optimization of non-smooth functions. This improves upon the more complex algorithms of Chin et al. (ITCS ’12), and Christiano et al. (STOC ’11) by a factor of at least $1/\epsilon^2$, and yields a truly efficient natural algorithm for the slime mold dynamics (Straszak-Vishnoi, SODA ’16, ITCS ’16, ITCS ’17).

paragraphs: Iteratively reweighted least squares solves a regression problem through a sequence of weighted least-squares problems. Although widely used in practice, its theoretical analyses had not fully reflected its practical effectiveness. This paper proposes a simple version for l1 regression, which aggregates absolute residuals, and l-infinity regression, which focuses on the largest absolute residual.

The method provably reaches a solution within a multiplicative factor of 1 + epsilon of the optimum. Its iteration bound is O(m^(1/3) log(1/epsilon)/epsilon^(2/3) + log(m)/epsilon^2), where m counts input-matrix rows. The stated running-time guarantee does not depend on input conditioning. The authors also highlight the sublinear dependence on inverse accuracy in the dominant term, an unusual feature for nonsmooth optimization.

The analysis improves on the cited, more complex algorithms by at least a factor of 1/epsilon^2. It also yields an efficient natural algorithm for slime mold dynamics. The contribution is therefore both a simpler regression procedure with stronger convergence guarantees and a connection to another computational process discussed in the paper.
summary.tldr: A simple reweighted least-squares method achieves improved approximation guarantees for l1 and l-infinity regression independently of input conditioning.

title: Improved Convergence for $\ell_1$ and $\ell_∞$ Regression via Iteratively Reweighted Least Squares

abstract: Owing to the extremely high expressive power of deep neural networks, their side effect is to totally memorize training data even when the labels are extremely noisy. To overcome overfitting on the noisy labels, we propose a novel robust training method called SELFIE. Our key idea is to selectively refurbish and exploit unclean samples that can be corrected with high precision, thereby gradually increasing the number of available training samples. Taking advantage of this design, SELFIE effectively prevents the risk of noise accumulation from the false correction and fully exploits the training data. To validate the superiority of SELFIE, we conducted extensive experimentation using four real-world or synthetic data sets. The result showed that SELFIE remarkably improved absolute test error compared with two state-of-the-art methods.

paragraphs: Deep neural networks can memorize training examples even when their labels are highly unreliable. This makes noisy labels a source of overfitting: fitting the supplied answers can reinforce mistakes in the data. SELFIE addresses the problem through a training method that selectively corrects and reuses unclean examples.

Its central idea is to refurbish samples whose labels can be corrected with high precision. As those examples become usable, the available training set grows gradually. Selectivity matters because mistaken corrections can introduce further noise; the method’s design aims to prevent that accumulation while making fuller use of the training data.

The authors evaluate SELFIE on four real-world or synthetic datasets and report substantial improvements in absolute test error compared with two state-of-the-art methods. These findings support the usefulness of recovering selected noisy examples during training. The contribution combines label correction with careful sample reuse, treating the reliability of a correction as important to whether an example should contribute to learning.
summary.tldr: SELFIE selectively corrects and reuses noisy-label examples, expanding usable training data and reducing test error in the reported experiments.

title: SELFIE: Refurbishing Unclean Samples for Robust Deep Learning

abstract: Multi-output Gaussian processes (MOGPs) leverage the flexibility and interpretability of GPs while capturing structure across outputs, which is desirable, for example, in spatio-temporal modelling. The key problem with MOGPs is their computational scaling $O(n^3 p^3)$, which is cubic in the number of both inputs $n$ (e.g., time points or locations) and outputs $p$. For this reason, a popular class of MOGPs assumes that the data live around a low-dimensional linear subspace, reducing the complexity to $O(n^3 m^3)$. However, this cost is still cubic in the dimensionality of the subspace $m$, which is still prohibitively expensive for many applications. We propose the use of a sufficient statistic of the data to accelerate inference and learning in MOGPs with orthogonal bases. The method achieves linear scaling in $m$ in practice, allowing these models to scale to large $m$ without sacrificing significant expressivity or requiring approximation. This advance opens up a wide range of real-world tasks and can be combined with existing GP approximations in a plug-and-play way. We demonstrate the efficacy of the method on various synthetic and real-world data sets.

paragraphs: Multi-output Gaussian processes model related outputs jointly, allowing them to capture shared structure. Their computational cost can be a major obstacle: conventional scaling is cubic in both the number of inputs and outputs. Assuming that observations lie near a lower-dimensional linear subspace reduces the problem, but the remaining cost is still cubic in the subspace dimension.

This paper accelerates inference and learning for models with orthogonal bases by using a sufficient statistic of the data. Such a statistic retains the information needed for the relevant inference. The method achieves linear scaling in the subspace dimension in practice, allowing larger subspaces without requiring an approximation or sacrificing significant expressivity.

The improvement specifically addresses dependence on subspace dimension; it does not claim linear scaling in every aspect of the problem. The authors demonstrate effectiveness on synthetic and real datasets and explain that the method can also be combined with existing Gaussian process approximations. This makes the contribution useful both for exact inference in the stated model class and as a component alongside other approaches to scaling.
summary.tldr: A sufficient-statistic method enables exact inference with practical linear scaling in subspace dimension for multi-output Gaussian processes with orthogonal bases.

title: Scalable Exact Inference in Multi-Output Gaussian Processes

abstract: We consider un-discounted reinforcement learning (RL) in Markov decision processes (MDPs) under drifting non-stationarity, \ie, both the reward and state transition distributions are allowed to evolve over time, as long as their respective total variations, quantified by suitable metrics, do not exceed certain \emph{variation budgets}. We first develop the Sliding Window Upper-Confidence bound for Reinforcement Learning with Confidence Widening (\texttt{SWUCRL2-CW}) algorithm, and establish its dynamic regret bound when the variation budgets are known. In addition, we propose the Bandit-over-Reinforcement Learning (\texttt{BORL}) algorithm to adaptively tune the \sw to achieve the same dynamic regret bound, but in a \emph{parameter-free} manner, \ie, without knowing the variation budgets. Notably, learning drifting MDPs via conventional optimistic exploration presents a unique challenge absent in existing (non-stationary) bandit learning settings. We overcome the challenge by a novel confidence widening technique that incorporates additional optimism.

We first develop the Sliding Window Upper-Confidence bound for Reinforcement Learning with Confidence Widening (\texttt{SWUCRL2-CW}) algorithm, and establish its dynamic regret bound when the variation budgets are known. paragraphs: This paper studies reinforcement learning when both rewards and state transition distributions change over time. The setting is undiscounted, and the total amount of change is bounded by variation budgets. The challenge is to keep learning effectively as the environment drifts, with performance measured through dynamic regret.

The first algorithm, SWUCRL2-CW, combines a sliding window with upper-confidence exploration and a technique called confidence widening. The authors establish a dynamic regret bound when the variation budgets are known. Confidence widening introduces additional optimism to address a difficulty specific to learning drifting Markov decision processes, where conventional optimistic exploration encounters challenges absent from the corresponding bandit setting.

The second algorithm, BORL, adaptively tunes the sliding window without knowing the variation budgets. It achieves the same stated dynamic regret bound in this parameter-free sense. Together, the methods show how additional optimism and adaptive window selection can support learning under bounded environmental drift, including when the amount of drift is not supplied beforehand.
summary.tldr: Confidence widening enables regret guarantees for drifting Markov decision processes, while adaptive window tuning achieves the same bound without knowing the variation budgets.

title: Reinforcement Learning for Non-Stationary Markov Decision Processes: The Blessing of (More) Optimism

abstract: Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) are known to rely more on local texture rather than global shape when making decisions. Recent work also indicates a close relationship between CNN’s texture-bias and its robustness against distribution shift, adversarial perturbation, random corruption, etc. In this work, we attempt at improving various kinds of robustness universally by alleviating CNN’s texture bias. With inspiration from the human visual system, we propose a light-weight model-agnostic method, namely Informative Dropout (InfoDrop), to improve interpretability and reduce texture bias. Specifically, we discriminate texture from shape based on local self-information in an image, and adopt a Dropout-like algorithm to decorrelate the model output from the local texture. Through extensive experiments, we observe enhanced robustness under various scenarios (domain generalization, few-shot classification, image corruption, and adversarial perturbation). To the best of our knowledge, this work is one of the earliest attempts to improve different kinds of robustness in a unified model, shedding new light on the relationship between shape-bias and robustness, also on new approaches to trustworthy machine learning algorithms. Code is available at https://github.com/bfshi/InfoDrop.

paragraphs: Convolutional networks often base decisions more on local texture than on overall shape. This paper investigates whether reducing that preference can improve robustness across several kinds of challenging conditions. Its motivation is the reported relationship between texture dependence and sensitivity to distribution shifts, image corruption, and adversarial perturbations.

The proposed Informative Dropout method uses local self-information in an image to distinguish texture from shape. A dropout-like procedure then reduces the dependence of the model’s output on local texture. The method is described as lightweight and model-agnostic, with the additional aim of improving interpretability. Its central intervention changes which visual information the model is encouraged to rely on.

Experiments report enhanced robustness in domain generalization, few-shot classification, image corruption, and adversarial perturbation scenarios. These observations support investigating shape bias as a shared route toward several kinds of robustness. The paper’s broad aim is a unified improvement, while its stated evidence is empirical improvement across the evaluated scenarios rather than a guarantee covering every possible disturbance.
summary.tldr: InfoDrop reduces CNN reliance on local texture and empirically improves robustness across several types of challenging visual conditions.

title: Informative Dropout for Robust Representation Learning: A Shape-bias Perspective

abstract: Deep neural networks are known to be fragile to small adversarial perturbations, which raises serious concerns when a neural network policy is interconnected with a physical system in a closed loop. In this paper, we show how to combine recent works on static neural network certification tools with robust control theory to certify a neural network policy in a control loop. We give a sufficient condition and an algorithm to ensure that the closed loop state and control constraints are satisfied when the persistent adversarial perturbation is l-infinity norm bounded. Our method is based on finding a positively invariant set of the closed loop dynamical system, and thus we do not require the continuity of the neural network policy. Along with the verification result, we also develop an effective attack strategy for neural network control systems that outperforms exhaustive Monte-Carlo search significantly. We show that our certification algorithm works well on learned models and could achieve 5 times better result than the traditional Lipschitz-based method to certify the robustness of a neural network policy on the cart-pole balance control problem.

paragraphs: A neural network controlling a physical system faces a different robustness question from a predictor used once: disturbances can persist while the controller and system repeatedly influence each other. This paper combines static neural network certification methods with robust control theory to study that closed-loop setting.

The authors give a sufficient condition and an algorithm for certifying that state and control constraints remain satisfied under persistent perturbations bounded in the infinity norm. The approach finds a positively invariant set, meaning a region the closed-loop dynamics continue to stay within. This construction does not require the neural network policy to be continuous.

The paper also develops an attack strategy that substantially outperforms exhaustive Monte Carlo search in the reported evaluation. Its certification algorithm works well on learned models and can achieve a fivefold improvement over a traditional Lipschitz-based method on cart-pole balance control. The certification condition is sufficient, so the result establishes robustness when that condition is met; it does not claim that every robust controller must satisfy it.
summary.tldr: Invariant-set analysis provides sufficient robustness certificates for neural controllers facing persistent infinity-norm-bounded adversarial disturbances.

title: Neural Network Control Policy Verification With Persistent Adversarial Perturbation

abstract: The performance of reinforcement learning depends upon designing an appropriate action space, where the effect of each action is measurable, yet, granular enough to permit flexible behavior. So far, this process involved non-trivial user choices in terms of the available actions and their execution frequency. We propose a novel framework for reinforcement learning that effectively lifts such constraints. Within our framework, agents learn effective behavior over a routine space: a new, higher-level action space, where each routine represents a set of ’equivalent’ sequences of granular actions with arbitrary length. Our routine space is learned end-to-end to facilitate the accomplishment of underlying off-policy reinforcement learning objectives. We apply our framework to two state-of-the-art off-policy algorithms and show that the resulting agents obtain relevant performance improvements while requiring fewer interactions with the environment per episode, improving computational efficiency.

So far, this process involved non-trivial user choices in terms of the available actions and their execution frequency. We propose a novel framework for reinforcement learning that effectively lifts such constraints. Within our framework, agents learn effective behavior over a routine space: a new, higher-level action space, where each routine represents a set of ’equivalent’ sequences of granular actions with arbitrary length. Our routine space is learned end-to-end to facilitate the accomplishment of underlying off-policy reinforcement learning objectives. paragraphs: The actions available to a reinforcement-learning agent shape what it can learn. Actions need effects large enough to evaluate, while retaining enough detail for flexible behavior. Choosing those actions and their execution frequency has traditionally required substantial manual decisions. This paper proposes learning a higher-level action space to reduce that design burden.

The new action space consists of routines. Each routine represents a set of equivalent sequences of granular actions, and those sequences can have arbitrary lengths. The routine space is learned end to end around the underlying off-policy learning objective. This ties the construction of higher-level behavior directly to the task rather than treating action grouping as a separate fixed choice.

The authors apply the framework to two leading off-policy algorithms. The resulting agents show performance improvements while requiring fewer interactions with the environment per episode, improving computational efficiency. These findings support learning the level at which an agent chooses behavior as a useful part of the reinforcement-learning problem itself.
summary.tldr: Agents learn higher-level routines of granular actions, improving off-policy learning performance and reducing interactions per episode.

title: Learning Routines for Effective Off-Policy Reinforcement Learning

abstract: We consider a distributed non-convex optimization where a network of agents aims at minimizing a global function over the Stiefel manifold. The global function is represented as a finite sum of smooth local functions, where each local function is associated with one agent and agents communicate with each other over an undirected connected graph. The problem is non-convex as local functions are possibly non-convex (but smooth) and the Steifel manifold is a non-convex set. We present a decentralized Riemannian stochastic gradient method (DRSGD) with the convergence rate of $\mathcal{O}(1/\sqrt{K})$ to a stationary point. To have exact convergence with constant stepsize, we also propose a decentralized Riemannian gradient tracking algorithm (DRGTA) with the convergence rate of $\mathcal{O}(1/K)$ to a stationary point. We use multi-step consensus to preserve the iteration in the local (consensus) region. DRGTA is the first decentralized algorithm with exact convergence for distributed optimization on Stiefel manifold.
originalAbstract: We consider a distributed non-convex optimization where a network of agents aims at minimizing a global function over the Stiefel manifold. The global function is represented as a finite sum of smooth local functions, where each local function is associated with one agent and agents communicate with each other over an undirected connected graph. The problem is non-convex as local functions are possibly non-convex (but smooth) and the Steifel manifold is a non-convex set. We present a decentralized Riemannian stochastic gradient method (DRSGD) with the convergence rate of $\mathcal{O}(1/\sqrt{K})$ to a stationary point. To have exact convergence with constant stepsize, we also propose a decentralized Riemannian gradient tracking algorithm (DRGTA) with the convergence rate of $\mathcal{O}(1/K)$ to a stationary point. We use multi-step consensus to preserve the iteration in the local (consensus) region. DRGTA is the first decentralized algorithm with exact convergence for distributed optimization on Stiefel manifold.

paragraphs: This paper studies optimization shared across a network of agents when the solution must lie on the Stiefel manifold. Each agent owns a smooth local objective, and together they minimize the sum of those objectives. Communication follows an undirected, connected graph. Both the potentially non-convex objectives and the non-convex constraint set make coordination more difficult.

The authors propose two decentralized methods that account for the geometry of the constraint. Their stochastic gradient method, DRSGD, has a convergence rate of O(1/√K) to a stationary point. Their gradient tracking method, DRGTA, achieves a rate of O(1/K) and supports exact convergence with a constant step size. These are stationary-point guarantees, rather than guarantees of finding a global optimum.

Both methods use multiple consensus steps to keep the iterates within a local region where agents remain sufficiently coordinated. The paper identifies DRGTA as the first decentralized algorithm providing exact convergence for this manifold-constrained distributed problem. Its contribution combines geometric optimization with communication mechanisms that sustain agreement among agents.
summary.tldr: Two decentralized methods provide stationary-point convergence guarantees for distributed optimization on the Stiefel manifold.

title: Decentralized Riemannian Gradient Descent on the Stiefel Manifold

abstract: Convolutional architectures have proven extremely successful for vision tasks. Their hard inductive biases enable sample-efficient learning, but come at the cost of a potentially lower performance ceiling. Vision Transformers (ViTs) rely on more flexible self-attention layers, and have recently outperformed CNNs for image classification. However, they require costly pre-training on large external datasets or distillation from pre-trained convolutional networks. In this paper, we ask the following question: is it possible to combine the strengths of these two architectures while avoiding their respective limitations? To this end, we introduce gated positional self-attention (GPSA), a form of positional self-attention which can be equipped with a “soft" convolutional inductive bias. We initialise the GPSA layers to mimic the locality of convolutional layers, then give each attention head the freedom to escape locality by adjusting a gating parameter regulating the attention paid to position versus content information. The resulting convolutional-like ViT architecture, ConViT, outperforms the DeiT on ImageNet, while offering a much improved sample efficiency. We further investigate the role of locality in learning by first quantifying how it is encouraged in vanilla self-attention layers, then analysing how it is escaped in GPSA layers. We conclude by presenting various ablations to better understand the success of the ConViT. Our code and models are released publicly at https://github.com/facebookresearch/convit.

Each attention head then adjusts a gate that controls the balance between positional information and image content. This lets learning retain locality where it is useful or move beyond it where content-based relationships are more useful.

On ImageNet, ConViT outperforms DeiT and shows substantially improved sample efficiency in the reported experiments. The authors also study how ordinary self-attention encourages locality and how the proposed layers move away from it, alongside ablation experiments examining the architecture. These findings support a soft inductive bias: a useful starting preference that the model can revise during learning.
summary.tldr: ConViT starts transformer attention with a learnable preference for locality, improving ImageNet performance and sample efficiency over DeiT.

title: ConViT: Improving Vision Transformers with Soft Convolutional Inductive Biases

abstract: We propose NeRF-VAE, a 3D scene generative model that incorporates geometric structure via Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) and differentiable volume rendering. In contrast to NeRF, our model takes into account shared structure across scenes, and is able to infer the structure of a novel scene—without the need to re-train—using amortized inference. NeRF-VAE’s explicit 3D rendering process further contrasts previous generative models with convolution-based rendering which lacks geometric structure. Our model is a VAE that learns a distribution over radiance fields by conditioning them on a latent scene representation. We show that, once trained, NeRF-VAE is able to infer and render geometrically-consistent scenes from previously unseen 3D environments of synthetic scenes using very few input images. We further demonstrate that NeRF-VAE generalizes well to out-of-distribution cameras, while convolutional models do not. Finally, we introduce and study an attention-based conditioning mechanism of NeRF-VAE’s decoder, which improves model performance.

Unlike fitting a separate NeRF for each scene, the model learns shared structure across scenes and uses amortized inference to infer a new scene without retraining.

The model is a variational autoencoder whose latent scene representation conditions a radiance field. Learning a distribution over those fields connects variation between scenes with the geometry used to render their images. This is a central distinction from the convolution-based rendering models discussed in the paper, which lack an explicit geometric rendering structure.

On previously unseen synthetic environments, the trained model infers and renders geometrically consistent scenes from very few input images. It also generalizes well to out-of-distribution cameras in the reported comparisons, where convolutional models do not. The findings support combining shared scene learning with explicit geometry for inference across scenes and camera configurations.
summary.tldr: NeRF-VAE learns shared scene structure to infer new synthetic 3D scenes without retraining and render them consistently across camera views.

title: NeRF-VAE: A Geometry Aware 3D Scene Generative Model

abstract: Continuous-time event sequences represent discrete events occurring in continuous time. Such sequences arise frequently in real-life. Usually we expect the sequences to follow some regular pattern over time. However, sometimes these patterns may be interrupted by unexpected absence or occurrences of events. Identification of these unexpected cases can be very important as they may point to abnormal situations that need human attention. In this work, we study and develop methods for detecting outliers in continuous-time event sequences, including unexpected absence and unexpected occurrences of events. Since the patterns that event sequences tend to follow may change in different contexts, we develop outlier detection methods based on point processes that can take context information into account. Our methods are based on Bayesian decision theory and hypothesis testing with theoretical guarantees. To test the performance of the methods, we conduct experiments on both synthetic data and real-world clinical data and show the effectiveness of the proposed methods.

paragraphs: The paper studies anomalies in sequences of discrete events that occur at continuous times. An unusual sequence can contain an unexpected event, but it can also be unusual because an expected event never happens. Detecting both types matters because either may indicate an abnormal situation deserving human attention.

The authors develop methods based on point processes that incorporate context. This allows the expected event pattern to depend on the surrounding circumstances, so the same occurrence or absence need not receive the same assessment everywhere. The methods use Bayesian decision theory and hypothesis testing, giving a principled basis for deciding when event behavior should be flagged.

The paper provides theoretical guarantees and evaluates the methods on synthetic sequences and real-world clinical data, reporting effective detection. Its central contribution is to bring unexpected occurrences and unexpected absences into a context-sensitive detection framework. This broadens the notion of an event outlier beyond unusual recorded events to include meaningful gaps in the sequence.
summary.tldr: Context-aware point-process methods detect both unexpected events and unexpected absences in continuous-time sequences.

title: Event Outlier Detection in Continuous Time

abstract: We study a fundamental problem in computational chemistry known as molecular conformation generation, trying to predict stable 3D structures from 2D molecular graphs. Existing machine learning approaches usually first predict distances between atoms and then generate a 3D structure satisfying the distances, where noise in predicted distances may induce extra errors during 3D coordinate generation. Inspired by the traditional force field methods for molecular dynamics simulation, in this paper, we propose a novel approach called ConfGF by directly estimating the gradient fields of the log density of atomic coordinates. The estimated gradient fields allow directly generating stable conformations via Langevin dynamics. However, the problem is very challenging as the gradient fields are roto-translation equivariant. We notice that estimating the gradient fields of atomic coordinates can be translated to estimating the gradient fields of interatomic distances, and hence develop a novel algorithm based on recent score-based generative models to effectively estimate these gradients. Experimental results across multiple tasks show that ConfGF outperforms previous state-of-the-art baselines by a significant margin.

paragraphs: Molecular conformation generation predicts stable three-dimensional structures from a two-dimensional molecular graph. Existing learning approaches often predict interatomic distances and then construct coordinates that satisfy them. The paper identifies a potential source of additional error in this pipeline: noisy distance predictions can create further errors during coordinate reconstruction.

ConfGF instead learns the gradient of the log probability density over atomic coordinates. This gradient field supplies directions for generating conformations through Langevin dynamics. The field must be equivariant to rotations and translations, so that changing a molecule’s orientation or position changes the predicted directions consistently with its geometry.

The authors show that estimating coordinate gradient fields can be translated into estimating gradient fields over interatomic distances. They use this relationship to develop an algorithm based on score-based generative modeling. Distances therefore help construct the coordinate field rather than serving only as constraints for a separate reconstruction stage. Across multiple evaluated tasks, ConfGF significantly outperforms previous state-of-the-art baselines, supporting this route to generating molecular structures.
summary.tldr: ConfGF learns geometry-consistent gradient fields to generate molecular conformations directly through Langevin dynamics.

title: Learning Gradient Fields for Molecular Conformation Generation

abstract: Recently, neural networks purely based on attention were shown to address image understanding tasks such as image classification. These high-performing vision transformers are pre-trained with hundreds of millions of images using a large infrastructure, thereby limiting their adoption. In this work, we produce competitive convolution-free transformers trained on ImageNet only using a single computer in less than 3 days. Our reference vision transformer (86M parameters) achieves top-1 accuracy of 83.1% (single-crop) on ImageNet with no external data. We also introduce a teacher-student strategy specific to transformers. It relies on a distillation token ensuring that the student learns from the teacher through attention, typically from a convnet teacher. The learned transformers are competitive (85.2% top-1 acc.) with the state of the art on ImageNet, and similarly when transferred to other tasks. We will share our code and models.

This paper demonstrates competitive convolution-free transformers trained using ImageNet alone, on one computer in less than three days. The work addresses the data and infrastructure demands that can make these architectures difficult to adopt.

The reference transformer contains 86 million parameters and reaches 83.1% single-crop top-1 accuracy on ImageNet without external data. The authors also introduce a teacher-student method tailored to transformers. A distillation token allows the student to learn from a teacher through attention, with a convolutional network typically serving as the teacher.

With the proposed approach, the learned transformers reach a reported 85.2% top-1 accuracy and are competitive with state-of-the-art ImageNet methods. They are similarly competitive when transferred to other tasks. The results demonstrate both a more accessible training setup and a way to communicate a teacher's knowledge through the transformer's attention mechanism, while keeping the student architecture convolution-free.
summary.tldr: ImageNet-only training and attention-based distillation produce competitive vision transformers without massive external pretraining datasets.

title: Training data-efficient image transformers & distillation through attention

abstract: Estimating counterfactual outcomes over time has the potential to unlock personalized healthcare by assisting decision-makers to answer "what-if" questions. Existing causal inference approaches typically consider regular, discrete-time intervals between observations and treatment decisions and hence are unable to naturally model irregularly sampled data, which is the common setting in practice. To handle arbitrary observation patterns, we interpret the data as samples from an underlying continuous-time process and propose to model its latent trajectory explicitly using the mathematics of controlled differential equations. This leads to a new approach, the Treatment Effect Neural Controlled Differential Equation (TE-CDE), that allows the potential outcomes to be evaluated at any time point. In addition, adversarial training is used to adjust for time-dependent confounding which is critical in longitudinal settings and is an added challenge not encountered in conventional time series. To assess solutions to this problem, we propose a controllable simulation environment based on a model of tumor growth for a range of scenarios with irregular sampling reflective of a variety of clinical scenarios. TE-CDE consistently outperforms existing approaches in all scenarios with irregular sampling.

paragraphs: Estimating counterfactual outcomes over time means asking how an outcome might evolve under different treatment choices. This is difficult when observations and treatment decisions arrive at irregular times. The paper addresses that timing problem by treating recorded measurements as samples from an underlying continuous process, rather than requiring regularly spaced steps.

The proposed Treatment Effect Neural Controlled Differential Equation, or TE-CDE, explicitly models a latent trajectory using controlled differential equations. This lets the model evaluate potential outcomes at arbitrary time points. It also uses adversarial training to adjust for time-dependent confounding: factors whose relationship with treatment and outcomes changes across a longitudinal record. Handling that issue is central to the causal prediction task.

The authors evaluate the approach in a controllable simulation environment based on tumor growth, with irregular observation patterns representing a variety of clinical scenarios. TE-CDE outperforms the existing approaches in every irregular-sampling scenario examined. The stated evidence therefore supports the method within these simulations, showing how continuous-time modeling can help answer treatment-related questions when measurements do not follow a fixed schedule.
summary.tldr: TE-CDE models treatment counterfactuals in continuous time and outperforms existing approaches across the evaluated irregularly sampled simulations.

title: Continuous-Time Modeling of Counterfactual Outcomes Using Neural Controlled Differential Equations

abstract: Differentially private algorithms for common metric aggregation tasks, such as clustering or averaging, often have limited practicality due to their complexity or to the large number of data points that is required for accurate results. We propose a simple and practical tool $\mathsf{FriendlyCore}$ that takes a set of points ${\cal D}$ from an unrestricted (pseudo) metric space as input. When ${\cal D}$ has effective diameter $r$, $\mathsf{FriendlyCore}$ returns a “stable” subset ${\cal C} \subseteq {\cal D}$ that includes all points, except possibly few outliers, and is guaranteed to have diameter $r$. $\mathsf{FriendlyCore}$ can be used to preprocess the input before privately aggregating it, potentially simplifying the aggregation or boosting its accuracy. Surprisingly, $\mathsf{FriendlyCore}$ is light-weight with no dependence on the dimension. We empirically demonstrate its advantages in boosting the accuracy of mean estimation and clustering tasks such as $k$-means and $k$-GMM, outperforming tailored methods.

paragraphs: Differentially private averaging and clustering can be difficult to use because algorithms are complex or require many observations for accurate results. FriendlyCore is a preprocessing tool intended to make these aggregation tasks easier. It accepts points from an unrestricted metric or pseudometric space, so its formulation does not require a particular coordinate representation.

When the input has effective diameter r, the method produces a stable subset with diameter guaranteed to be r. That subset retains all the points except possibly a few outliers. The construction therefore supplies a controlled collection of points for subsequent private aggregation, potentially simplifying that aggregation or improving its accuracy.

The authors emphasize that FriendlyCore is lightweight and has no dependence on dimension. Experiments show improved accuracy for mean estimation and clustering, including k-means and Gaussian mixture clustering, with performance exceeding tailored methods in the reported evaluations. Its central contribution is a reusable preprocessing step: establishing useful structure in the input can improve multiple private aggregation procedures rather than requiring a separate specialized construction for each task.
summary.tldr: FriendlyCore extracts a stable subset with controlled diameter to simplify or improve differentially private averaging and clustering.

title: FriendlyCore: Practical Differentially Private Aggregation

abstract: Present-day federated learning (FL) systems deployed over edge networks consists of a large number of workers with high degrees of heterogeneity in data and/or computing capabilities, which call for flexible worker participation in terms of timing, effort, data heterogeneity, etc. To satisfy the need for flexible worker participation, we consider a new FL paradigm called “Anarchic Federated Learning” (AFL) in this paper. In stark contrast to conventional FL models, each worker in AFL has the freedom to choose i) when to participate in FL, and ii) the number of local steps to perform in each round based on its current situation (e.g., battery level, communication channels, privacy concerns). However, such chaotic worker behaviors in AFL impose many new open questions in algorithm design. In particular, it remains unclear whether one could develop convergent AFL training algorithms, and if yes, under what conditions and how fast the achievable convergence speed is. Toward this end, we propose two Anarchic Federated Averaging (AFA) algorithms with two-sided learning rates for both cross-device and cross-silo settings, which are named AFA-CD and AFA-CS, respectively. Somewhat surprisingly, we show that, under mild anarchic assumptions, both AFL algorithms achieve the best known convergence rate as the state-of-the-art algorithms for conventional FL. Moreover, they retain the highly desirable linear speedup effect with respect of both the number of workers and local steps in the new AFL paradigm. We validate the proposed algorithms with extensive experiments on real-world datasets.

paragraphs: Federated learning brings together workers whose data and computing resources can differ substantially. A worker’s ability to contribute may also change with battery level, communication conditions, or privacy concerns. This paper introduces Anarchic Federated Learning, where workers choose both when to participate and how many local training steps to perform in a round.

Such flexibility raises a mathematical question: can training still converge when participation and effort vary this way? They also retain linear speedup with respect to worker count and local steps. Experiments on real-world datasets validate the proposed algorithms. The contribution is therefore both a flexible participation framework and conditional evidence that this flexibility can coexist with strong convergence properties.
summary.tldr: Two federated averaging algorithms allow workers to choose their participation and effort while retaining strong convergence rates under stated assumptions.

title: Anarchic Federated Learning

abstract: Constrained reinforcement learning (CRL) has gained significant interest recently, since safety constraints satisfaction is critical for real-world problems. However, existing CRL methods constraining discounted cumulative costs generally lack rigorous definition and guarantee of safety. In contrast, in the safe control research, safety is defined as persistently satisfying certain state constraints. Such persistent safety is possible only on a subset of the state space, called feasible set, where an optimal largest feasible set exists for a given environment. Recent studies incorporate feasible sets into CRL with energy-based methods such as control barrier function (CBF), safety index (SI), and leverage prior conservative estimations of feasible sets, which harms the performance of the learned policy. To deal with this problem, this paper proposes the reachability CRL (RCRL) method by using reachability analysis to establish the novel self-consistency condition and characterize the feasible sets. The feasible sets are represented by the safety value function, which is used as the constraint in CRL. We use the multi-time scale stochastic approximation theory to prove that the proposed algorithm converges to a local optimum, where the largest feasible set can be guaranteed. Empirical results on different benchmarks validate the learned feasible set, the policy performance, and constraint satisfaction of RCRL, compared to CRL and safe control baselines.

paragraphs: Keeping a discounted total cost small does not by itself rigorously express persistent safety. This paper uses the safe-control view that safety means continually satisfying state constraints. Such behavior is possible only from a feasible subset of states, and a given environment has a largest feasible set.

Reachability Constrained Reinforcement Learning, or RCRL, uses reachability analysis to formulate a self-consistency condition characterizing these sets. A safety value function represents the feasible set and becomes a constraint in reinforcement learning. This addresses the performance loss that can arise when learning relies on an overly conservative prior estimate of which states permit safe behavior.

Using multi-time-scale stochastic approximation, the authors prove convergence to a local optimum where the largest feasible set can be guaranteed. This is a local policy optimization result alongside a guarantee about the feasible set, rather than a claim of globally optimal policy performance. Benchmark experiments evaluate the learned set, policy performance, and constraint satisfaction against constrained reinforcement learning and safe-control baselines, supporting the proposed integration of reachability and learning.
summary.tldr: RCRL uses reachability-based safety constraints and proves convergence to a local optimum where the largest feasible set is guaranteed.

title: Reachability Constrained Reinforcement Learning

abstract: An important milestone for AI is the development of algorithms that can produce drawings that are indistinguishable from those of humans. Here, we adapt the ”diversity vs. recognizability” scoring framework from Boutin et al (2022) and find that one-shot diffusion models have indeed started to close the gap between humans and machines. However, using a finer-grained measure of the originality of individual samples, we show that strengthening the guidance of diffusion models helps improve the humanness of their drawings, but they still fall short of approximating the originality and recognizability of human drawings. Comparing human category diagnostic features, collected through an online psychophysics experiment, against those derived from diffusion models reveals that humans rely on fewer and more localized features. Overall, our study suggests that diffusion models have significantly helped improve the quality of machine-generated drawings; however, a gap between humans and machines remains – in part explainable by discrepancies in visual strategies.

paragraphs: How close are machine-generated drawings to human drawings? This paper evaluates that question through several complementary measures. It adapts a framework that considers both the variety of drawings and how recognisable they are, finding that one-shot diffusion models have begun to narrow the gap between machine and human output.

A more detailed assessment of individual drawings reveals a remaining difference. Stronger guidance makes diffusion-generated drawings appear more human, but the models still do not match the originality and recognisability of human drawings. This matters because improvements in an overall assessment can coexist with shortcomings in the particular qualities that distinguish individual examples.

The authors also compare the visual features humans and models use to identify categories. Human features, collected through an online psychophysics experiment, are fewer and more concentrated in particular locations than those derived from the diffusion models. The study suggests that differences in these visual strategies partly explain the remaining gap. Its findings support meaningful progress in drawing quality while distinguishing that progress from matching human originality and recognition.
summary.tldr: Diffusion models produce increasingly human-like drawings, but differences in originality, recognisability, and visual strategies leave a measurable gap.

title: Diffusion Models as Artists: Are we Closing the Gap between Humans and Machines?

abstract: Diffusion models achieve state-of-the-art performance in various generation tasks. However, their theoretical foundations fall far behind. This paper studies score approximation, estimation, and distribution recovery of diffusion models, when data are supported on an unknown low-dimensional linear subspace. Our result provides sample complexity bounds for distribution estimation using diffusion models. We show that with a properly chosen neural network architecture, the score function can be both accurately approximated and efficiently estimated. Further, the generated distribution based on the estimated score function captures the data geometric structures and converges to a close vicinity of the data distribution. The convergence rate depends on subspace dimension, implying that diffusion models can circumvent the curse of data ambient dimensionality.

paragraphs: This paper develops theory for diffusion models when data lie on an unknown low-dimensional linear subspace. The analysis connects learning the score function to recovering both the distribution and its geometry.

The authors establish sample-complexity bounds for distribution estimation and show that a properly selected neural architecture can approximate the score accurately and estimate it efficiently. These are complementary requirements: the network must be capable of representing the needed function, and available samples must support learning that representation with controlled error.

The convergence rate depends on the subspace dimension, indicating that diffusion models can avoid the curse of ambient dimensionality in this setting. That conclusion is tied to the stated linear-subspace assumption and appropriate architecture, rather than being a guarantee for arbitrary data geometry.
summary.tldr: For data on an unknown low-dimensional linear subspace, diffusion-model recovery guarantees can depend on intrinsic rather than ambient dimension.

title: Score Approximation, Estimation and Distribution Recovery of Diffusion Models on Low-Dimensional Data

abstract: We present a shape-guided expert-learning framework to tackle the problem of unsupervised 3D anomaly detection. Our method is established on the effectiveness of two specialized expert models and their synergy to localize anomalous regions from color and shape modalities. The first expert utilizes geometric information to probe 3D structural anomalies by modeling the implicit distance fields around local shapes. The second expert considers the 2D RGB features associated with the first expert to identify color appearance irregularities on the local shapes. We use the two experts to build the dual memory banks from the anomaly-free training samples and perform shape-guided inference to pinpoint the defects in the testing samples. Owing to the per-point 3D representation and the effective fusion scheme of complementary modalities, our method efficiently achieves state-of-the-art performance on the MVTec 3D-AD dataset with better recall and lower false positive rates, as preferred in real applications.

This paper develops an unsupervised anomaly detection framework that combines two specialized experts to locate such defects. Training uses anomaly-free samples, from which the method builds separate memory banks for the two complementary sources of information.

The first expert models implicit distance fields around local shapes to capture geometric structure and detect structural irregularities. The second examines associated RGB features to identify unusual color appearance on those shapes. At test time, shape-guided inference brings these representations together to locate anomalous regions in the input.

The method's per-point 3D representation and fusion of shape and color support detailed defect localization. On the MVTec 3D-AD dataset, the authors report efficient, state-of-the-art performance with higher recall and fewer false positives. Those improvements mean more defects are detected while fewer normal regions are incorrectly flagged in the reported evaluation. The findings support combining complementary experts and memories for this anomaly detection task.
summary.tldr: Two experts combine shape and color memories learned from normal samples to improve 3D defect detection on MVTec 3D-AD.

title: Shape-Guided Dual-Memory Learning for 3D Anomaly Detection

abstract: Continuous monitoring with an ever-increasing number of sensors has become ubiquitous across many application domains. However, acquired time series are typically high-dimensional and difficult to interpret. Expressive deep learning (DL) models have gained popularity for dimensionality reduction, but the resulting latent space often remains difficult to interpret. In this work we propose SOM-CPC, a model that visualizes data in an organized 2D manifold, while preserving higher-dimensional information. We address a largely unexplored and challenging set of scenarios comprising high-rate time series, and show on both synthetic and real-life data (physiological data and audio recordings) that SOM-CPC outperforms strong baselines like DL-based feature extraction, followed by conventional dimensionality reduction techniques, and models that jointly optimize a DL model and a Self-Organizing Map (SOM). SOM-CPC has great potential to acquire a better understanding of latent patterns in high-rate data streams.

paragraphs: High-rate sensor streams can contain many measurements that are difficult to inspect directly. Deep learning can compress those measurements, but the resulting latent representations may still be hard to interpret. SOM-CPC addresses this gap by seeking a representation that supports an organized two-dimensional visualization while preserving information from higher dimensions.

The model combines unsupervised contrastive learning with self-organizing maps. Its purpose is to make the structure of high-rate time series easier to examine, rather than treating dimensionality reduction alone as sufficient for understanding. The paper focuses on this challenging setting across both synthetic data and real recordings.

The evaluation includes physiological signals and audio. The authors report that SOM-CPC outperforms strong alternatives, including deep feature extraction followed by conventional dimensionality reduction and models that jointly train a deep network with a self-organizing map. These comparisons support the usefulness of the proposed combination for the tested data. The broader implication is a promising way to study latent patterns in continuous streams, with improved understanding presented as potential rather than as a guaranteed outcome of every visualization.
summary.tldr: SOM-CPC combines contrastive learning and self-organizing maps to create structured two-dimensional representations of high-rate time series.

title: SOM-CPC: Unsupervised Contrastive Learning with Self-Organizing Maps for Structured Representations of High-Rate Time Series

abstract: Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) are one of the most powerful tools for prediction, but many of them implicitly assume that the data are statistically independent. However, in the real world, it is common for large-scale data to be clustered with temporal-spatial correlation structures. Variational approaches and integrated likelihood approaches have been proposed to obtain approximate maximum likelihood estimators (MLEs) for correlated data. However, due to the large size of data, they cannot provide exact MLEs. In this study, we propose a new hierarchical likelihood approach to DNNs with correlated random effects for clustered data. By jointly optimizing the the negative h-likelihood loss, we can provide exact MLEs for both mean and dispersion parameters, as well as the best linear unbiased predictors for the random effects. Moreover, the hierarchical likelihood allows a computable procedure for restricted maximum likelihood estimators of dispersion parameters. The proposed two-step algorithm enables online learning for the neural networks, whereas the integrated likelihood cannot decompose like a widely-used loss function in DNNs. The proposed h-likelihood approach offers several advantages, which we demonstrate through numerical studies and real data analyses.

paragraphs: Many neural-network approaches implicitly treat observations as statistically independent, while real datasets often contain clusters connected through time or space. This paper incorporates correlated random effects into deep neural networks to represent that dependence. The setting also concerns categorical features with many possible values, where a model must account for substantial group structure.

The authors propose optimizing a hierarchical likelihood, or h-likelihood, objective. They state that joint optimization provides exact maximum likelihood estimates for mean and dispersion parameters, together with best linear unbiased predictions of the random effects. The approach also supplies a computable procedure for restricted maximum likelihood estimation of dispersion parameters, addressing several statistical estimation tasks within the same framework.

A two-step algorithm enables online learning for the neural-network component. The authors contrast this with integrated likelihood, which does not decompose like commonly used neural-network losses. Numerical studies and analyses of real data demonstrate advantages of the approach. Its significance is the combination of explicit dependence modeling, the stated estimation properties, and a training procedure compatible with online neural-network learning.
summary.tldr: The paper uses hierarchical likelihood to train neural networks with correlated random effects, providing stated exact estimation results and an online-learning procedure.

title: H-Likelihood Approach to Deep Neural Networks with Temporal-Spatial Random Effects for High-Cardinality Categorical Features

abstract: In online reinforcement learning (RL), instead of employing standard structural assumptions on Markov decision processes (MDPs), using a certain coverage condition (original from offline RL) is enough to ensure sample-efficient guarantees (Xie et al. 2023). In this work, we focus on this new direction by digging more possible and general coverage conditions, and study the potential and the utility of them in efficient online RL. We identify more concepts, including the $L^p$ variant of concentrability, the density ratio realizability, and trade-off on the partial/rest coverage condition, that can be also beneficial to sample-efficient online RL, achieving improved regret bound. Furthermore, if exploratory offline data are used, under our coverage conditions, both statistically and computationally efficient guarantees can be achieved for online RL. Besides, even though the MDP structure is given, e.g., linear MDP, we elucidate that, good coverage conditions are still beneficial to obtain faster regret bound beyond $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\sqrt{T})$ and even a logarithmic order regret. These results provide a good justification for the usage of general coverage conditions in efficient online RL.

paragraphs: Efficient online reinforcement learning is often analyzed using structural assumptions about the environment. This paper explores a different route: coverage conditions that describe how well relevant distributions are represented. Building on the sufficiency of a coverage condition for sample-efficient learning, the authors investigate broader conditions and the benefits they can provide.

The analysis considers Lᵖ concentrability, realizability of density ratios, and trade-offs involving partial and remaining coverage. These concepts give additional ways to control the distributional relationships that matter for learning, leading to improved regret bounds. When exploratory offline data are also available, the paper establishes both statistical and computational efficiency under its coverage conditions.

The benefits can persist even when the environment already has a known structure, such as a linear Markov decision process. With good coverage, the authors obtain regret rates faster than square-root growth and even logarithmic regret in the covered settings. These are conditional guarantees that show coverage can complement structural assumptions as well as provide an alternative analytical foundation.
summary.tldr: General coverage conditions can improve online reinforcement learning guarantees, including computational efficiency with exploratory offline data and faster conditional regret rates.

title: What can online reinforcement learning with function approximation benefit from general coverage conditions?

abstract: We explore algorithms to select actions in the causal bandit setting where the learner can choose to intervene on a set of random variables related by a causal graph, and the learner sequentially chooses interventions and observes a sample from the interventional distribution. The learner’s goal is to quickly find the intervention, among all interventions on observable variables, that maximizes the expectation of an outcome variable. We depart from previous literature by assuming no knowledge of the causal graph except that latent confounders between the outcome and its ancestors are not present. We first show that the unknown graph problem can be exponentially hard in the parents of the outcome. To remedy this, we adopt an additional additive assumption on the outcome which allows us to solve the problem by casting it as an additive combinatorial linear bandit problem with full-bandit feedback. We propose a novel action-elimination algorithm for this setting, show how to apply this algorithm to the causal bandit problem, provide sample complexity bounds, and empirically validate our findings on a suite of randomly generated causal models, effectively showing that one does not need to explicitly learn the parents of the outcome to identify the best intervention.

paragraphs: A causal bandit learner repeatedly changes selected variables, observes the resulting outcomes, and tries to identify the intervention with the highest expected reward. This paper studies that task without knowing the causal graph. It does assume that there are no latent confounders between the outcome and its ancestors.

The authors first show that the unknown-graph problem can require effort growing exponentially with the number of direct causes of the outcome. They then introduce an additional assumption: the outcome has an additive structure. This lets them reformulate intervention selection as a combinatorial linear bandit problem in which feedback describes the overall selected action.

For this formulation, the paper develops an action-elimination algorithm and gives sample complexity bounds. Experiments on randomly generated causal models support the approach. The central finding is that, under the stated assumptions, identifying the best intervention does not require explicitly discovering the outcome’s parents. Additivity provides a way to make the decision problem manageable without first solving that causal structure learning task.
summary.tldr: With an additive outcome and no specified latent confounding, a learner can identify the best intervention without explicitly learning the outcome’s parents.

title: Additive Causal Bandits with Unknown Graph

abstract: Many, if not most, systems of interest in science are naturally described as nonlinear dynamical systems. Empirically, we commonly access these systems through time series measurements. Often such time series may consist of discrete random variables rather than continuous measurements, or may be composed of measurements from multiple data modalities observed simultaneously. For instance, in neuroscience we may have behavioral labels in addition to spike counts and continuous physiological recordings. While by now there is a burgeoning literature on deep learning for dynamical systems reconstruction (DSR), multimodal data integration has hardly been considered in this context. Here we provide such an efficient and flexible algorithmic framework that rests on a multimodal variational autoencoder for generating a sparse teacher signal that guides training of a reconstruction model, exploiting recent advances in DSR training techniques. It enables to combine various sources of information for optimal reconstruction, even allows for reconstruction from symbolic data (class labels) alone, and connects different types of observations within a common latent dynamics space. In contrast to previous multimodal data integration techniques for scientific applications, our framework is fully generative, producing, after training, trajectories with the same geometrical and temporal structure as those of the ground truth system.

paragraphs: Reconstructing a nonlinear dynamical system from observations becomes more complicated when measurements come in different forms. A scientific dataset might combine continuous recordings, counts, and categorical labels. This paper develops a framework that brings such observations together to learn a shared account of the underlying dynamics, addressing multimodal integration within dynamical systems reconstruction.

The method uses a multimodal variational autoencoder to produce a sparse teaching signal for a reconstruction model. That signal guides training through recent dynamical reconstruction techniques. Different kinds of observations are connected within one latent dynamical space, allowing information from several measurement sources to contribute to the reconstructed system.

The framework can also reconstruct dynamics from symbolic class labels alone. After training, it is fully generative: the authors report trajectories with the same geometric and temporal structure as the ground-truth system. This makes the contribution more than an alignment of different observation types; the learned representation supports generating evolving behavior with the structure of the system being studied.
summary.tldr: A multimodal autoencoder guides dynamical reconstruction, enabling joint generative modelling from mixed measurements or even class labels alone.

title: Integrating Multimodal Data for Joint Generative Modeling of Complex Dynamics

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in language generation, understanding, and few-shot learning in recent years. An extensive body of work has explored how their performance may be further improved through the tools of prompting, ranging from verification, self-consistency, or intermediate scratchpads. In this paper, we present a complementary approach to improve language responses where multiple language model instances propose and debate their individual responses and reasoning processes over multiple rounds to arrive at a common final answer. Our findings indicate that this approach significantly enhances mathematical and strategic reasoning across a number of tasks. We also demonstrate that our approach improves the factual validity of generated content, reducing fallacious answers and hallucinations that contemporary models are prone to. Our approach may be directly applied to existing black-box models and uses identical procedure and prompts for all tasks we investigate. Overall, our findings suggest that such "society of minds" approach has the potential to significantly advance the capabilities of LLMs and pave the way for further breakthroughs in language generation and understanding.

paragraphs: This paper studies whether language models can improve their answers through discussion among multiple model instances. Each instance first proposes its own response and reasoning. The instances then debate over several rounds, working toward a shared final answer. This adds an interaction process around existing models as another way to improve their responses.

The approach complements prompting methods such as checking an answer, considering multiple responses, or writing intermediate reasoning. Here, the proposed answers and explanations become material for further exchanges among the instances. The method can be applied directly to black-box models, and the authors use the same procedure and prompts across all tasks they investigate.

The reported findings show significant improvements in mathematical and strategic reasoning across several tasks. The authors also find improved factual validity, with fewer fallacious answers and hallucinations. These results support debate as a useful way to organize model inference in the evaluated settings. The broader suggestion is that structured interaction among instances may unlock capabilities beyond those obtained from an individual response.
summary.tldr: Multiple language-model instances debating their answers improve reasoning and factual accuracy across the tasks studied.

title: Improving Factuality and Reasoning in Language Models through Multiagent Debate

abstract: Training and validating models for semantic segmentation require datasets with pixel-wise annotations, which are notoriously labor-intensive. Although useful priors such as foundation models or crowdsourced datasets are available, they are error-prone. We hence propose an effective framework of active label correction (ALC) based on a design of correction query to rectify pseudo labels of pixels, which in turn is more annotator-friendly than the standard one inquiring to classify a pixel directly according to our theoretical analysis and user study. Specifically, leveraging foundation models providing useful zero-shot predictions on pseudo labels and superpixels, our method comprises two key techniques: (i) an annotator-friendly design of correction query with the pseudo labels, and (ii) an acquisition function looking ahead label expansions based on the superpixels. Experimental results on PASCAL, Cityscapes, and Kvasir-SEG datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our ALC framework, outperforming prior methods for active semantic segmentation and label correction. Notably, utilizing our method, we obtained a revised dataset of PASCAL by rectifying errors in 2.6 million pixels in PASCAL dataset.

paragraphs: Semantic segmentation assigns a category to each image pixel, making reliable annotation labor-intensive. Foundation models and existing crowdsourced datasets offer useful starting labels, but those labels can contain errors. This paper studies how to direct human effort toward correcting them efficiently.

The framework combines two choices: how to ask for a correction and which correction to request next. Instead of asking an annotator to classify a pixel directly, it presents a correction query based on an existing pseudo label. The authors support this design with theoretical analysis and a user study. The selection rule also looks ahead to how a correction can expand through superpixels, which group pixels into regions.

Foundation models supply zero-shot pseudo labels and superpixels for this process. Experiments on PASCAL, Cityscapes, and Kvasir-SEG show improvements over previous active segmentation and label-correction methods. The authors also use the framework to revise PASCAL, correcting errors across 2.6 million pixels. The contribution therefore concerns both making annotation interactions easier and selecting interactions with broader corrective value.
summary.tldr: A foundation-model-assisted annotation framework improves semantic segmentation label correction through easier queries and superpixel-aware selection.

title: Active Label Correction for Semantic Segmentation with Foundation Models

abstract: Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) has emerged as the main paradigm for aligning large language models (LLMs) with human preferences. Traditionally, RLHF involves the initial step of learning a reward model from pairwise human feedback, i.e., expressed as preferences between pairs of text generations. Subsequently, the LLM’s policy is fine-tuned to maximize the reward through a reinforcement learning algorithm. In this study, we introduce an alternative pipeline for the fine-tuning of LLMs using pairwise human feedback. Our approach entails the initial learning of a pairwise preference model, which is conditioned on two inputs (instead of a single input in the case of a reward model) given a prompt, followed by the pursuit of a policy that consistently generates responses preferred over those generated by any competing policy, thus defining the Nash equilibrium of this preference model. We term this approach Nash learning from human feedback (NLHF). In the context of a tabular policy representation, we present a novel algorithmic solution, Nash-MD, founded on the principles of mirror descent. This algorithm produces a sequence of policies, with the last iteration converging to the regularized Nash equilibrium. Additionally, we explore parametric representations of policies and introduce gradient descent algorithms for deep-learning architectures. We illustrate the effectiveness of our approach by presenting experimental results on a text summarization task. We believe NLHF offers a compelling avenue for fine-tuning LLMs and enhancing the alignment of LLMs with human preferences.

paragraphs: Traditional reinforcement learning from human feedback converts pairwise judgments into a reward model that scores individual responses. Nash learning from human feedback instead learns a model that directly compares two responses to the same prompt. It then uses that comparison model to define the objective for language model fine-tuning.

The target is a policy whose responses are preferred against those from competing policies, expressed through a Nash equilibrium of the preference model. For tabular policy representations, the authors introduce Nash-MD, an algorithm based on mirror descent. They prove convergence of its last policy iterate to a regularized Nash equilibrium, rather than stating this guarantee only for an average of earlier policies.

The paper also explores parameterized policies and develops gradient descent algorithms for deep-learning architectures. Experiments on text summarization illustrate the approach’s effectiveness. The tabular convergence result and the summarization experiments provide different forms of support for a pipeline that keeps pairwise preferences central throughout learning.
summary.tldr: NLHF fine-tunes language models using a pairwise preference model and a Nash-equilibrium objective, with tabular convergence guarantees.

title: Nash Learning from Human Feedback

abstract: We give extensive empirical evidence against the common belief that variational learning is ineffective for large neural networks. We show that an optimizer called Improved Variational Online Newton (IVON) consistently matches or outperforms Adam for training large networks such as GPT-2 and ResNets from scratch. IVON’s computational costs are nearly identical to Adam but its predictive uncertainty is better. We show several new use cases of IVON where we improve finetuning and model merging in Large Language Models, accurately predict generalization error, and faithfully estimate sensitivity to data. We find overwhelming evidence that variational learning is effective. Code is available at https://github.com/team-approx-bayes/ivon.
