paragraphs: This paper tests the belief that variational learning is ineffective for large neural networks. Its evidence centers on Improved Variational Online Newton, or IVON, an optimizer used to train networks including GPT-2 and ResNets from scratch. Across the reported evaluations, IVON consistently matches or exceeds Adam's performance.

The comparison also considers practical cost and uncertainty. IVON's computational requirements are nearly the same as Adam's, while its predictive uncertainty is better. This combination matters because the reported uncertainty improvement accompanies competitive training performance without a substantial increase in computational expense.

The authors extend the investigation beyond training from scratch. They report improvements in language-model fine-tuning and model merging, along with accurate prediction of generalization error and faithful estimation of sensitivity to data. These uses show how the method's value can extend to analyzing and adapting trained models. Taken together, the extensive empirical results challenge a broad dismissal of variational learning for large networks and demonstrate its effectiveness in the studied settings.
summary.tldr: IVON matches or beats Adam in reported large-network training experiments at similar cost, with better predictive uncertainty and useful adaptation capabilities.

title: Variational Learning is Effective for Large Deep Networks

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable proficiency in understanding and generating natural language. However, their capabilities wane in highly specialized domains underrepresented in the pretraining corpus, such as physical and biomedical sciences. This work explores how to repurpose general LLMs into effective task solvers for specialized domains. We introduce a novel, model-agnostic framework for learning custom input tags, which are parameterized as continuous vectors appended to the LLM’s embedding layer, to condition the LLM. We design two types of input tags: domain tags are used to delimit specialized representations (e.g., chemical formulas) and provide domain-relevant context; function tags are used to represent specific functions (e.g., predicting molecular properties) and compress function-solving instructions. We develop a three-stage protocol to learn these tags using auxiliary data and domain knowledge. By explicitly disentangling task domains from task functions, our method enables zero-shot generalization to unseen problems through diverse combinations of the input tags. It also boosts LLM’s performance in various specialized domains, such as predicting protein or chemical properties and modeling drug-target interactions, outperforming expert models tailored to these tasks.

paragraphs: General-purpose language models can struggle with specialized scientific domains that are underrepresented in pretraining. Tag-LLM addresses this by learning custom input tags that condition the model. These tags are continuous vectors added at the embedding layer, giving the model learned signals about the material and task it should handle.

The framework separates domain tags from function tags. Domain tags mark specialized representations, such as chemical formulas, and supply relevant context. Function tags represent operations, such as molecular property prediction, and compress the instructions needed to perform them. A three-stage learning protocol uses auxiliary data and domain knowledge to train the tags.

Separating domain and function allows learned tags to be recombined for unseen problems, enabling the stated zero-shot generalization. The authors report improvements on specialized tasks including protein and chemical property prediction and drug-target interaction modeling, outperforming expert models tailored to the evaluated tasks. The approach offers a model-agnostic way to organize specialized knowledge and task instructions into reusable conditioning components.
summary.tldr: Tag-LLM learns separate domain and function tags that improve specialized task performance and can be recombined for unseen problems.

title: Tag-LLM: Repurposing General-Purpose LLMs for Specialized Domains

abstract: While supervised federated learning approaches have enjoyed significant success, the domain of unsupervised federated learning remains relatively underexplored. Several federated EM algorithms have gained popularity in practice, however, their theoretical foundations are often lacking. In this paper, we first introduce a federated gradient EM algorithm (FedGrEM) designed for the unsupervised learning of mixture models, which supplements the existing federated EM algorithms by considering task heterogeneity and potential adversarial attacks. We present a comprehensive finite-sample theory that holds for general mixture models, then apply this general theory on specific statistical models to characterize the explicit estimation error of model parameters and mixture proportions. Our theory elucidates when and how FedGrEM outperforms local single-task learning with insights extending to existing federated EM algorithms. This bridges the gap between their practical success and theoretical understanding. Our numerical results validate our theory, and demonstrate FedGrEM’s superiority over existing unsupervised federated learning benchmarks.

paragraphs: Federated expectation-maximization methods have been used for unsupervised learning, but their practical success has outpaced their theoretical explanation. This paper studies federated learning of mixture models, where the aim is to infer underlying components without supervised labels. It introduces FedGrEM, a federated gradient EM algorithm that accounts for differences between tasks and potential adversarial attacks.

The authors develop a finite-sample theory for general mixture models. They then apply that theory to specific statistical models to characterize errors in estimated model parameters and mixture proportions. This moves the analysis toward what can be learned from a finite amount of data, including how accurately the component structure and its relative weights can be recovered.

The theory explains when and how FedGrEM can outperform learning each task locally, with insights that also extend to existing federated EM algorithms. Numerical results support the analysis and show better performance than the evaluated unsupervised federated-learning benchmarks. The key contribution is a connection between collaborative estimation, task heterogeneity, and finite-sample accuracy, with conditions governing the benefit of collaboration.
summary.tldr: FedGrEM combines unsupervised federated mixture learning with finite-sample theory explaining when collaboration improves estimation.

title: Towards the Theory of Unsupervised Federated Learning: Non-asymptotic Analysis of Federated EM Algorithms

abstract: The field of hypothesis generation promises to reduce costs in neuroscience by narrowing the range of interventional studies needed to study various phenomena. Existing machine learning methods can generate scientific hypotheses from complex datasets, but many approaches assume causal relationships are static over time, limiting their applicability to systems with dynamic, state-dependent behavior, such as the brain. While some techniques attempt dynamic causal discovery through factor models, they often restrict relationships to linear patterns or impose other simplifying assumptions. We propose a novel method that models dynamic graphs as a conditionally weighted superposition of static graphs, where each static graph can capture nonlinear relationships. This approach enables the detection of complex, time-varying interactions between variables beyond linear limitations. Our method improves f1-scores of predicted dynamic causal patterns by roughly 22-28% on average over baselines in some of our experiments, with some improvements reaching well over 60%. A case study on real brain data demonstrates our method’s ability to uncover relationships linked to specific behavioral states, offering valuable insights into neural dynamics.

paragraphs: Relationships between brain variables can change with behavioral state, making a single fixed causal graph an incomplete description. This paper develops a method for generating hypotheses about these changing relationships from observed time series. Its motivation is to narrow the set of interventions that neuroscientists need to investigate.

The method represents a dynamic graph as a condition-dependent weighted combination of static graphs. Each component graph can describe nonlinear relationships, so the changing mixture can capture interactions beyond linear patterns. This provides a structured way to express both recurring relationships and changes in their importance as the system's state varies.

In some experiments, the method improves F1 scores for predicted dynamic causal patterns by roughly 22–28% on average over baselines, with some improvements exceeding 60%. A case study using real brain data identifies relationships associated with particular behavioral states. These results support the approach as a tool for proposing state-sensitive causal hypotheses. Its role in the stated neuroscience workflow is to guide subsequent investigation through patterns inferred from observational data.
summary.tldr: A weighted combination of nonlinear static graphs generates hypotheses about changing causal relationships in neural time series.

title: Generating Hypotheses of Dynamic Causal Graphs in Neuroscience: Leveraging Generative Factor Models of Observed Time Series

abstract: Pretraining robust vision or multimodal foundation models (e.g., CLIP) relies on large-scale datasets that may be noisy, potentially misaligned, and have long-tail distributions. Previous works have shown promising results in augmenting datasets by generating synthetic samples. However, they only support domain-specific ad hoc use cases (e.g., either image or text only, but not both), and are limited in data diversity due to a lack of fine-grained control over the synthesis process. In this paper, we design a controllable image-text synthesis pipeline, CtrlSynth, for data-efficient and robust multimodal learning. The key idea is to decompose the visual semantics of an image into basic elements, apply user-specified control policies (e.g., remove, add, or replace operations), and recompose them to synthesize images or texts. The decompose and recompose feature in CtrlSynth allows users to control data synthesis in a fine-grained manner by defining customized control policies to manipulate the basic elements. CtrlSynth leverages the capabilities of pretrained foundation models such as large language models or diffusion models to reason and recompose basic elements such that synthetic samples are natural and composed in diverse ways. CtrlSynth is a closed-loop, training-free, and modular framework, making it easy to support different pretrained models. With extensive experiments on 31 datasets spanning different vision and vision-language tasks, we show that CtrlSynth substantially improves zero-shot classification, image-text retrieval, and compositional reasoning performance of CLIP models.

paragraphs: CtrlSynth addresses a problem in training vision-language models: large image-text datasets can contain noise, mismatched pairs, and uneven coverage. Synthetic data can help, but generating useful variety requires control over what changes. The paper introduces a pipeline that supports fine-grained manipulation when synthesizing either images or text.

The pipeline breaks an image’s visual meaning into basic elements. Users specify policies that add, remove, or replace elements, and pretrained foundation models reason about and recombine them into natural, varied samples. This decomposition makes control explicit at the level of content, instead of leaving the entire synthesis process to an undirected generation request.

The authors evaluate its use across 31 datasets covering vision and vision-language tasks. They report substantial improvements in CLIP’s zero-shot classification, image-text retrieval, and compositional reasoning. These results connect control over generated content to better use of synthetic data for multimodal learning.
summary.tldr: CtrlSynth improves multimodal learning by generating images and text through controllable edits to basic visual-semantic elements.

title: CtrlSynth: Controllable Image Text Synthesis for Data-Efficient Multimodal Learning

abstract: Scaling laws predict the loss of a target machine learning model by extrapolating from easier-to-train models with fewer parameters or smaller training sets. This provides an efficient way for practitioners and researchers alike to compare pretraining decisions involving optimizers, datasets, and model architectures. Despite the widespread use of scaling laws to model the dynamics of language model training, there has been little work on understanding how to best estimate and interpret them. We collect (and release) a large-scale dataset containing losses and downstream evaluations for 485 previously published pretrained models. We use these to estimate more than 1000 scaling laws, then derive a set of best practices for estimating scaling laws in new model families. We find that fitting scaling laws to intermediate checkpoints of training runs (and not just their final losses) substantially improves accuracy, and that—all else equal—estimates of performance are generally most accurate when derived from other models of similar sizes. However, because there is a significant degree of variability across model seeds, training multiple small models is sometimes more useful than training a single large one. Moreover, while different model families differ in scaling behavior, they are often similar enough that a target model’s behavior can be predicted from a single model with the same architecture, along with scaling parameter estimates derived from other model families.

paragraphs: Scaling laws help researchers predict how a larger model will perform using results from smaller, cheaper training runs. Their usefulness depends on how those relationships are estimated. This paper examines that estimation process using a released collection of losses and downstream evaluations from 485 previously published pretrained models, fitting more than 1,000 scaling laws.

One finding is that measurements taken during training contain valuable information: including intermediate checkpoints substantially improves prediction accuracy compared with using final losses alone. Holding other factors equal, predictions are generally most accurate when they come from models near the target model’s size. However, variation between random seeds means that several small training runs can sometimes provide more useful evidence than one large run.

The authors also find that differences between model families need not prevent useful transfer. A single model with the target architecture, combined with scaling parameters estimated from other families, can often predict the target’s behavior. Together, these findings guide how to allocate training experiments and extract more information from their results.
summary.tldr: A large study of scaling-law estimation identifies practical ways to improve predictions using intermediate checkpoints, nearby model sizes, repeated runs, and information from other model families.

title: A Hitchhiker’s Guide to Scaling Law Estimation

abstract: Recent advances in test-time adaptation (TTA) for Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have garnered increasing attention, particularly through the use of multiple augmented views of a single image to boost zero-shot generalization. Unfortunately, existing methods fail to strike a satisfactory balance between performance and efficiency, either due to excessive overhead of tuning text prompts or unstable benefits from handcrafted, training-free visual feature enhancement. In this paper, we present Global-Spatial Bias Learner (GS-Bias), an efficient and effective TTA paradigm that incorporates two learnable biases during TTA, unfolded as the global bias and spatial bias. Particularly, the global bias captures the global semantic features of a test image by learning consistency across augmented views, while spatial bias learns the semantic coherence between regions in the image’s spatial visual representation. It is worth highlighting that these two sets of biases are directly added to the logits outputed by the pretrained VLMs, which circumvent the full backpropagation through VLM that hinders the efficiency of existing TTA methods. This endows GS-Bias with extremely high efficiency while achieving state-of-the-art performance on 15 benchmark datasets. For example, it achieves a 2.23% improvement over TPT in cross-dataset generalization and a 2.72% improvement in domain generalization, while requiring only 6.5% of TPT’s memory usage on ImageNet.

paragraphs: Vision-language models can adapt to a test image by examining several augmented versions of it. Existing approaches face a performance-efficiency tradeoff: tuning text prompts creates substantial overhead, while handcrafted visual-feature adjustments can provide unstable benefits. GS-Bias introduces a small set of learned corrections intended to make this adaptation effective and inexpensive.

The method learns two biases. A global bias captures the image’s overall semantics by encouraging consistency across augmented views. A spatial bias learns semantic coherence among regions in the image’s visual representation. The results indicate that adapting output scores using global and regional information can provide substantial benefits without the computational burden of tuning through the full model.
summary.tldr: GS-Bias adapts vision-language predictions with global and spatial output corrections, achieving strong benchmark performance with low memory use.

title: GS-Bias: Global-Spatial Bias Learner for Single-Image Test-Time Adaptation of Vision-Language Models

abstract: Applications of machine learning often involve making predictions based on both model outputs and the opinions of human experts. In this context, we investigate the problem of querying experts for class label predictions, using as few human queries as possible, and leveraging the class probability estimates of pre-trained classifiers. We develop a general Bayesian framework for this problem, modeling expert correlation via a joint latent representation, enabling simulation-based inference about the utility of additional expert queries, as well as inference of posterior distributions over unobserved expert labels. We apply our approach to two real-world medical classification problems, as well as to CIFAR-10H and ImageNet-16H, demonstrating substantial reductions relative to baselines in the cost of querying human experts while maintaining high prediction accuracy.

paragraphs: When a prediction system can consult both classifiers and human experts, each additional human opinion has a cost. This paper studies how to maintain accurate class predictions while asking fewer questions. It combines probability estimates from pretrained classifiers with a Bayesian model of the labels that experts would provide.

A central feature is that the framework represents correlations among experts through shared hidden variables. This lets it reason jointly about their opinions instead of treating every response as unrelated evidence. Using simulations, the system estimates how useful another expert query would be. It also maintains probability distributions over the responses of experts who have not yet been consulted.

The authors evaluate the approach on two medical classification problems and on CIFAR-10H and ImageNet-16H. They report substantially lower human-query costs than the compared baselines while maintaining high prediction accuracy. The practical contribution is a framework for deciding when further consultation is valuable, using both the classifier’s uncertainty and relationships among human judgments.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian framework models correlated expert opinions to reduce human queries while maintaining high classification accuracy in the reported evaluations.

title: Bayesian Inference for Correlated Human Experts and Classifiers

abstract: Both PAC-Bayesian and Sample Compress learning frameworks have been shown instrumental for deriving tight (non-vacuous) generalization bounds for neural networks. We leverage these results in a meta-learning scheme, relying on a hypernetwork that outputs the parameters of a downstream predictor from a dataset input. The originality of our approach lies in the investigated hypernetwork architectures that encode the dataset before decoding the parameters: (1) a PAC-Bayesian encoder that expresses a posterior distribution over a latent space, (2) a Sample Compress encoder that selects a small sample of the dataset input along with a message from a discrete set, and (3) a hybrid between both approaches motivated by a new Sample Compress theorem handling continuous messages. The latter theorem exploits the pivotal information transiting at the encoder-decoder junction in order to compute generalization guarantees for each downstream predictor obtained by our meta-learning scheme.

paragraphs: This paper studies generalization guarantees for a system that learns to produce predictors from datasets. Its central component is a hypernetwork: a network that takes a dataset as input and outputs the parameters of another model. The authors investigate how the representation passed between the hypernetwork's encoder and decoder can support guarantees for each resulting predictor.

They develop three encoding approaches. A PAC-Bayesian encoder represents the dataset through a probability distribution in a latent space. A sample-compression encoder selects a small subset of the data together with a message from a discrete set. A third architecture combines the two ideas, supported by a new sample-compression theorem that permits continuous messages.

The new theorem uses information passing through the encoder-decoder junction to calculate generalization guarantees. This connects the design of a learned model representation with analysis of the downstream predictor it generates. The contribution brings PAC-Bayesian and sample-compression tools into a meta-learning framework, making the way a dataset is encoded central to the resulting guarantees.
summary.tldr: Hypernetwork encoders combine PAC-Bayesian and sample-compression ideas to derive generalization guarantees for generated predictors.

title: Generalization Bounds via Meta-Learned Model Representations: PAC-Bayes and Sample Compression Hypernetworks

abstract: Diffusion-based re-ranking methods are effective in modeling the data manifolds through similarity propagation in affinity graphs. However, positive signals tend to diminish over several steps away from the source, reducing discriminative power beyond local regions. To address this issue, we introduce the Locality Preserving Markovian Transition (LPMT) framework, which employs a long-term thermodynamic transition process with multiple states for accurate manifold distance measurement. The proposed LPMT first integrates diffusion processes across separate graphs using Bidirectional Collaborative Diffusion (BCD) to establish strong similarity relationships. Afterwards, Locality State Embedding (LSE) encodes each instance into a distribution for enhanced local consistency. These distributions are interconnected via the Thermodynamic Markovian Transition (TMT) process, enabling efficient global retrieval while maintaining local effectiveness. Experimental results across diverse tasks confirm the effectiveness of LPMT for instance retrieval.

paragraphs: Diffusion-based retrieval reranks candidates by propagating similarities through a graph, helping capture the data manifold. But useful signals can fade several steps from their source, weakening discrimination outside local neighborhoods. This paper develops a transition framework intended to maintain local quality while supporting broader retrieval.

Locality Preserving Markovian Transition combines three components. Bidirectional Collaborative Diffusion connects similarity information across separate graphs. Locality State Embedding represents each instance as a distribution to preserve local consistency. A Thermodynamic Markovian Transition then links those distributions through a multi-state, long-term transition process for measuring manifold relationships.

Experiments across diverse retrieval tasks support the effectiveness of LPMT. The contribution is a coordinated re-ranking framework that addresses how similarity information travels beyond immediate neighbors. The abstract does not provide the detailed transition equations or numerical gains, so it supports the method’s structure and tested utility without establishing an identical improvement for every affinity-graph construction.
summary.tldr: LPMT combines collaborative diffusion, local distribution embeddings, and Markovian transitions to improve instance-retrieval re-ranking.

title: Locality Preserving Markovian Transition for Instance Retrieval

abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models mostly use a router to assign tokens to specific expert modules, activating only partial parameters and often outperforming dense models. We argue that the separation between the router’s decision-making and the experts’ execution is a critical yet overlooked issue, leading to suboptimal expert selection and learning. To address this, we propose Autonomy-of-Expert (AoE), a novel MoE paradigm in which experts autonomously select themselves to process inputs. AoE is based on the insight that an expert is aware of its own capacity to effectively process a token, an awareness reflected in the scale of its internal activations. In AoE, routers are removed; instead, experts pre-compute internal activations for inputs and are ranked based on their activation norms. Only the top-ranking experts proceed with the forward pass, while the others abort. The overhead of pre-computing activations is reduced through a low-rank weight factorization. This self-evaluating-then-partner-comparing approach ensures improved expert selection and effective learning. We pre-train language models having 700M up to 4B parameters, demonstrating that AoE outperforms traditional MoE models with comparable efficiency.

paragraphs: Mixture-of-experts models process each token with only some of their available expert modules. A separate router usually decides which experts should participate. This paper argues that separating selection from execution can produce poor matches between tokens and experts, weakening both immediate processing and the learning of expert capabilities.

Autonomy-of-Expert replaces the router with an expert-driven selection procedure. Each expert first computes internal activations for an input, and the experts are ranked by the norms of those activations. The highest-ranking experts finish their forward passes; the others stop. The underlying idea is that activation scale reflects an expert’s capacity to handle a token, allowing the expert’s own computation to inform selection.

Evaluating every expert even partially introduces overhead, so the method uses low-rank weight factorization to reduce that cost. In language-model pretraining experiments spanning 700 million to 4 billion parameters, the approach outperforms traditional mixture-of-experts models with comparable efficiency. The results support using internal expert responses as a practical basis for allocating computation.
summary.tldr: Autonomy-of-Expert selects experts using their own preliminary activations, improving tested language models while retaining comparable efficiency.

title: Autonomy-of-Experts Models

abstract: Federated recommender system (FedRec) has emerged as a solution to protect user data through collaborative training techniques. A typical FedRec involves transmitting the full model and entire weight updates between edge devices and the server, causing significant burdens to edge devices with limited bandwidth and computational power. The sparsity of embedding updates provides opportunity for payload optimization, while existing sparsity-aware federated protocols generally sacrifice privacy for efficiency. A key challenge in designing a secure sparsity-aware efficient protocol is to protect the rated item indices from the server. In this paper, we propose a lossless secure recommender systems with on sparse embedding updates (SecEmb). SecEmb reduces user payload while ensuring that the server learns no information about both rated item indices and individual updates except the aggregated model. The protocol consists of two correlated modules: (1) a privacy-preserving embedding retrieval module that allows users to download relevant embeddings from the server, and (2) an update aggregation module that securely aggregates updates at the server. Empirical analysis demonstrates that SecEmb reduces both download and upload communication costs by up to 90x and decreases user-side computation time by up to 70x compared with secure FedRec protocols. Additionally, it offers non-negligible utility advantages compared with lossy message compression methods.

In this paper, we propose a lossless secure recommender systems with on sparse embedding updates (SecEmb). SecEmb reduces user payload while ensuring that the server learns no information about both rated item indices and individual updates except the aggregated model. The protocol consists of two correlated modules: (1) a privacy-preserving embedding retrieval module that allows users to download relevant embeddings from the server, and (2) an update aggregation module that securely aggregates updates at the server. Empirical analysis demonstrates that SecEmb reduces both download and upload communication costs by up to 90x and decreases user-side computation time by up to 70x compared with secure FedRec protocols. Additionally, it offers non-negligible utility advantages compared with lossy message compression methods.

paragraphs: Federated recommenders let devices collaborate in training, but transferring full embedding models and updates can overwhelm limited bandwidth and computation. Individual users change only a sparse portion of these embeddings. Exploiting that sparsity can save resources, yet revealing which entries a user accesses can expose the indices of items they rated.

SecEmb combines private embedding retrieval with secure update aggregation. Devices download the embeddings relevant to them, and the server aggregates their updates. The protocol is lossless and is designed so the server learns no information about rated-item indices or individual updates beyond the aggregated model. Protecting both stages is central to making sparse communication compatible with the stated privacy goal.

Empirical results show reductions of up to 90 times in both download and upload communication, and up to 70 times in device-side computation time compared with secure federated recommendation protocols. The authors also report utility advantages over lossy compression methods. These are reported maximum improvements, supporting the potential of secure sparse processing without implying the same savings in every setting.
summary.tldr: SecEmb reduces federated recommendation costs through lossless sparse embedding transfers while protecting rated-item indices and individual updates.

title: SecEmb: Sparsity-Aware Secure Federated Learning of On-Device Recommender System with Large Embedding

abstract: We study the computational complexity of approximating general constrained Markov decision processes. Our primary contribution is the design of a polynomial time $(0,\epsilon)$-additive bicriteria approximation algorithm for finding optimal constrained policies across a broad class of recursively computable constraints, including almost-sure, chance, expectation, and their anytime variants. Matching lower bounds imply our approximation guarantees are optimal so long as $P \neq NP$. The generality of our approach results in answers to several long-standing open complexity questions in the constrained reinforcement learning literature. Specifically, we are the first to prove polynomial-time approximability for the following settings: policies under chance constraints, deterministic policies under multiple expectation constraints, policies under non-homogeneous constraints (i.e., constraints of different types), and policies under constraints for continuous-state processes.

These problems require balancing a policy's objective with restrictions on its behavior, and the computational difficulty can depend strongly on how those restrictions are expressed.

The main result is a polynomial-time algorithm with a (0, ε) additive bicriteria guarantee. Its framework covers a broad family of recursively computable constraints, including almost-sure, chance, expectation, and anytime forms. Using a common formulation allows the authors to address multiple constraint types within one approximation approach.

They cover policies under chance constraints, deterministic policies with multiple expectation constraints, policies facing a mixture of constraint types, and constrained policies in continuous-state processes. Matching lower bounds show that the approximation guarantees are optimal if P differs from NP. The significance is therefore both constructive and limiting: the paper supplies efficient approximation algorithms while establishing why stronger guarantees cannot generally be expected under that complexity assumption.
summary.tldr: A polynomial-time approximation framework covers broad constrained decision problems with guarantees that matching lower bounds show are optimal if P differs from NP.

title: Polynomial-Time Approximability of Constrained Reinforcement Learning

abstract: We study the out-of-sample performance of multi-pass stochastic gradient descent (SGD) in the fundamental stochastic convex optimization (SCO) model. While one-pass SGD is known to achieve an optimal $\Theta(1/\sqrt{n})$ excess population loss given a sample of size $n$, much less is understood about the multi-pass version of the algorithm which is widely used in practice. Somewhat surprisingly, we show that in the general non-smooth case of SCO, just a few epochs of SGD can already hurt its out-of-sample performance significantly and lead to overfitting. In particular, using a step size $\eta = \Theta(1/\sqrt{n})$, which gives the optimal rate after one pass, can lead to population loss as large as $\Omega(1)$ after just one additional pass. More generally, we show that the population loss from the second pass onward is of the order $\Theta(1/(\eta T) + \eta \sqrt{T})$, where $T$ is the total number of steps. These results reveal a certain phase-transition in the out-of-sample behavior of SGD after the first epoch, as well as a sharp separation between the rates of overfitting in the smooth and non-smooth cases of SCO. Additionally, we extend our results to with-replacement SGD, proving that the same asymptotic bounds hold after $O(n \log n)$ steps. Finally, we also prove a lower bound of $\Omega(\eta \sqrt{n})$ on the generalization gap of one-pass SGD in dimension $d = {\widetilde O}(n)$, improving on recent results of Koren et al. (2022) and Schliserman et al. (2024).

paragraphs: This paper analyzes how repeated passes over a dataset affect stochastic gradient descent’s performance on unseen data. In stochastic convex optimization, one pass can achieve optimal excess population loss proportional to one over the square root of the sample size. The authors show that this favorable behavior can deteriorate rapidly in the general nonsmooth setting.

With a step size proportional to one over the square root of n, just a second pass can produce population loss bounded below by a constant. More generally, the stated second-pass-onward loss order combines 1/(ηT) with η√T, where η is the step size and T the total steps. The growing term exposes a tradeoff that additional optimization steps can worsen.

It also extends the asymptotic bounds to sampling with replacement after O(n log n) steps and strengthens a one-pass generalization-gap lower bound. summary.tldr: In general nonsmooth stochastic convex optimization, a step size optimal for one-pass SGD can lead to substantial overfitting after only one additional pass.

title: Rapid Overfitting of Multi-Pass SGD in Stochastic Convex Optimization

abstract: The rise of LLMs has increased concerns over source tracing and copyright protection for AIGC, highlighting the need for advanced detection technologies. Passive detection methods usually face high false positives, while active watermarking techniques using logits or sampling manipulation offer more effective protection. Existing LLM watermarking methods, though effective on unaltered content, suffer significant performance drops when the text is modified and could introduce biases that degrade LLM performance in downstream tasks. These methods fail to achieve an optimal tradeoff between text quality and robustness, particularly due to the lack of end-to-end optimization of the encoder and decoder. In this paper, we introduce a novel end-to-end logits perturbation method for watermarking LLM-generated text. By joint optimization, our approach achieves a better balance between quality and robustness. To address non-differentiable operations in the end-to-end training pipeline, we introduce an online-prompting technique that leverages the on-the-fly LLM as a differentiable surrogate. Our method achieves superior robustness, outperforming distortion-free methods by 37–39% under paraphrasing and 17.2% on average, while maintaining text quality on par with the distortion-free methods in terms of text perplexity and downstream tasks. Our method can be easily generalized to different LLMs. Code is available at https://github.com/KAHIMWONG/E2E_LLM_WM.

Existing methods can lose effectiveness after text is modified, while the changes used to insert a watermark may also harm output quality. This paper addresses the tradeoff between making a watermark survive editing and preserving useful language-model behavior.

The proposed method perturbs logits, the scores a model assigns to possible next tokens. It jointly optimizes the watermark encoder and decoder so that inserting and recognizing the watermark are trained together. Because some operations in this pipeline are not differentiable, an online-prompting technique uses the on-the-fly language model as a differentiable surrogate.

The abstract also states that the approach can be generalized to different language models.
summary.tldr: Jointly training watermark insertion and detection improves robustness to text changes while maintaining comparable measured text quality.

title: An End-to-End Model for Logits-Based Large Language Models Watermarking

abstract: Policy learning under action constraints plays a central role in ensuring safe behaviors in various robot control and resource allocation applications. In this paper, we study a new problem setting termed Action-Constrained Imitation Learning (ACIL), where an action-constrained imitator aims to learn from a demonstrative expert with larger action space. The fundamental challenge of ACIL lies in the unavoidable mismatch of occupancy measure between the expert and the imitator caused by the action constraints. We tackle this mismatch through trajectory alignment and propose DTWIL, which replaces the original expert demonstrations with a surrogate dataset that follows similar state trajectories while adhering to the action constraints. Specifically, we recast trajectory alignment as a planning problem and solve it via Model Predictive Control, which aligns the surrogate trajectories with the expert trajectories based on the Dynamic Time Warping (DTW) distance. Through extensive experiments, we demonstrate that learning from the dataset generated by DTWIL significantly enhances performance across multiple robot control tasks and outperforms various benchmark imitation learning algorithms in terms of sample efficiency.

paragraphs: Imitation learning becomes difficult when the learner cannot perform every action available to the expert. The paper formalizes this situation as Action-Constrained Imitation Learning. Because the learner has a smaller action space, it cannot exactly reproduce the expert’s pattern of visited states and actions. This creates a mismatch that ordinary imitation objectives must contend with.

The proposed method, DTWIL, builds replacement demonstrations that obey the learner’s action constraints while following state trajectories similar to the expert’s. It treats the construction of these trajectories as a planning problem and solves it using Model Predictive Control. Dynamic Time Warping supplies the alignment distance, allowing the comparison to accommodate differences in how trajectories progress over time.

The learner then trains on the feasible replacement dataset. Experiments across several robot control tasks show improved performance and greater sample efficiency than the benchmark imitation methods considered. The central idea is to adapt the demonstrations to the learner’s capabilities, preserving useful trajectory information even when the original expert actions are unavailable.
summary.tldr: DTWIL converts expert demonstrations into similar, feasible trajectories so action-constrained learners can imitate more effectively.

title: Action-Constrained Imitation Learning

abstract: Large language model inference is both memory-intensive and time-consuming, often requiring distributed algorithms to efficiently scale. Various model parallelism strategies are used in multi-gpu training and inference to partition computation across multiple devices, reducing memory load and computation time. However, using model parallelism necessitates communication of information between GPUs, which has been a major bottleneck and limits the gains obtained by scaling up the number of devices. We introduce Ladder Residual, a simple architectural modification applicable to all residual-based models that enables straightforward overlapping that effectively hides the latency of communication. Our insight is that in addition to systems optimization, one can also redesign the model architecture to decouple communication from computation. While Ladder Residual can allow communication-computation decoupling in conventional parallelism patterns, we focus on Tensor Parallelism in this paper, which is particularly bottlenecked by its heavy communication. For a Transformer model with 70B parameters, applying Ladder Residual to all its layers can achieve 29% end-to-end wall clock speed up at inference time with TP sharding over 8 devices. We refer the resulting Transformer model as the Ladder Transformer. We train a 1B and 3B Ladder Transformer from scratch and observe comparable performance to a standard dense transformer baseline. We also show that it is possible to convert parts of the Llama-3.1 8B model to our Ladder Residual architecture with minimal accuracy degradation by only retraining for 3B tokens.

summary.tldr: Ladder Residual changes model architecture to overlap GPU communication with computation, achieving a reported 29% inference speedup in a 70B-model setting.

title: Ladder-Residual: Parallelism-Aware Architecture for Accelerating Large Model Inference with Communication Overlapping

abstract: Handcrafting heuristics for solving complex optimization tasks (e.g., route planning and task allocation) is a common practice but requires extensive domain knowledge. Recently, Large Language Model (LLM)-based automatic heuristic design (AHD) methods have shown promise in generating high-quality heuristics without manual interventions. Existing LLM-based AHD methods employ a population to maintain a fixed number of top-performing LLM-generated heuristics and introduce evolutionary computation (EC) to iteratively enhance the population. However, these population-based procedures cannot fully develop the potential of each heuristic and are prone to converge into local optima. To more comprehensively explore the space of heuristics, this paper proposes to use Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) for LLM-based heuristic evolution. The proposed MCTS-AHD method organizes all LLM-generated heuristics in a tree structure and can better develop the potential of temporarily underperforming heuristics. In experiments, MCTS-AHD delivers significantly higher-quality heuristics on various complex tasks. Our code is available.

paragraphs: Heuristics help solve complex optimization problems, but designing them manually requires considerable domain expertise. Language models offer a way to generate heuristics automatically. The tree-based approach can continue developing such candidates rather than focusing exclusively on current top performers.

The findings support broader exploration of the heuristic space as a useful complement to language-model generation. The contribution is principally a change in how candidate heuristics are organized and explored, allowing the search to better investigate potential that immediate performance alone may not reveal.
summary.tldr: MCTS-AHD uses tree search to develop language-model-generated heuristics, including temporarily weak candidates, and finds better heuristics in the reported experiments.

title: Monte Carlo Tree Search for Comprehensive Exploration in LLM-Based Automatic Heuristic Design

abstract: We are born with the ability to learn concepts by comparing diverse observations. This helps us to understand the new world in a compositional manner and facilitates extrapolation, as objects naturally consist of multiple concepts. In this work, we argue that the cognitive mechanism of comparison, fundamental to human learning, is also vital for machines to recover true concepts underlying the data. This offers correctness guarantees for the field of concept learning, which, despite its impressive empirical successes, still lacks general theoretical support. Specifically, we aim to develop a theoretical framework for the identifiability of concepts with multiple classes of observations. We show that with sufficient diversity across classes, hidden concepts can be identified without assuming specific concept types, functional relations, or parametric generative models. Interestingly, even when conditions are not globally satisfied, we can still provide alternative guarantees for as many concepts as possible based on local comparisons, thereby extending the applicability of our theory to more flexible scenarios. Moreover, the hidden structure between classes and concepts can also be identified nonparametrically. We validate our theoretical results in both synthetic and real-world settings.

paragraphs: Concept learning aims to recover the hidden concepts that explain observations. Strong empirical performance alone does not establish whether those recovered concepts correspond to the underlying ones. This paper develops an identifiability framework based on comparing multiple classes of observations, asking when such comparisons provide enough information to recover latent concepts.

The main result requires sufficient diversity across observation classes. Under that condition, concepts can be identified without specifying their types, the functional relationships involved, or a parametric model for generating the data. The significance is that the guarantee rests on informative variation across classes rather than a narrowly prescribed form for the hidden concepts.

The theory also addresses cases where its conditions do not hold globally. Local comparisons can provide alternative guarantees for as many concepts as possible, extending identification to more flexible settings. The authors additionally show that the hidden relationships between classes and concepts can be identified nonparametrically. Synthetic and real-world evaluations support the theoretical results, connecting the comparison-based framework with observed data.
summary.tldr: Sufficient diversity across observation classes enables nonparametric identification of hidden concepts, with local guarantees when global conditions fail.

title: Nonparametric Identification of Latent Concepts

abstract: Spatial transcriptomics offers spatially resolved gene expression profiling within tissue sections, but its cost and limited throughput hinder large-scale deployment. To extend this capability to routine practice, recent computational methods aim to infer spatial gene expression directly from ubiquitous hematoxylin and eosin-stained histology slides. However, most existing models assume Cartesian or geometry-agnostic locality, despite the hexagonal sampling of widely used spot-array platforms, and point-wise regression objectives often yield over-smoothed gene expression profiles, obscuring gene-specific spatial heterogeneity. To address these, we propose HEXST, a geometry-aligned Transformer for spatial gene expression prediction from histology. HEXST operates directly on hexagonal spot coordinates to enable efficient local-to-global contextual modeling via a tailored shifted-window attention mechanism and hexagonal rotary positional encoding. To enhance gene-wise spatial contrast, HEXST complements point-wise regression with a contrast-sensitive differential objective and transcriptomic priors from a pretrained single-cell foundation model during training. Across seven spatial transcriptomics datasets, HEXST consistently outperforms state-of-the-art models, providing accurate and robust spatial gene expression predictions while preserving gene-wise contrast and spatial heterogeneity.

paragraphs: Spatial transcriptomics measures gene expression at locations within tissue, but cost and throughput limit its use at scale. HEXST aims to predict those spatial expression patterns from routine stained histology images. It addresses two modeling problems: mismatched spatial geometry and predictions that smooth away meaningful differences between locations.

Many spot-array platforms sample tissue on a hexagonal layout. HEXST works directly with those coordinates, using a tailored shifted-window attention mechanism and hexagonal rotary positional encoding to connect local information with broader context. During training, it supplements point-wise regression with an objective sensitive to spatial differences and with transcriptomic priors from a pretrained single-cell foundation model. These additions target gene-specific contrast that ordinary regression can blur.

The predicted profiles are described as accurate and robust while preserving gene-wise contrast and spatial heterogeneity. The contribution combines geometry-aware contextual modeling with training signals that value spatial variation, so performance reflects both prediction accuracy and the preservation of expression patterns across tissue.
summary.tldr: HEXST aligns attention with hexagonal tissue sampling and trains for spatial contrast to improve gene-expression predictions from histology.

title: HEXST: Hexagonal Shifted-Window Transformer for Spatial Transcriptomics Gene Expression Prediction

abstract: Linear bandits have long been a central topic in online learning, with applications ranging from recommendation systems to adaptive clinical trials. Their general learnability has been established when the objective is to minimise the inner product between a cost parameter and the decision variable. While this is highly general, this reliance on an inner product structure belies the name of linear bandits, and fails to account for problems such as Optimal Transport. Using the Kantorovich formulation of Optimal Transport as an example, this article shows that an inner product structure is not necessary to achieve efficient learning in linear bandits. We propose a refinement of the classical OFUL algorithm that operates by embedding the action set into a Hilbertian subspace, where confidence sets can be built via least-squares estimation. Actions are then constrained to this subspace by penalising optimism. The analysis is completed by leveraging convergence results from penalised (entropic) transport to the Kantorovich problem. Up to this approximation term, the resulting algorithm achieves the same trajectorial regret upper bounds as the OFUL algorithm, which we turn into worst-case regret using functional regression techniques. Its regret interpolates between $\tilde{\mathcal O}(\sqrt{T})$ and ${\mathcal O}(T)$, depending on the regularity of the cost function, and recovers the parametric rate $\tilde{\mathcal O}(\sqrt{dT})$ in finite-dimensional settings.

paragraphs: Standard linear-bandit theory assumes that costs arise from an inner product between an unknown parameter and a chosen action. This paper uses the Kantorovich formulation of optimal transport to show that efficient learning can extend beyond that structure. The question is how to learn when the original decision space lacks the usual geometry.

The proposed refinement of OFUL embeds the action set into a Hilbertian subspace, where least-squares estimation can support confidence sets. A penalty on optimism constrains action selection to that subspace. The analysis then uses convergence from penalized entropic transport to the Kantorovich problem, accounting for the approximation introduced by this construction.

Up to that approximation term, the algorithm obtains the same trajectory-dependent regret upper bounds as OFUL. Functional regression techniques turn these into worst-case bounds. Depending on the cost function's regularity, regret ranges from approximately square-root growth in the number of rounds to linear growth. In finite dimensions, the method recovers the usual square-root dependence on dimension times rounds, showing how familiar rates emerge within the broader framework.
summary.tldr: An OFUL extension learns optimal-transport decisions beyond standard inner-product spaces, with regret depending on cost regularity and approximation error.

title: Linear Bandits beyond Inner Product Spaces, the case of Bandit Optimal Transport

abstract: Photoplethysmography (PPG), a non-invasive measure of changes in blood volume, is widely used in both wearable devices and clinical settings. Recent PPG foundation models either use open-source ICU datasets with pretraining paradigms that require curated data and thus complicate generalization to field-like data, or use closed-source field-like PPG data. In contrast, we propose a PPG foundation model that does not require high-quality or field-like pretraining data, and instead leverages accompanying electrocardiogram and respiratory signals in ICU datasets to select contrastive samples during pretraining. Our approach allows the model to retain and learn from noisy PPG segments, improving robustness at inference. Our model, pretrained on 3x fewer subjects than existing state-of-the-art approaches, achieves performance improvements on 14 out of 15 diverse downstream tasks, including field-like daily activity and heart rate prediction. Our results demonstrate that multimodal supervision can integrate complementary physiological information to improve the robustness of PPG foundation models and enhance their generalization to consumer-grade data.

A model trained that way may struggle with the noisier signals encountered during daily activities.

These additional physiological signals help select samples for contrastive learning, which learns representations by comparing examples. The approach retains noisy PPG segments as useful training material instead of requiring high-quality or field-like recordings.

The tasks include daily activity and heart rate prediction under field-like conditions. summary.tldr: Using accompanying heart and respiratory signals during pretraining helps a PPG foundation model learn from noisy data and improve across most evaluated tasks.

title: A robust PPG foundation model using multimodal physiological supervision

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown promise in assisting cybersecurity tasks, yet existing approaches struggle with automatic vulnerability discovery and exploitation due to limited interaction, weak execution grounding, and a lack of experience reuse. We propose Co-RedTeam, a security-aware multi-agent framework designed to mirror real-world red-teaming workflows by integrating security-domain knowledge, code-aware analysis, execution-grounded iterative reasoning, and long-term memory. Co-RedTeam decomposes vulnerability analysis into coordinated discovery and exploitation stages, enabling agents to plan, execute, validate, and refine actions based on real execution feedback while learning from prior trajectories. Extensive evaluations on challenging security benchmarks demonstrate that Co-RedTeam consistently outperforms strong baselines across diverse backbone models, achieving over 60% success rate in vulnerability exploitation and over 10% absolute improvement in vulnerability detection. Ablation and iteration studies further confirm the critical role of execution feedback, structured interaction, and memory for building robust and generalizable cybersecurity agents.

paragraphs: Language-model security agents can struggle when they reason without enough execution feedback or repeatedly discard lessons from previous attempts. Co-RedTeam organizes vulnerability analysis into coordinated stages intended to address those weaknesses. The framework combines security knowledge, code analysis, interaction, and reusable experience.

Separate discovery and exploitation stages allow agents to plan, execute, validate, and refine actions using observed execution results. Long-term memory stores prior trajectories so later work can benefit from earlier experience. The architecture is intended to mirror an iterative red-teaming workflow rather than a single static prediction about whether code is vulnerable.

Across security benchmarks and multiple backbone models, the system reports exploitation success above 60% and more than a ten-percentage-point improvement in detection. Ablations support the importance of execution feedback, structured interaction, and memory. These are benchmark capability results; the abstract does not establish the same success on arbitrary live systems or provide an unrestricted guarantee of security-analysis reliability.
summary.tldr: Co-RedTeam coordinates discovery, validation, and experience reuse to improve benchmark vulnerability detection and exploitation performance.

title: Co-RedTeam: Orchestrated Security Discovery and Exploitation with LLM Agents

abstract: Physics-informed diffusion models typically enforce PDE constraints only on final outputs, leaving intermediate representations unconstrained and prone to shortcut learning under shifted boundary conditions. We introduce REPA-P, a teacher-free, architecture-agnostic framework that aligns intermediate features with physical states using first-principles residuals. REPA-P attaches lightweight $1{\times}1$ projection heads to selected layers, decodes hidden activations into physical quantities, and applies PDE residual losses during training. These heads are discarded at inference, introducing zero overhead. Across four PDE tasks, including Darcy flow, topology optimization, electrostatic potential, and turbulent channel flow, REPA-P accelerates convergence by up to $2{\times}$, reduces physics residuals by up to $66.4%$, and improves out-of-distribution robustness by up to $49.3%$, with consistent gains on both U-Net and Diffusion Transformer backbones. Ablations show that supervising a small set of intermediate layers captures most benefits and complements output-level physics losses. Code is available at https://github.com/Hxxxz0/REPA-P.

paragraphs: REPA-P addresses a weakness in physics-informed diffusion models: applying physical constraints only to final outputs leaves intermediate representations unconstrained. The paper connects this gap to shortcut learning when boundary conditions change. Its approach teaches selected internal layers to represent physical states during training.

Lightweight 1×1 projection heads convert hidden activations into physical quantities. The training objective then applies partial differential equation residual losses to those quantities, measuring their agreement with the governing equations. The method requires no teacher model and can be attached to different architectures. The heads are removed for inference, so this extra supervision adds no inference overhead.

Across Darcy flow, topology optimization, electrostatic potential, and turbulent channel flow, REPA-P reports up to twice-faster convergence, up to 66.4% lower physics residuals, and up to 49.3% better out-of-distribution robustness. Gains appear on both U-Net and Diffusion Transformer backbones. Ablations indicate that supervising only a small selection of intermediate layers captures most benefits and complements physical constraints on final outputs.
summary.tldr: REPA-P supervises diffusion models’ intermediate features with physical equations, improving reported robustness and convergence without adding inference cost.

title: Learning to Think in Physics: Breaking Shortcut Learning in Scientific Diffusion via Representation Alignment

abstract: Despite the success of parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods in reducing parameter-related overhead, fine-tuning large language models (LLMs) is still bottlenecked by significant memory and computational demands. In this paper, we propose TokenDrop, a token-level importance-aware backpropagation skipping method that reduces activation memory and accelerates LLM fine-tuning by skipping backward computations for less informative tokens. TokenDrop evaluates token importance based on the magnitude of residual updates during the forward pass, enabling lightweight, gradient-free importance estimation. Furthermore, we introduce cumulative token selection to preserve gradient continuity across layers and lazy selection scheduling that defers token selection to facilitate globally informed importance scoring under memory constraints. Across a range of experiments, TokenDrop achieves up to 42.9% reduction in memory usage and up to 1.50$\times$ training speedup, while preserving accuracy and outperforming existing backpropagation-skipping baselines. The code is available at https://github.com/kimbss470/tokendrop_official.

paragraphs: Fine-tuning can remain expensive even when only a small subset of model parameters is updated. Storing activations and computing gradients still consumes memory and processing time. TokenDrop addresses those costs by deciding which tokens warrant backward computation, allowing less informative tokens to skip that part of training.

The method estimates importance from the magnitude of residual updates observed during the forward pass. This produces a lightweight score without first calculating gradients. Cumulative token selection is designed to preserve gradient continuity across layers, while a delayed selection schedule allows importance decisions to incorporate broader information under memory constraints. These mechanisms coordinate skipping so that it follows token importance rather than applying an isolated decision at every layer.

Across the reported experiments, TokenDrop reduces memory usage by up to 42.9% and accelerates training by up to 1.50 times while preserving accuracy. It also outperforms existing backward-skipping baselines. These are reported maxima across experiments, not promised savings for every setting. The results show that token-level decisions can address training costs that parameter-efficient methods alone leave substantial.
summary.tldr: TokenDrop reduces fine-tuning costs by using forward-pass importance estimates to skip backward computation for less informative tokens.

title: TokenDrop: Token-Level Importance-Aware Backward Propagation Skipping for Efficient LLM Fine-Tuning

abstract: Offline goal-conditioned RL (GCRL) learns goal-reaching policies from static datasets, but real-world environments are often partially observable, so the collected trajectories are only partly consistent with the Markov assumption while other segments remain history-dependent. History-aware sequence models such as Decision Transformer (DT) are a natural fit for long-term dependency modeling, yet pure attention is inefficient and brittle when handling local Markovian structure and long-range context simultaneously. Although recent hybrid architectures (e.g., LSDT) introduce local extractors, their fixed-window extraction cannot adapt the effective memory to varying dependency lengths, often truncating long-range context instead of compressing it. Moreover, under sparse rewards, return-to-go (RTG) becomes non-discriminative across sub-trajectories, offering little guidance for stitching goal-reaching behaviors from diverse demonstrations. To address these limitations, we propose QHyer (Q-conditioned Hybrid Attention-Mamba Transformer), which replaces RTG with a Normalizing Flows (NFs) parameterized goal-reaching Q-estimator used directly as conditioning tokens, and a gated Hybrid Attention-Mamba backbone whose selective state-space dynamics enable content-adaptive history compression while attention captures global goal-directed dependencies. Extensive experiments on OGBench and D4RL demonstrate that QHyer achieves state-of-the-art performance on both non-Markovian and Markovian datasets, validating its effectiveness for diverse scenarios.

paragraphs: Learning to reach goals from a fixed dataset becomes difficult when observations do not fully reveal the environment’s state. Some trajectory segments can be understood locally, while others require longer histories. QHyer addresses this mixture alongside a second difficulty: sparse rewards can make return-to-go signals too similar across sub-trajectories to guide the combination of demonstrated behaviors.

The method replaces return-to-go conditioning with tokens from a goal-reaching Q-estimator parameterized by normalizing flows. Its sequence backbone combines attention with Mamba through a gated hybrid architecture. Selective state-space dynamics compress history according to its content, while attention captures global dependencies relevant to the goal. This is intended to accommodate varying memory needs without relying on a fixed extraction window.

Experiments on OGBench and D4RL report state-of-the-art performance on both Markovian and non-Markovian datasets. These findings support the combined design across settings with different dependence on history. The approach links more discriminative goal-reaching guidance with adaptive memory compression, addressing both what information should condition an action and how past observations should remain available.
summary.tldr: QHyer combines goal-reaching Q-value conditioning with attention–Mamba history processing to improve offline goal-conditioned reinforcement learning.

title: QHyer: Q-conditioned Hybrid Attention-mamba Transformer for Offline Goal-conditioned RL

abstract: Research idea innovation is a fundamental engine of scientific progress, yet it remains difficult to generate and evaluate in a scalable and controllable way. This challenge lies in its inherently open-ended and multi-objective nature, where ideas should balance novelty, plausibility and feasibility. While recent LLM-based approaches have made progress through carefully designed prompts or agent pipelines, they are constrained by predefined, static ideation workflows. To address this limitation, we propose MindFlow, a framework that explicitly formulates ideation as a graph-structured Flow in Mind, which is composed of modular thinking operators and modeled by a probabilistic mind supernet. Given a research topic, a controller dynamically samples thinking flows to generate candidate ideas. This open-ended problem is optimized using a tournament-based relative ranking, enabling the controller to progressively favor higher-quality thinking flows. We further introduce an evaluation protocol that jointly assesses problem finding and problem solving, going beyond title- or abstract-only judgments. Across diverse topics, MindFlow shows its superiority as an explicit, controllable and optimizable research idea innovator.

paragraphs: Generating research ideas requires balancing novelty, plausibility, and feasibility, which makes both generation and evaluation open-ended. MindFlow addresses the rigidity of language-model systems that use a predetermined ideation workflow. It represents the workflow itself as something that can be sampled, evaluated, and improved for a given research topic.

The framework builds graph-structured thinking flows from modular thinking operators. A probabilistic mind supernet represents possible flows, and a controller samples among them to produce candidate ideas. Tournament-based relative rankings then train the controller to favor flows associated with better ideas. This makes the organization of the thinking process an explicit target of optimization.

The paper also introduces an evaluation protocol covering both problem finding and problem solving, extending assessment beyond judgments based only on titles or abstracts. Across diverse topics, the authors report that MindFlow outperforms the compared approaches. The stated contribution is a controllable framework that adapts its ideation process, linking the choice of thinking operations to comparative feedback about the resulting research ideas.
summary.tldr: MindFlow learns to select graph-structured thinking workflows for research ideation using tournament-based comparisons of candidate ideas.

title: MindFlow: Mind Supernet Powered Thinking Flows for Research Idea Innovation

abstract: We study the problem of learning the optimal policy in a discounted, infinite-horizon reinforcement learning (RL) setting in the presence of adversarially corrupted rewards. To address this problem, we develop a novel robust variant of the Q-learning algorithm and analyze it under the challenging asynchronous sampling model with time-correlated data. Despite corruption, we prove that the finite-time guarantees of our approach match existing bounds, up to an additive term that scales with the fraction of corrupted samples. We also establish an information-theoretic lower bound, revealing that our guarantees are near-optimal. Notably, our algorithm is agnostic to the underlying reward distribution and provides the first finite-time robustness guarantees for asynchronous Q-learning. A key element of our analysis is a refined Azuma-Hoeffding inequality for almost-martingales, which may have broader applicability in the study of RL algorithms.

paragraphs: This paper studies reinforcement learning when an adversary can corrupt some observed rewards. The objective is to learn an optimal policy for an infinite-horizon problem with discounted future rewards. The authors consider asynchronous sampling with time-correlated observations, bringing dependence between samples directly into the robustness analysis.

They develop a robust variant of Q-learning and prove finite-time guarantees that match existing bounds except for an additional term scaling with the fraction of corrupted samples. This separates ordinary learning error from the cost of reward corruption. Its analysis also develops a refined Azuma-Hoeffding inequality for almost-martingales, a mathematical tool for controlling dependent fluctuations. The authors identify possible applications of that inequality to the analysis of other reinforcement learning algorithms.
summary.tldr: Robust asynchronous Q-learning achieves near-optimal finite-time guarantees with an added error term tied to reward corruption.

title: Corruption-Tolerant Asynchronous Q-Learning with Near-Optimal Rates

abstract: Predicting spatial gene expression from routine H&E enables large-scale molecular profiling, yet current models treat this as isolated pointwise tasks, thereby overlooking essential biological structures like gene coordination and spatial distribution. To preserve these relationships, we introduce FLAG, a diffusion-based framework that redefines this task as structured distribution modeling. At the same time, we identify the critical Gene Dimension Curse, where joint modeling gene expression and their spatial interactions fail in high-dimensional spaces, and FLAG solves this challenge by integrating a spatial graph encoder for topological consistency and utilizing Gene Foundation Model (GFM) alignment for gene-gene fidelity in the generation process. To rigorously assess model performance, we propose a set of novel structural evaluation metrics, including Gene Structural Correlation (GSC) and Spatial Structural Correlation (SSC). Our experiments demonstrate that FLAG is highly competitive in traditional accuracy (PCC/MSE) while achieving significantly enhanced structural fidelity in capturing both gene-gene and gene-spatial relationships. The code is available at https://github.com/darkflash03/FLAG.

paragraphs: FLAG predicts spatial gene expression from routine H&E tissue images while explicitly considering relationships among genes and tissue locations. The paper argues that treating each prediction as an isolated value overlooks biological organization. It therefore frames the task as modeling a structured distribution, where the relationships among predicted values matter alongside their individual accuracy.

The authors identify a high-dimensional difficulty they call the Gene Dimension Curse: jointly modeling many genes and their spatial interactions can fail as dimensionality grows. FLAG combines diffusion modeling with a spatial graph encoder to preserve spatial topology. It also aligns generation with a Gene Foundation Model to support faithful relationships between genes.

The paper introduces Gene Structural Correlation and Spatial Structural Correlation to evaluate these aspects directly. Experiments show competitive performance on conventional correlation and squared-error measures, alongside significantly better fidelity to gene–gene and gene–spatial relationships. The contribution is therefore both a modeling approach and an evaluation perspective: predictions should reproduce coordinated biological patterns, as well as estimate individual expression values accurately.
summary.tldr: FLAG combines diffusion, spatial graphs, and gene foundation-model alignment to predict expression while better preserving biological relationships.

title: FLAG: Foundation model representation with Latent diffusion Alignment via Graph for spatial gene expression prediction

abstract: The scalability of world models is currently bottlenecked by the scarcity of action annotations. While self-supervised latent action learning offers a potential solution, existing single-view paradigms—relying on information bottlenecks or Vector Quantization (VQ)—often conflate superficial 2D pixel displacements with the underlying physical-spatial dynamics of an action. Consequently, these methods remain highly susceptible to view-dependent noise, such as camera shake. We introduce MuCoLA (Multi-view Consistent Latent Action learning), a framework that learns robust, view-invariant action representations by enforcing semantic consistency across synchronized video streams. MuCoLA utilizes a Student-Teacher network with DINO-style self-distillation to align action distributions across viewpoints, effectively filtering high-frequency visual noise while preserving motion semantics. Theoretical analysis reveals that our multi-view objective functions as a spectral filter, isolating agent dynamics from environmental nuisances. Empirically, MuCoLA significantly outperforms baselines in action regression, video reconstruction, and downstream visual control tasks. Furthermore, we demonstrate that MuCoLA exhibits favorable scaling properties with respect to model capacity and data volume, paving the way for large-scale action-free world modeling.

paragraphs: World models need representations of actions, but action labels are scarce. Learning hidden action representations from video could help, yet a single camera view can confuse physical motion with superficial pixel changes such as camera shake. MuCoLA uses synchronized views to identify action information that remains consistent across different visual perspectives.

The framework trains a student-teacher network with DINO-style self-distillation, aligning action distributions across viewpoints. Shared motion semantics provide the agreement signal, while viewpoint-dependent disturbances are filtered out. The paper’s theoretical analysis describes the multi-view objective as a spectral filter that separates agent dynamics from environmental nuisances, explaining why consistency across cameras can improve the learned representation.

Experiments show significant improvements over baselines in action regression, video reconstruction, and downstream visual control. The method also exhibits favorable scaling as model capacity and data volume increase. Together, the results support synchronized multi-view video as useful supervision for learning actions without explicit action annotations. The approach’s central resource is agreement across video streams, which supplies information that a single view may not reliably reveal.
summary.tldr: MuCoLA learns action representations from synchronized camera views, reducing viewpoint noise and improving world modeling and control.

title: Multi-view Consistent Latent Action Learning for World Modeling and Control

abstract: Multimodal reasoning for ultra-high-resolution (UHR) remote sensing (RS) is usually bottlenecked by visual evidence acquisition: the model necessities localizing tiny task-relevant regions in massive pixel spaces. While Agentic Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) using zoom-in tools offers a path forward, we find that standard reinforcement learning struggles to navigate these vast visual spaces without structured domain priors. In this paper, we investigate the interplay between post-training paradigms: comparing Cold-start Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT), RLVR, and Agentic RLVR on the UHR RS benchmark. Our controlled studies yield a counter-intuitive finding: high-quality Earth-science text-only QA is a primary driver of UHR visual reasoning gains. Despite lacking images, domain-specific text injects the concepts, mechanistic explanations, and decision rules necessary to guide visual evidence retrieval. Based on this, we propose a staged knowledge injection recipe: (1) cold-starting with scalable, knowledge-graph-verified Earth-science text QA to instill reasoning structures; and (2) "pre-warming” on the same hard UHR image–text examples during SFT to stabilize and amplify subsequent tool-based RL. This approach achieves a 60.04% Pass@1 on XLRS-Bench, significantly outperforming larger general-purpose models (e.g., GPT-5.2, Gemini 3.0 Pro, Intern-S1) and establishing a new state-of-the-art. We provide both the automated data pipeline and the rigorous ablation studies that validate this "Text-Before-Vision” paradigm. Datasets and code will be released.
