paragraphs: Understanding extremely high-resolution remote-sensing images often depends on finding tiny relevant regions within a vast image. Zoom tools can help, but the authors find that reinforcement learning struggles to direct that search without domain knowledge. Their controlled comparisons examine supervised fine-tuning, reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, and tool-using reinforcement learning.

A central finding is that high-quality Earth-science question-answer data containing only text drives substantial visual reasoning gains. Such data provides concepts, causal explanations, and decision rules that help guide evidence retrieval. The proposed recipe first teaches these structures using knowledge-graph-verified text questions. It then exposes the model to the same difficult image-text examples during supervised training before tool-based reinforcement learning.

This staged approach achieves 60.04% Pass@1 on XLRS-Bench, outperforming the larger general-purpose models named in the study and establishing a reported state of the art. Ablation studies support the training sequence. The findings show that, in this setting, teaching what evidence matters can improve the subsequent process of learning where to look.
summary.tldr: Teaching Earth-science reasoning through text before visual and tool-based training improves ultra-high-resolution remote-sensing understanding.

title: Text Before Vision: Staged Knowledge Injection Matters for Agentic RLVR in Ultra-High-Resolution Remote Sensing Understanding

abstract: Discovering atom-level phenomena requires molecular dynamics (MD) simulations with ab initio accuracy. Machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) enable stable, high-accuracy MD simulations, and their models exhibit scaling-law trends similar to large language models. However, the lack of scalable and efficient distributed training systems for conservative MLIPs makes them difficult to scale. This is because conservative MLIPs inherently follow a double-backward execution pattern, which involves computing gradients during the forward pass. This pattern creates a mismatch with existing distributed training systems, especially for pipeline parallelism. Therefore, we present JanusPipe, an efficient 3D-parallel (PP/DP/GP) training system tailored for conservative MLIPs. It integrates SymFold to enable memory-efficient pipeline parallelism for conservative MLIPs, and WaveK to reduce pipeline bubbles by balancing the four-phase compute time. Experimental results on 32 GPUs show that JanusPipe improves throughput by $1.51\times$ and $1.45\times$ on average over 1F1B and Hanayo, respectively.
originalAbstract: Discovering atom-level phenomena requires molecular dynamics (MD) simulations with ab initio accuracy. Machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) enable stable, high-accuracy MD simulations, and their models exhibit scaling-law trends similar to large language models. However, the lack of scalable and efficient distributed training systems for conservative MLIPs makes them difficult to scale. This is because conservative MLIPs inherently follow a double-backward execution pattern, which involves computing gradients during the forward pass. This pattern creates a mismatch with existing distributed training systems, especially for pipeline parallelism. Therefore, we present JanusPipe, an efficient 3D-parallel (PP/DP/GP) training system tailored for conservative MLIPs. It integrates SymFold to enable memory-efficient pipeline parallelism for conservative MLIPs, and WaveK to reduce pipeline bubbles by balancing the four-phase compute time. Experimental results on 32 GPUs show that JanusPipe improves throughput by $1.51\times$ and $1.45\times$ on average over 1F1B and Hanayo, respectively.

Conservative models compute gradients within their forward pass, creating a double-backward execution pattern. Distributed training systems designed around more conventional execution do not naturally accommodate this pattern, particularly when model stages are spread across a pipeline.

JanusPipe is a three-dimensional parallel training system tailored to these conservative models. Its SymFold component enables memory-efficient pipeline parallelism. Its WaveK component balances computation across four phases to reduce pipeline bubbles, the periods when parts of the pipeline are idle. These components address both the memory demands and scheduling imbalance created by the unusual execution pattern.

In experiments using 32 GPUs, JanusPipe delivers average throughput improvements of 1.51 times over 1F1B and 1.45 times over Hanayo. The contribution is a training-system design that matches the computation of conservative interatomic potentials, making the reported scaling benefits a consequence of specialized execution and scheduling.
summary.tldr: JanusPipe adapts distributed training to conservative interatomic potentials’ double-backward computation, improving throughput in 32-GPU experiments.

title: JanusPipe: Efficient Pipeline Parallel Training for Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials

abstract: Constrained clustering incorporates prior knowledge in the form of pairwise constraints to guide data partitioning. While effective, existing Bayesian approaches are often limited in scalability to large datasets and provide weak interpretability due to the lack of explicit feature relevance modeling. We propose BASIL, a scalable Bayesian semi-supervised clustering framework that leverages stochastic variational inference to jointly infer cluster assignments and feature importance weights. This joint formulation enables the identification of discriminative features consistent with the imposed constraints. To robustly handle noisy or inconsistent supervision, BASIL introduces an adaptive constraint-weighting mechanism that down-weights unreliable constraints. Experiments on synthetic and real-world benchmarks show BASIL attains competitive accuracy while reducing training time by over $96%$ on large datasets, learns interpretable cluster-specific feature importance maps, and remains robust to up to $30%$ noisy constraints under sufficient supervision. We further demonstrate applicability to large-scale health data, including medical imaging and electronic health records.

paragraphs: Constrained clustering uses information about pairs of examples to guide how data is grouped. Bayesian versions can struggle with large datasets and may offer little explanation of which features define each group. BASIL addresses these problems by learning cluster assignments and feature importance together, rather than treating feature relevance as a separate concern.

The framework uses stochastic variational inference to make this joint learning scalable. Its feature weights identify dimensions that distinguish clusters in ways consistent with the supplied constraints. Because those constraints can be noisy or contradictory, BASIL also adjusts their influence during training, reducing the weight given to unreliable supervision instead of treating every constraint equally.

Experiments on synthetic and real data report competitive clustering accuracy and more than 96% less training time on large datasets. The learned feature maps provide cluster-specific explanations. Robustness to as much as 30% noisy constraints is reported under sufficient supervision, an important condition on that finding. Applications include large-scale medical imaging and electronic health records.
summary.tldr: BASIL jointly learns clusters, relevant features, and constraint reliability to make Bayesian constrained clustering faster and more interpretable.

title: BASIL: Scalable Bayesian Semi-supervised Clustering with Feature Selection and Adaptive Constraint Weighting

abstract: The quality of both the environment and the reward model fundamentally governs the effectiveness of reinforcement learning. Accordingly, we propose RLAnything, a reinforcement learning framework that dynamically optimizes each component through closed-loop optimization, amplifying learning signals and strengthening the overall system. Specifically, the policy is trained with integrated feedback from step-wise and outcome signals, while the reward model is jointly optimized via consistency feedback, which in turn further improves policy training. Moreover, our theory-motivated automatic environment adaptation improves training for both the reward and policy models by leveraging critic feedback from each, enabling learning from experience. Empirically, each added component consistently improves the overall system, and RLAnything yields substantial gains in practical applications, boosting Qwen3-VL-8B-Thinking by 8.5% on OSWorld and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct by 21.2% and 12.1% on AlfWorld and LiveBench, respectively.

Its framework links policy training, reward-model training, and environment adaptation in a feedback loop intended to strengthen the overall learning process.

The paper reports gains of 8.5% for Qwen3-VL-8B-Thinking on OSWorld and 21.2% and 12.1% for Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct on AlfWorld and LiveBench, respectively. These results support coordinating improvements across the environment, evaluator, and acting model instead of treating the learning signal as fixed throughout training.
summary.tldr: RLAnything jointly adapts the policy, reward model, and environment, producing reported gains across three practical evaluation settings.

title: RLAnything: Forge Environment, Policy, and Reward Model in Completely Dynamic RL System

abstract: Cross-subject emotion recognition aims to improve a model’s generalization to previously unseen subjects. Existing methods are mainly built upon domain generalization or data augmentation, but suffer from two major limitations: 1) heavy dependence on modality-specific feature designs—almost exclusively tailored to EEG signals—resulting in limited generalizability; and 2) the widespread assumption of independently and identically distributed data, which restricts the diversity of generated samples. To address these challenges, we systematically analyze the heterogeneous distribution characteristics of emotion data and propose MixEmo, a framework that integrates heterogeneous distribution augmentation and collaborative learning. Specifically, a well-trained backbone is used to extract representations and partition them into multiple single-distribution subsets as distribution prototypes. These prototypes are randomly combined to synthesize unseen distributions, thereby enhancing distributional diversity. Finally, heterogeneous distribution collaborative learning jointly optimizes the model across subsets. Extensive experiments demonstrate that MixEmo substantially improves generalization performance in cross-subject emotion recognition.

paragraphs: Cross-subject emotion recognition asks a model to work for people it did not encounter during training. The paper identifies two barriers in existing approaches: dependence on features designed largely for EEG signals, and assumptions that samples follow a common independent distribution. These choices can restrict both generalizability and the variety of augmented data.

MixEmo explicitly models heterogeneous distributions in emotion data. A trained backbone first extracts representations, which are divided into subsets corresponding to individual distributions. These subsets serve as distribution prototypes. Randomly combining prototypes then creates synthetic distributions that expand the range of variation available during training.

The framework pairs this augmentation with collaborative learning that jointly optimizes the model across the subsets. Its central idea is to prepare the model for distribution differences between people by exposing it to a broader collection of such differences during learning. Extensive experiments report substantial improvements in cross-subject generalization, supporting the combination of distribution-level augmentation and coordinated training.
summary.tldr: MixEmo improves recognition of unseen subjects’ emotions by synthesizing diverse distributions and learning collaboratively across them.

title: Enhancing Cross-subject Emotion Recognition via Heterogeneous Distribution Augmentation and Collaborative Learning

abstract: Perception for embodied agents is video-based, often multi-view (ego, exo, or both), and inherently continual, with simultaneous task and viewpoint shifts. Yet continual learning (CL) remains dominated by exo-only recognition tasks, obscuring behavior under these real-world coupled shifts. We introduce Continual Ego, Exo, and Ego-Exo Learning (CE$^4$L), a unified multi-view CL benchmark spanning four representative tasks: cross-view referenced skill assessment, temporal action segmentation, cross-view association, and action anticipation & planning. CE$^4$L highlights challenges largely absent in prior CL benchmarks, including cross-view correspondence, view-dependent asynchrony, and heterogeneous semantic objectives. To this end, we propose Video Incremental Subspace-routed Task Adapters (VISTA), a parameter-efficient baseline method that stores task-specific updates in lightweight adapters and performs training-free routing via residual distance to task-specific whitened subspaces estimated from second-order statistics. Extensive experiments demonstrate the significantly varied efficacy of representative CL methods across CE$^4$L settings, while VISTA is consistently competitive and achieves state-of-the-art overall performance.

CE⁴L studies these changes together, covering first-person views, external views, and combinations of both. The motivation is that benchmarks centered on external-view recognition leave important aspects of continual learning for embodied perception insufficiently tested.

The benchmark includes cross-view skill assessment, temporal action segmentation, cross-view association, and action anticipation and planning. Together, these tasks require more than recognizing an activity: models must connect observations across viewpoints, cope with timing differences, and handle different kinds of semantic objectives. This makes the evaluation sensitive to coupled changes in what a model must do and how it observes the scene.

The paper also proposes VISTA, a parameter-efficient baseline that stores task-specific changes in small adapters. It selects adapters without training a router, using distances to task-specific subspaces estimated from second-order statistics. Experiments show that existing continual-learning methods vary substantially across benchmark settings. VISTA remains consistently competitive and achieves the strongest reported overall performance, providing a baseline suited to this broader evaluation.
summary.tldr: CE⁴L benchmarks continual video learning across changing tasks and viewpoints, while VISTA provides a competitive lightweight adapter baseline.

title: CE$^4$L: Continual Ego, Exo, and Ego-Exo Learning

abstract: Graph Federated Learning (GFL) enables distributed graph representation learning while preserving graph data privacy. However, it suffers from heterogeneity in node features and graph structures across clients. To address this challenge, we propose a novel graph Federated learning method via Semantic and Structural Alignment (FedSSA). For node feature heterogeneity, FedSSA infers class-wise node distributions through a variational model, clusters clients according to the inferred distributions, and aligns local distributions with cluster-level representatives. For structural heterogeneity, FedSSA employs spectral Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) and introduces a spectral energy measure to characterize graph topology, enabling structural alignment between local and cluster-level spectral GNNs. Experiments on eleven homophilic and heterophilic graph datasets under non-overlapping and overlapping partitioning settings demonstrate that FedSSA consistently outperforms eleven state-of-the-art methods. Our code is available at https://github.com/blgpb/FedSSA.

paragraphs: Federated graph learning lets clients collaborate on graph representations while preserving the privacy of their graph data. Collaboration becomes harder when clients differ in both node features and connection patterns. FedSSA addresses these two sources of heterogeneity separately, aligning semantic information and structural information within a shared learning framework.

For node features, a variational model estimates class-specific node distributions. Clients are grouped according to these distributions, and each client’s local distributions are aligned with representatives of its cluster. For graph structure, the method uses spectral graph neural networks and a spectral energy measure to characterize topology. This supports alignment between local and cluster-level spectral models.

Experiments evaluate eleven datasets covering homophilic and heterophilic graphs, with both overlapping and non-overlapping client partitions. FedSSA consistently outperforms eleven compared state-of-the-art methods in those evaluations. The findings support organizing knowledge sharing around differences among clients, using distribution-based grouping for node information and a separate structural alignment mechanism for graph topology.
summary.tldr: FedSSA improves federated graph learning by aligning client groups separately on node-feature distributions and graph structure.

title: Heterogeneity-Aware Knowledge Sharing for Graph Federated Learning

abstract: Text-to-Image Person Re-Identification (TI-ReID) retrieves visible pedestrian images using text queries. Yet in low-light or nighttime settings, visible images lack sufficient identity details, while infrared images effectively capture pedestrian contours and textures. To enable all-day surveillance, we propose a dual cross-modal retrieval task called Text-to-Visible-Infrared Re-Identification (TVI-ReID) and construct corresponding tri-modal datasets. Compared to TI-ReID, TVI-ReID faces two key challenges: (1) complex hybrid discrepancies in dual cross-modal retrieval from three modalities, and (2) semantic inconsistency between pretraining and downstream tasks. To address these issues, we propose a Cross-Modal Semantic Decoupling and Transfer (CSDT) framework. CSDT constructs color-related and color-irrelevant feature subspaces via Semantic Decoupling Learning (SDL) to align shared semantics across text and dual image modalities, reducing hybrid discrepancies. Moreover, Semantic Distribution Transfer (SDT) adapts pretrained text-visible alignment to text-infrared matching. Extensive experiments on tri-modal datasets show our approach outperforms existing state-of-the-art TI-ReID methods.

paragraphs: Retrieving pedestrian images from text descriptions becomes harder when visible-light images lose identity details at night. Infrared images can provide useful contours and textures in these conditions. This paper introduces text-to-visible-infrared person re-identification, along with datasets connecting text, visible images, and infrared images for this dual retrieval task.

The proposed Cross-Modal Semantic Decoupling and Transfer framework separates features into color-related and color-irrelevant subspaces. The contribution combines a broader retrieval setting with a method that explicitly addresses both differences among modalities and the gap between pretraining and the downstream matching task.
summary.tldr: CSDT separates color-dependent semantics and transfers pretrained alignment to retrieve both visible and infrared pedestrian images from text.

title: Cross-Modal Semantic Decoupling and Transfer for Text-to-Visible-Infrared Person Re-Identification

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are vulnerable to backdoor attacks, yet we observe that many LLM backdoors do not survive when end users perform supervised fine-tuning (SFT). In this work, we provide a geometric explanation: by probing the backdoor objective under controlled weight perturbations, we find that conventional poisoning often drives the backdoor loss to a narrow and sharp basin; consequently, even modest parameter drift induced by downstream SFT can push the model out of the low-loss and high-ASR region, leading to rapid backdoor forgetting. Motivated by this insight, we propose BAD-BOOM, a resilient backdoor attack via broader smoothness minimization, which explicitly broadens and smooths the backdoor basin. BAD-BOOM extends sharpness-aware minimization with a Fisher-induced ellipsoidal constraint that allocates larger perturbation budgets to backdoor-sensitive parameters, encouraging solutions whose neighborhoods also maintain low backdoor loss. Across two threat settings, three attack scenarios, three open-source LLMs, and three trigger-free downstream SFT tasks, BAD-BOOM consistently preserves high ASR while maintaining competitive utility. The code is available at https://github.com/xingyizhao/BAD-BOOM.

Conventional poisoning often produces a narrow region in parameter space where the backdoor remains effective.

If that region is sharp and narrow, relatively modest changes during downstream training can move the model outside it, causing the backdoor to be forgotten. The proposed attack, BAD-BOOM, instead encourages a broader, smoother region of low backdoor loss. It extends sharpness-aware minimization with a Fisher-based ellipsoidal constraint that gives backdoor-sensitive parameters larger perturbation budgets.

The findings connect backdoor persistence to the geometry surrounding the learned parameters and show why downstream fine-tuning may remove conventional backdoors yet leave deliberately broadened ones effective.
summary.tldr: The paper links backdoor forgetting to narrow loss basins and demonstrates an attack that broadens them to survive downstream fine-tuning.

title: Broadening the Backdoor Basin: Understanding LLM Backdoors Collapse and Making Backdoors Persistent

abstract: The proliferation of large language models (LLMs) and autonomous AI agents has given rise to a rapidly growing methodological paradigm: "in silico" behavioral experiments. Originally conceived as a way to use AI agents as proxies for human participants in studies of cognition, decision-making, and social dynamics, this approach has taken on new significance—as AI agents increasingly negotiate, transact, and make consequential decisions on behalf of people and organizations, understanding their behavior has become a research priority in its own right. While these experiments with AI agents offer unprecedented advantages in terms of scalability, cost efficiency, and experimental control, they also inherit—and in some cases amplify—methodological vulnerabilities that have long plagued human subjects research. To address these issues, this position paper argues that preregistration practices—central to improving the credibility of human subjects experiments—should now be extended to experiments with AI agents. We systematically catalog the researcher degrees of freedom that experiments with AI agents introduce—model selection, prompt wording, settings, and outcome-contingent redesign, for example—and show how the low cost of iteration and lack of reporting norms make these choices both easy to exploit and difficult to detect. We propose a preregistration template tailored to experiments with AI agents and call on conferences, journals, and funding agencies to make preregistration standard practice for this emerging research paradigm.

paragraphs: Experiments with AI agents increasingly investigate both simulated human behavior and the behavior of agents acting on behalf of people or organizations. The paper argues that this growing research area needs preregistration: recording experimental plans before outcomes can influence those plans. Although agent experiments offer low costs, scale, and substantial control, they can inherit or amplify methodological vulnerabilities familiar from human research.

The authors catalog choices researchers can make, including model selection, prompt wording, settings, and redesign in response to observed outcomes. This creates a credibility problem even when the experimental process is technically easy to repeat.

The paper proposes a preregistration template specifically for AI-agent experiments and asks conferences, journals, and funders to establish preregistration as standard practice. Its contribution is a methodological response to the flexibility of agent-based research. Documenting planned choices would make the relationship between the original experimental design and the reported findings easier to assess.
summary.tldr: The paper proposes tailored preregistration for AI-agent experiments to make flexible research choices more transparent and findings more credible.

Discriminative cluster analysis

abstract: We provide a framework to exploit dependencies among arms in multi-armed bandit problems, when the dependencies are in the form of a generative model on clusters of arms. We find an optimal MDP-based policy for the discounted reward case, and also give an approximation of it with formal error guarantee. We discuss lower bounds on regret in the undiscounted reward scenario, and propose a general two-level bandit policy for it. We propose three different instantiations of our general policy and provide theoretical justifications of how the regret of the instantiated policies depend on the characteristics of the clusters. Finally, we empirically demonstrate the efficacy of our policies on large-scale realworld and synthetic data, and show that they significantly outperform classical policies designed for bandits with independent arms.

paragraphs: The paper studies multi-armed bandits whose choices are statistically related. It assumes that these dependencies are described by a generative model over clusters of arms. This structure gives the decision policy information about relationships among choices, creating an opportunity to improve on methods designed for independent arms.

For discounted rewards, the authors identify an optimal policy based on a Markov decision process and provide an approximation with a formal error guarantee. For undiscounted rewards, they discuss lower bounds on regret and propose a general two-level bandit policy. These separate treatments address different ways of evaluating reward over time.

The paper develops three versions of the two-level policy and theoretically explains how their regret depends on cluster characteristics. Experiments on large-scale real-world and synthetic data show significant improvements over classical independent-arm policies. The contribution links the usefulness of dependency information to both policy design and theoretical analysis, with empirical support under the studied clustered-arm settings.
summary.tldr: Policies that exploit modeled dependencies within arm clusters gain theoretical support and outperform independent-arm bandit policies in the reported experiments.

title: Multi-armed bandit problems with dependent arms

abstract: We propose a family of clustering algorithms based on the maximization of dependence between the input variables and their cluster labels, as expressed by the Hilbert-Schmidt Independence Criterion (HSIC). Under this framework, we unify the geometric, spectral, and statistical dependence views of clustering, and subsume many existing algorithms as special cases (e.g. k-means and spectral clustering). Distinctive to our framework is that kernels can also be applied on the labels, which can endow them with particular structures. We also obtain a perturbation bound on the change in k-means clustering.

Under this framework, we unify the geometric, spectral, and statistical dependence views of clustering, and subsume many existing algorithms as special cases (e.g. k-means and spectral clustering). Distinctive to our framework is that kernels can also be applied on the labels, which can endow them with particular structures. We also obtain a perturbation bound on the change in k-means clustering.

paragraphs: Clustering assigns examples to groups without starting from known class labels. This paper proposes choosing those assignments by maximizing statistical dependence between the input variables and the assigned cluster labels. It measures that dependence with the Hilbert-Schmidt Independence Criterion, or HSIC. The central idea is that a useful grouping should have a strong statistical relationship with the data it describes.

This objective brings several perspectives on clustering into one framework. Geometric approaches emphasize the arrangement of points, spectral approaches use matrix-based representations, and dependence-based approaches emphasize statistical relationships. The authors show that their framework includes many existing algorithms, including k-means and spectral clustering, as special cases. This provides a common language for methods that otherwise appear different.

A distinctive feature is that kernels can describe the cluster labels as well as the inputs, allowing particular structures to be imposed on the labels. The paper also derives a perturbation bound for changes in k-means clustering. Together, these contributions connect the design of clustering objectives with an analysis of how clustering can change under perturbations.
summary.tldr: The paper unifies several clustering methods by maximizing statistical dependence between data and cluster labels.

title: A dependence maximization view of clustering

abstract: Supervised learning is difficult with high dimensional input spaces and very small training sets, but accurate classification may be possible if the data lie on a low-dimensional manifold. Gaussian Process Latent Variable Models can discover low dimensional manifolds given only a small number of examples, but learn a latent space without regard for class labels. Existing methods for discriminative manifold learning (e.g., LDA, GDA) do constrain the class distribution in the latent space, but are generally deterministic and may not generalize well with limited training data. We introduce a method for Gaussian Process Classification using latent variable models trained with discriminative priors over the latent space, which can learn a discriminative latent space from a small training set.

Existing methods for discriminative manifold learning (e.g., LDA, GDA) do constrain the class distribution in the latent space, but are generally deterministic and may not generalize well with limited training data. We introduce a method for Gaussian Process Classification using latent variable models trained with discriminative priors over the latent space, which can learn a discriminative latent space from a small training set.

paragraphs: Classification becomes difficult when examples have many input dimensions but only a small training set is available. The paper starts from the possibility that accurate prediction may still be achievable if the data occupy a low-dimensional manifold. A useful representation would capture that smaller underlying space while retaining the information needed to distinguish classes.

Gaussian Process Latent Variable Models can discover low-dimensional manifolds from relatively few examples, but their usual latent representation does not account for class labels. Other discriminative manifold-learning methods constrain how classes are arranged, yet the abstract notes that their generally deterministic formulations may generalize poorly with limited training data. These observations motivate combining latent-space learning with explicit class information.

The proposed method performs Gaussian process classification using latent-variable models trained with discriminative priors over the latent space. Those priors guide the hidden representation toward distinctions relevant to classification. The stated contribution is the ability to learn a discriminative latent space from a small training set, addressing the joint need for dimensionality reduction and label-aware representation learning.
summary.tldr: Discriminative priors guide a Gaussian process latent-variable model toward class-relevant representations from small training sets.

title: Discriminative Gaussian process latent variable model for classification

abstract: In multi-task learning our goal is to design regression or classification models for each of the tasks and appropriately share information between tasks. A Dirichlet process (DP) prior can be used to encourage task clustering. However, the DP prior does not allow local clustering of tasks with respect to a subset of the feature vector without making independence assumptions. Motivated by this problem, we develop a new multitask-learning prior, termed the matrix stickbreaking process (MSBP), which encourages cross-task sharing of data. However, the MSBP allows separate clustering and borrowing of information for the different feature components. This is important when tasks are more closely related for certain features than for others. Bayesian inference proceeds by a Gibbs sampling algorithm and the approach is illustrated using a simulated example and a multi-national application.

paragraphs: Multi-task learning builds models for several tasks while sharing information where appropriate. A difficulty is that tasks may resemble one another for some features but differ for others. This paper addresses that uneven relatedness, which cannot always be captured by assigning each task to a single overall cluster.

The authors explain that a Dirichlet-process prior can encourage task clustering, but cannot provide clustering over feature subsets without independence assumptions. They introduce the matrix stick-breaking process as a new prior that allows separate clustering and information sharing for different feature components. Tasks can consequently borrow information according to which part of their feature representation is being considered.

Bayesian inference is performed using Gibbs sampling. The paper illustrates the approach with a simulated example and a multinational application. Its central contribution is a more flexible structure for deciding how tasks share data: relatedness can vary across feature components. The examples demonstrate this formulation, while the motivation is the specific situation in which a single task-level grouping misses meaningful differences among features.
summary.tldr: The matrix stick-breaking process lets tasks cluster and share information differently across feature components.

title: The matrix stick-breaking process for flexible multi-task learning

abstract: This paper introduces the Banditron, a variant of the Perceptron, for the multiclass bandit setting. The multiclass bandit setting models a wide range of practical supervised learning applications where the learner only receives partial feedback (referred to as "bandit" feedback, in the spirit of multi-armed bandit models) with respect to the true label (e.g. in many web applications users often only provide positive "click" feedback which does not necessarily fully disclose a true label). The Banditron has the ability to learn in a multiclass classification setting with the "bandit" feedback which only reveals whether or not the prediction made by the algorithm was correct or not (but does not necessarily reveal the true label). We provide (relative) mistake bounds which show how the Banditron enjoys favorable performance, and our experiments demonstrate the practicality of the algorithm. Furthermore, this paper pays close attention to the important special case when the data is linearly separable --- a problem which has been exhaustively studied in the full information setting yet is novel in the bandit setting.

paragraphs: In some prediction systems, feedback says only whether the chosen answer was correct. When the answer was wrong, the learner may never discover the true class. This paper studies that multiclass bandit setting and introduces Banditron, a variant of the Perceptron designed to learn from this restricted feedback.

The restriction matters because an incorrect prediction does not provide the full correction available in ordinary supervised learning. The abstract uses web interactions as motivation: a user's click may supply useful positive feedback without fully identifying the correct label. Banditron addresses the resulting learning problem directly, using feedback about its own prediction while operating across multiple possible classes.

The authors establish relative mistake bounds that show favorable performance and provide experiments demonstrating practicality. They also give particular attention to linearly separable data, a familiar case under full feedback whose bandit version presents a distinct problem. The contribution combines an efficient algorithm with theoretical and empirical evidence for learning when the true label is only partially revealed.
summary.tldr: Banditron adapts Perceptron-style multiclass learning to feedback that reveals only whether the learner's prediction was correct.

title: Efficient bandit algorithms for online multiclass prediction

abstract: The nu-support vector classification (nu-SVC) algorithm was shown to work well and provide intuitive interpretations, e.g., the parameter nu roughly specifies the fraction of support vectors. Although nu corresponds to a fraction, it cannot take the entire range between 0 and 1 in its original form. This problem was settled by a non-convex extension of nu-SVC and the extended method was experimentally shown to generalize better than original nu-SVC. However, its good generalization performance and convergence properties of the optimization algorithm have not been studied yet. In this paper, we provide new theoretical insights into these issues and propose a novel nu-SVC algorithm that has guaranteed generalization performance and convergence properties.

paragraphs: The nu-support vector classifier has a parameter with an intuitive interpretation: nu roughly describes the fraction of support vectors. Yet the original formulation does not allow every value between zero and one. That mismatch between interpretation and permitted values motivates the extension considered in this paper.

An earlier non-convex extension resolved the parameter-range issue and had shown better generalization experimentally than the original classifier. However, the reasons for its generalization behavior and the convergence properties of its optimization algorithm had not been established. The paper addresses those theoretical questions, connecting observed performance with the need to understand how the algorithm behaves.

The authors provide new theoretical insights and propose a new nu-SVC algorithm with guarantees for both generalization performance and convergence. The title frames the work through conditional value-at-risk minimization. The stated advance is therefore a theoretically supported algorithm for this classification setting; the abstract does not claim that the new method universally improves accuracy or specify the precise form of its guarantees.
summary.tldr: The paper develops theoretical support for extended nu-SVC and proposes an algorithm with generalization and convergence guarantees.

title: nu-support vector machine as conditional value-at-risk minimization

abstract: In the context of large space MDPs with linear value function approximation, we introduce a new approximate version of Λ-Policy Iteration (Berteskas and Ioffe, 1996), a method that generalizes Value Iteration and Policy Iteration. Our approach, called Least-Squares Λ Policy Iteration, generalizes LSPI (Lagoudakis & Parr, 2003) which makes efficient use of training samples compared to classical temporal-differences methods. The motivation of our work is to exploit the Λ parameter within the least-squares context, and without having to generate new sample sat each iteration or to know a model of the MDP. We provide a performance bound that shows the soundness of the algorithm. We show empirically on a simple chain problem and on the Tetris game that this Λ parameter acts as a bias-variance trade-off that may improve the convergence and the performance of the policy obtained.

paragraphs: This paper addresses control in large Markov decision processes using linear approximations to value functions. It introduces Least-Squares Lambda Policy Iteration, extending least-squares policy iteration through a parameterized approach that generalizes value iteration and policy iteration. The motivation is to bring the flexibility of the lambda parameter into sample-efficient least-squares learning.

The method is designed to work without knowing the process model and without generating a fresh set of samples at every iteration. This makes sample reuse part of the approach, alongside the adjustable policy-iteration procedure. The authors also provide a performance bound supporting the algorithm's theoretical soundness.

Experiments on a simple chain problem and Tetris show that lambda controls a bias-variance trade-off. In practical terms, the parameter changes the balance between systematic approximation error and variability in learning from samples. Adjusting this balance may improve convergence and the performance of the resulting policy. The reported finding is a potential benefit of the parameter, rather than a guarantee that every choice of lambda improves control.
summary.tldr: Least-Squares Lambda Policy Iteration reuses samples while exposing a bias-variance trade-off that may improve convergence and policy performance.

title: Least-Squares Policy Iteration: Bias-Variance Trade-off in Control Problems

abstract: We study the convergence rate of stochastic optimization of exact (NP-hard) objectives, for which only biased estimates of the gradient are available. We motivate this problem in the context of learning the structure and parameters of Ising models. We first provide a convergence-rate analysis of deterministic errors for forward-backward splitting (FBS). We then extend our analysis to biased stochastic errors, by first characterizing a family of samplers and providing a high probability bound that allows understanding not only FBS, but also proximal gradient (PG) methods. We derive some interesting conclusions: FBS requires only a logarithmically increasing number of random samples in order to converge (although at a very low rate); the required number of random samples is the same for the deterministic and the biased stochastic setting for FBS and basic PG; accelerated PG is not guaranteed to converge in the biased stochastic setting.
originalAbstract: We study the convergence rate of stochastic optimization of exact (NP-hard) objectives, for which only biased estimates of the gradient are available. We motivate this problem in the context of learning the structure and parameters of Ising models. We first provide a convergence-rate analysis of deterministic errors for forward-backward splitting (FBS). We then extend our analysis to biased stochastic errors, by first characterizing a family of samplers and providing a high probability bound that allows understanding not only FBS, but also proximal gradient (PG) methods. We derive some interesting conclusions: FBS requires only a logarithmically increasing number of random samples in order to converge (although at a very low rate); the required number of random samples is the same for the deterministic and the biased stochastic setting for FBS and basic PG; accelerated PG is not guaranteed to converge in the biased stochastic setting.

paragraphs: The paper studies optimization when the exact objective is computationally hard and only biased gradient estimates are available. Its motivating application is learning the structure and parameters of Ising models. Bias matters because errors in the estimated direction need not cancel out, so convergence analysis must account for more than random variation.

The authors first analyze deterministic errors in forward-backward splitting, then extend the analysis to biased stochastic errors. They characterize a family of samplers and establish a high-probability bound. This framework supports analysis of both forward-backward splitting and proximal gradient methods, connecting the amount of sampling to the behavior of the optimization algorithm.

Forward-backward splitting can converge with a sample count that grows only logarithmically, although the resulting convergence can be very slow. For this method and basic proximal gradient, the required sample counts match between the deterministic and biased stochastic settings studied. Accelerated proximal gradient has no convergence guarantee in the biased stochastic setting analyzed; this is a lack of assurance, rather than a claim that it always fails.
summary.tldr: An analysis of biased gradient estimates shows how sampling supports convergence and why acceleration lacks a guarantee in the studied stochastic setting.

title: Convergence Rates of Biased Stochastic Optimization for Learning Sparse Ising Models
